There were times when I was playing RE6 where I thought "this is really cool". Unfortunately, most of the time, it's either boring, irritating, or plain bad. To be clear, this is not a Resident Evil game. It has the skin of a Resident Evil game, but it is not a survival horror game. 

The best part of this game is the disjointed story. The game is split across four ~5 hours on average campaigns, and you get the whole picture if you play all four, and you're supposed to play all four. The dialogue is not great, and the story is very predictable, but I found it was really the only decent part of the experience.

Leon's Campaign isn't very good. If he wasn't in resident evil 6, nothing would change. It does atleast try to have a couple chapters of survival horror, but it gets thrown out the window relatively quickly. The game also tries to have you play his campaign first, but you get nearly every plot twist shown in this campaign, so the others won't hit very well.

Chris's campaign is just a straight shooter, without any survival horror. There are some really annoying parts of his campaign, but overall, isn't terrible if you like shooters.

Jake's campaign starts out really rough, but I did end up liking his campaign more towards the end.

The Ada campaign also starts out rough, but ends up being one of the more enjoyable campaigns.

For the bad, this game has a lot of it. One of the most restrictive cameras in any resident evil game, constantly being pulled and yanked, even in the middle of combat. Resource management can also be horribly balanced. At some points, you're showered in ammo for no real reason, and others, when you actually need ammo because the game is no longer a survival horror but you are expected to play it like a shooter, you have no ammo. Some sections of the game are very janky, and can lead to weird deaths. Lots of quick time events, but not as bad as the RE5 ones are. It also takes about ~20 hours to finish all four campaigns, and oh my god it drags so much. Leon's campaign is especially bad, dragging it out so long when there isn't a lot of real substance. If you do end up playing all the campaigns, you'll be running through sections that you've ran through in previous campaigns but switched up, which, when you're on your second campaign, is cool, but after a while gets a bit boring.

This isn't the worst game I've played, but it's certainly below average.

tl;dr - Good zombie shooter, bad RE title.

Pros: Everything RE5 got wrong, RE6 did right. QTE events are less oppressive. Your AI partner didn't get any smarter, so they made them effectively immortal, reducing the number of game overs out of your control. Control scheme, inventory and melee action was a lot more streamlined. The stop-to-shoot meme officially ended. The core mechanics of this game are honestly great.

Cons: Story is awful. The villain is a joke. Unleashed another virus because his waifu rejected him. RE has never taken its narrative super seriously prior to 6 but everything here is a mess. You have three separate campaigns that occasionally intersect but it makes for a messy story that doesn't come together in a very satisfying way unless you read through all of the extra UNLOCKABLE material. If your story only makes sense by reading the extra material, it wasn't a good story.

-The game continues straying from its survival horror roots in exchange for fast-paced action. Personally I don't mind this but many fans disliked it and that criticism is valid. If you started on the more recent titles (or the very old titles), then 6 is going to feel significantly different. 

It is a great co-op experience and a mediocre single-player experience.

[h1]This isn’t Resident Evil[/h1]
This is a hyperactive action fever dream wearing Resident Evil’s corpse like a cheap Halloween costume. It feels like a movie co-directed by Michael Bay and Uwe Boll.

You’ve probably heard that before, but let me clarify just how wildly and insanely bad it actually is.

[h2]The "Logic" of RE6[/h2]
[list]
[*]Every 5 to 10 minutes, something explodes, crashes, or falls down and then explodes.
[*]Leon can pilot commercial jets and helicopters now.
[*]Chris can fly fighter jets like a pro.
[*]Umbrella was supposedly in hiding after Raccoon City, yet they managed to own two aircraft carriers.
[*]You outrun a zombie-piloted Apache on a motorcycle while shooting barrels AND rockets.
[*]You outrun 10 different bosses or tanks (yes, tanks) while running TOWARDS the camera, because whoever made this game clearly loved Crash Bandicoot.
[*]While you run for your life, the camera switches angles so suddenly that you end up running backwards into your death.
[*]The game is super easy on Professional, but don't worry—you will still die A LOT due to QTEs, weird AI, bugs, or being frozen during dumb cutscenes.
[*]Sometimes you will die 20 times in a row simply because you were one second late with a QTE.

[h1]Tries to satisfy every type of player but fails immensely. Still, a very fun action COOP game that is worth your time. But it isn't a Resident Evil game. [/h1]

[b]Ah, RE6, so much potential; wasted for what reason? Trying to please every crowd? This easily proves how almost   all games after 2010s and especially after 2012 just try to be action hollywood games with very "serious" characters and mediocre/forced one liners.[/b]
i have played this game a lot through PS3 and PC, just like with RE5.

This game's story is the most easily forgettable one there is. But the worst part is actually that your favourite characters are ruined. Leon and Ada are limited to forced bad one liners and generic lines(outside of funny COOP lines, i mean story lines). Chris is way too serious and i see why because of his losses. Perhaps he along with Piers are the most normal duo in the game.
Jake and Sherry are a good duo in theory but they just force boring one liners and a implied  "romance" at the end; however as always, RE6 fails to have closure in that.

Gameplay wise: It is very fun action shooter with very questionable enemy designs and irritating gameplay. This is due to how some enemies can easily one shot you especially on QTEs. On higher settings, some mini-boss or bosses are way too tough.
Ranged enemies with firearms are the worst aspects of this game due that their bullets will stun you if you get hit fully from their burst. This shouldn't be in the game but it is one of the many aspects in this game that is there to annoy you fully.

Perhaps the worst aspect of this game that shows the irony of this abomination is the lack of ammo. If you try this on higher difficulty or specifically  No hope as i did when i played it on PC; you will very easily come across a lack of ammo IN A SHOOTER GAME.

COOP aspect
This is the reason i dislike RE6 and much prefer RE5. This game has turned into a generic coop game where your partner is just  there to shoot enemies along with you and revive you incase of being downed. You even get back up on your own if you survive your downed status. This game has literally turned into COD.  
Your gear is also seperated from your partner's; the only thing you can share is health tablets and first aid spray. NOTHING ELSE. 
Your weapon progress is also linear and incase you replay the game, you will already have the later weapons that will ruin the flow of the game. Who designed this really?
Not only that but the invetory is totally ruined. This system was purely designed for consoles.  

To switch weapons you got to mouse scroll several times to get to the weapon you want, so it is a linear selection in a fast paced game. WHO DESIGNED THIS?
And also, since your slots are very limited, you can't pick up herbs and combine them. You got to have the space of that and you have to remove your spare ammo, delete it i mean. 
This game especially on higher difficulty wants you to play it without being damaged at all. And also hoard ammo for specific gun you want to use, preferrably a sniper,grenade launcher  or a shotgun.

RE6 is better played on "No Hope" since the useless "skills"  makes this game literally a cake walk. They thought it would be good idea to introduce  "gold" as skill points so you can do better at X thing. But the only good thing it has is the "defense" skill and infinite ammo. With the defense skill maxed, even on professional, you will only receive 50% less damage from any source.
Makes you wonder WHO THOUGHT this was a good idea? 
The QTEs in this game are 100+ times worse than on RE5, thankfully for both games, in game settings you can make the cutscenes QTEs automatic. Saves you a lot  of trouble because this games loves to ruin the flow of a first timer in this game.

The campaigns are really bad; both from a Resident Evil and a shooter game point of view.
You start with a very slow and forced "Tutorial" which is the prologue that truly shows the  bad design of this game, or rather the mediocre story and story flow. Since the game design is bad but at least it is unique.
Then you have 3 choices.
Start Leon which is mainly vs zombies and other monsters. A very slow start with an awful partner that doesn't make sense. i will have to say this, all of the voice actors did an excellent perfomance; the problem is the director behind the story and their scripts.

Chris' side is mainly all about humanoid enemies with firearms and the occasional monsters. This along with Jake's is the main point of RE6, this is where RE6 shines in its action. As along of course you remove the stupid snipers and enemies that can deal huge damage for unfair reasons.

Jake's is very similar to Chris' but more varied; it does have a forced stealth section which reminds me of 2-3 in RE5. It just breaks the flow of action for no reason.

And once you complete all those; what do you think you might get? You get the most unifnished or rushed campaign ever. And its Ada's.

Not only that, you also get to hear very boring mologues of Ada which doesn't fit her character(like with Leon) unlike RE2 and RE4. This is easily the worst part of the game.

This game tries to be "UNIQUE" by introducing intersection parts where campaigns meet up and you can play with 4 COOP partners. However the huge issue of that is the fact that these parts can only be played if you already have 4 players ready. 
They can't be found publically because people need to be at the same point before the level, with the same DIFFICULTY PARAMETERS and probably same settings regarding Friendly fire and other settings.
Why your most unique aspect of the game is so badly hidden? WHO DESIGNED THIS?
The best parts of this game is ruined by oversights.

i recommend this game for people who like action and COOP action, as along you forget the awful story and its characters(only Sherry and Piers saves this game) and remember that this game isn't really Resident evil. [h1]For context, I wish there was more of an informative/conditional review rating.[/h1]

This game for how much fun I had with it, is an atrocious dumpsterfire of a Resident Evil game and if it wasn't for the fact I played it cooperatively with a friend, I think this would have never been a fully finished completion review due to just how much it breaks away from both the horror parts while giving too little action due to how often it'll just be a QTE or a "Run Away from the Bad Thing!" sequence.

From the start the flash forward prologue is a mess that paints a very obnoxious picture, cinematic forced slow walking with a camera pan that forces you to go at the game's pace not your own, immediately going into the first campaign if you don't know that exiting after the prologue is finished you're given 4 options of story; 
Leon's campaign is arguably the best but the most egregious about locking you into those slow story moments between the hordes of zombies that feel pretty fun to deal with, when the BOW mutations aren't obnoxious as hell in between. 
Chris's campaign is a lot less fun as the majority of it is shooting galleries between you and a new enemy in the series called the J'avo, which [i]functionally[/i] act as the plagas from RE4/RE5 but the starting levels they open fire with guns and the only big difference is later they can start mutating on the fly if you don't instant kill them in some way.
Jake's Campaign is my personal favorite but the most divisive I feel due to having a diet Nemesis clone chasing him and Sherry throughout the entire experience, it also features the J'avo but they tend to have more sharp and blunt weapons than firearms until the near end of his story, couple that with the fact he has his bare fists as a melee weapon and he can be hilariously fun as a meme tenderizing badass.
Ada's Campaign is my least favorite, and weaves in between each campaign to offer some exposition about certain situations being XYZ thing when each character gets there, but offers nothing uniquely interesting in her story outside of some background information about the two major antagonists.

Gameplay and controls is comparably just RE5 but improved on in some ways while bloated/downgraded in others,  like having more 3D movement and ways to dodge through sliding, side rolling, and backdropping to lay on your back to avoid things like overheads, as well as a slight return to inventory management due to one of the downsides listed here. Controls I think are a serious downgrade from RE5 if you play KB/M, controller feels fine and more or less the same but managing your inventory on the former is nightmarishly uncomfortable.
Aforementioned downsides being; There is no trader and upgrading firearms is not a thing, you keep all of your weapons between each playthrough so the only way to replay "Fresh" is to disable cloud saving and debone the save in your files yourself, since there's no trader there is no real value to guns you feel might be filler at best outside of stuns/staggers, there's a skill point system giving you a build customization thing - but it's hilariously limited to just 3 slots per "perk deck" with all of the infinite ammo or specialized skills being 1 slot each as your "reward" for going through all the campaigns.

OST is actually not bad, I would say this is one of the more solid positives of this game, each character actually has a couple unique tracks to experience that aren't shared from campaign to campaign, and every sequence has somewhat noteworthy tracks - aside the weird genre mixes that Jake has for some reason.


All in all, I personally love this game even with all of the glaring faults and how "bad" the action hero era was for Resident Evil, but objectively I think this game isn't something you should get for 20 - a massive discount and a friend who's willing to [strike]suffer[/strike] play through the entire experience with you is what's needed to really make this game pop past just being a dark relic of the Bro-shooter Resident Evil titles.

[h1] This is not Resident Evil — and it’s not a particularly good game either. [/h1]

I marked it as “negative”, but if there were a “mixed” option, that would be more accurate. Don’t get me wrong: it can be fun, and it’s not outright bad. It’s just wildly inconsistent. Let’s start with the positives:

[h3] Pros: [/h3]

1. A lot of content. The campaign runs around 20 hours, which is huge for a RE title. You’ve got solo, co-op, Mercenaries, extra online modes, and collectibles. It’s undeniably a big production.
2. High production values. Solid voice acting and impressive graphics for its time. I also recommend the texture mod by Evgeshajk — not perfect, but a noticeable improvement.
3. Great in co-op. No surprises here: playing with a friend makes the experience much more enjoyable.
4. Responsive controls. Movement and shooting feel smooth and satisfying.

[h3] Cons: [/h3]

1. Lack of cohesion. The campaigns feel uneven, and progression is poorly designed. Your first campaign ends up being the hardest simply because you lack upgrades — which makes little sense.
2. The story is a mess (and forgettable). It tries to be epic and ends up being meaningless. You could skip this game entirely and miss nothing. Special mention to Leon’s campaign, which builds up a “big reveal” for hours… and then delivers nothing.

It defies all logic that this game has an mostly positive rating on Steam. This game is so much crappier compared to other entries in the series it's unreal. None of the characters really have any personality, the story seems completely unnecessary in the overarching story of Resident Evil, and this game can easily be skipped without losing anything for anyone who wants to play through the entire series. 

I've played through Leon and Chris' campaigns entirely and I played about a chapter or so of Ada's (who's chapter by the way adds another person who seems to not be canon to the actual plot of the game - it's insanely jarring), before my friend and I decided it was too insufferable to continue. 

Neo-umbrella as an organization seems so random and just a cheap attempt to get the same feeling as the original umbrella without any work to set it up. I've played hours of this game and still don't really feel as though I understand their motives or backstory, and I certainly don't understand how they were able to establish the same sort of facilities as the original umbrella without being stopped or mentioned at all prior to RE6.

The movement has so many unnecessary mechanics that I don't use 90 percent of the time and they don't really even feel that good or natural to do. The combat is clunky, especially in Chris' campaign when Piers gets his arm electricity weapon, and don't even remind me about how bad and clunky the inventory itself is as well as managing it or the controls for doing anything in it. By the end of Chris' campaign, I had like 5 guns and like 8 types of ammo that were taking up space in my limited inventory, as well as flash grenades which I never find useful so I end up getting stacks of them piled up in my inventory doing nothing. 

The only redeeming qualities that this game has are some of the enemy designs which are generally either not too bad or very inspired, and some of the action can be enjoyable at times. Otherwise this game tends to be a tedious slog that throws a bunch of arbitrary mechanics and objectives that don't coalesce into something that was as fun as the rest of the series. Even Code Veronica, which is a pretty campy and clunky title (still fun though overall imo) felt better than this game in many respects. Get this game for really cheap and to laugh at with your friend, but don't put much stock into it as a very serious entry.

Last thing is that the action-heavy, xbox 360 oriented nature of this game really shines through. Everything is dark and gritty and desaturated and colorless. I would definitely recommend this game but it does have a few caveats to be aware of, but I will cover this in order.
General gameplay: The controls are similar but unlike previous and in some respects future resident evil games, however once you get a feel for it I genuinely think that it's one of the most fun combat systems that has been done outside of the sequels. Herbs are present but they do not heal the same way previous games do instead having a segmented health system which seems arbitrary for the sake of being arbitrary but ultimately it's harmless. Melee combat is damn fun but be wary that outside of one character the melee attacks use a stamina system.
Now onto the campaigns
Leon: If I had to describe this campaign think of every spy movie with a zombie twist. It's probably the one campaign where you do fight the more traditional zombie hordes. 
Story: 4/5       Gameplay: 4/5

Chris: A fun campaign that sadly crashes and burns at the finale. I'm not gonna sugarcoat this one, I experienced the most frustration with this campaign due to the chase sequence and boss battle at the end, as for whatever reason during the chase sequence they decide to flip-flop your controls to tank controls and the controls you've been familiar with the entire game. A damn shame it ended the way it did for it soured any expectation of replayability.
Story: 3/5       Gameplay: 2/5

Jake: This campaign feels like a party bag you get at a birthday party. There are some things that are good, others confusing, but overall a fun time. I am going to say that Jake as a character gets so much unnecessary hate that's generally unwarranted if you view this game as the cheesy B-action movie it was meant to be. So if your into cheesy action flicks with a bit of even cheesier romance tropes sprinkled in, this is for you.
Story: 4/5       Gameplay: 5/5

Ada: At the present time of writing I have yet to experience Ada's campaign, but I will edit this review once the time comes.
Story: ?/5       Gameplay: ?/5

Agent Hunt: A fun little side gamemode in the extra content that allows you to take control of the many infected and/or zombie enemies in other peoples campaigns if allowed. Just don't expect to win everytime, however you will still be rewarded once the mode ends.
Gameplay 3/5

The Mercenaries: I'm 90% sure this was the whole reason this game was even considered because this is honestly one of the most fun mercenaries experiences I've played in a while, especially if you have a friend to bring along. It truly allows you to feel the full experience of the combat system in this game and play to it's full potential
Gameplay 5/5

Singleplayer vs Multiplayer: I'll be honest, RE6 is much more fun when you have a friend to play with. While the AI companion is not useless in singleplayer, the game feels much more like multiplayer was the true intended experence. While it may anger fans of the older RE experience, I'd argue it's best to frame the game much like Left 4 Dead, where the true experience can really only be felt with a friend along for the ride.

Overall review:
Story: 3.5/5       Multiplayer Gameplay: 4/5       Singleplayer Gameplay: 3/5

[h1]Resident Evil 6 is an everything game.[/h1]
I stop trusting steam reviews a some time ago considering games like Crimson Desert, Resident Evil 9 and more are sitting are overwhelmingly positive for some reason(very average games). People's standards have gotten so low at this point that they'll take anything that is a 5/10 or a remake that is a demake in every way possible(Silent hill 2) and call it a "masterpiece".  Don't get me wrong this game it's fun in some ways, but overall it's a very bad experience to play and doesn't do anything groundbreaking for the franchise as a whole.

[h2]The Story[/h2]
The story itself isn't the problem, but the execution and how it's told to the player. By the time you finish Leon's campaign you basically know 85% of the plotline of the game. While you could play all the campaigns anyway you want, most players start from top to bottom. A really easy way you could of fixed this issue is just reorder the campaigns(Jake>Chris>Leon>Ada) considering jake's story has fewer reveals and his campaign can set the tone for the rest of the game. But i'm not writing a fanfiction about this game but a review about how bad the game is so leave it to another person for that.

-Ada having a clone and revealing it to be Carla in the Leon campaign was to sudden. This is why this game has bad execution of story-telling. When Chris reveals to Leon that "Ada" is dead, we don't really care because we already know that it's Carla that died not Ada. We don't have to question any of Ada's motives. The attack on Chris's men? Ada. The missile in Taichi? Also Ada. Were just waiting for the characters to catch up with the story that we are already aware of.
-Leon's obsession with Ada draws some parallels to Simmons and the story should confronted with the fact Ada doesn't need Leon to save her and maybe it would of been time to let her go.
-Chris development takes entirely in his own head. First he is a kind of rude amnesiac, then having recovered his memory in the end of chapter 1, he goes from a guy hell bent on revenge until he's inches away from getting it to being introspective and humble for some reason? The guy should be mad at Leon, nobody cares that you have feelings for her, when Carla infected Chris and piers team with C-virus mutating them into horrific monsters right before their eyes. Yet I'm supposed to believe he has a instant change of heart?
-Jake hating Chris storyline. It makes absolutely no sense, Jake went from not knowing who his father was to finding out that his dad was a terrorist trying to destroy the world and he’s upset that Chris killed him? Like what? When I first played it that literally made me hate the character and hoped they never brought him back. This could of worked but Jake never once showed any hint of wanting to meet his dad. Jake's story sound good on paper, but execution is terrible. Also Chris not even trying to explain WHY he killed him makes no sense.
- Carla and Simmons. I think they should have been a side story rather than the main villains. Simmons obsessing over Ada and damn near causing the apocalypse just felt so weak to me. On top of that, Simmons just had no charisma. Ada's campaign basically just shows what happened behind the scenes of all 3 other campaigns. There are few revelations and most of her story is spent musing about how she has an evil twin and making sure she shows up in time to cameo in other campaigns.

-JAKE'S CHAPTER 2 CAMPAIGN HAS A ♥♥♥♥!ING FORCE STEALTH SECTION IN A ACTION GAME. ARE YOUT KIDDING ME>>>>>>. I think I almost quit the game at this point, who thought that was a good idea?
-There are a lot of moments in the game where you’re supposed to protect your AI or player companion, which sounds good in theory. Because of that, every situation where you’re meant to cover or defend them feels pointless. There’s no real tension or adrenaline since they’re never actually in danger. You can just sit back and relax without worrying about what happens to them. For example, in Ada’s campaign chapter 3, there’s a section where you have to protect Jake and Sherry from chainsaw-wielding enemies and J’avo. Boring, and a dilution of weapon identity/actual choices to make.

Evolution is typically understood as a blind, natural process driven by genetic variation, environmental pressure, and survival. Over billions of years, it has produced everything from single-celled organisms to complex, conscious beings capable of abstract thought. Scientists often argue that evolution has no goal—that it is not working toward any predetermined endpoint. However, if one were to momentarily suspend strict scientific objectivity and examine human progress through a more imaginative lens, an amusing and oddly compelling argument emerges: that the ultimate outcome of evolution is the creation of complex entertainment systems, culminating in one of the most ambitious video games ever produced—Resident Evil 6.

To understand this argument, we must first consider what evolution has actually enabled. Through countless generations, evolution has refined the human brain into an extraordinarily powerful organ. Humans developed not only the ability to survive but also to create, imagine, and innovate. Language, art, and technology are all byproducts of this evolutionary process. While early humans focused on survival tasks such as hunting and shelter-building, modern humans have moved beyond mere survival and now dedicate significant time to entertainment and storytelling. This shift suggests that once basic needs are met, evolution allows for—and perhaps even encourages—the pursuit of increasingly complex forms of stimulation.

Video games represent one of the most sophisticated forms of entertainment ever created. They combine visual art, music, storytelling, mathematics, and interactive design into a single experience. Unlike passive forms of media such as books or films, video games require active participation. This interactivity engages multiple cognitive systems simultaneously, making gaming a uniquely immersive activity. From this perspective, video games can be seen as a natural extension of evolutionary progress: they are tools that challenge and stimulate the highly developed human brain.

Among these creations, Resident Evil 6 stands out as a particularly interesting case study. Released as part of a long-running survival horror franchise, the game attempted to push boundaries by combining multiple gameplay styles, intertwining storylines, and large-scale action sequences. While it received mixed critical reception, its ambition cannot be denied. It features four distinct campaigns, each with its own characters, mechanics, and tone, all interconnected within a single narrative. This level of complexity reflects the incredible capabilities of human creativity and technological advancement.

If we trace the evolutionary chain backward, we see a fascinating progression. Early organisms developed basic sensory systems to detect light and movement. Over time, these systems became more advanced, eventually leading to the human visual and auditory systems. These senses allow players to perceive the detailed environments, sound design, and cinematic elements present in games like Resident Evil 6. Similarly, the evolution of fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination enables players to interact with controllers and execute complex in-game actions. Even the development of social behavior plays a role, as cooperative gameplay and shared experiences are central to modern gaming culture.

From this perspective, it becomes possible to argue—albeit humorously—that evolution has been gradually assembling the necessary components for the creation and enjoyment of such games. The human brain evolved to recognize patterns, solve problems, and respond to challenges. These traits are directly engaged when playing a video game. The emotional responses triggered by narrative elements—fear, excitement, tension—are also products of evolutionary survival mechanisms. In a survival horror game, these instincts are simulated rather than life-threatening, allowing players to experience them in a controlled environment.

Furthermore, the development of modern technology is itself a product of evolutionary intelligence. The ability to design computers, write code, and create digital worlds requires advanced reasoning and collaboration. Thousands of individuals contribute their expertise to produce a single video game. This collective effort highlights another key outcome of evolution: the capacity for large-scale cooperation. Without this, a project as complex as Resident Evil 6 would not be possible.

Critics might argue that calling Resident Evil 6 the “best game ever” is highly subjective. Indeed, opinions on its quality vary widely. Some praise its ambition and variety, while others criticize its departure from traditional survival horror elements. However, the purpose of this argument is not to definitively rank video games but to illustrate how something like Resident Evil 6 could symbolically represent the peak of evolutionary achievement. It embodies the culmination of biological development, cultural evolution, and technological innovation.

Additionally, the game’s themes themselves align intriguingly with the concept of evolution. The Resident Evil series frequently explores genetic mutation, viral outbreaks, and the consequences of manipulating biological systems. In this sense, the game reflects humanity’s fascination with—and fear of—evolutionary processes. It serves as both a product of evolution and a commentary on it, creating a recursive relationship between the creator and the created.

One could even extend this argument further by considering the future of evolution. As technology continues to advance, humans are increasingly integrating with machines through virtual reality, artificial intelligence, and biotechnology. These developments may lead to entirely new forms of entertainment that surpass current video games. However, Resident Evil 6 represents a significant milestone along this path—a moment where multiple strands of progress converged to produce a highly complex and immersive experience.

In conclusion, while evolution does not have a conscious goal, it has undeniably led to the development of beings capable of creating extraordinary works of art and technology. By examining this process through a playful and unconventional lens, one can argue that evolution has been working toward the creation of increasingly sophisticated forms of entertainment. Resident Evil 6, with its ambition, complexity, and integration of multiple disciplines, can be seen as a symbolic culmination of this journey. Though the claim may not hold up under strict scientific scrutiny, it offers an engaging way to appreciate both the power of evolution and the creativity of humanity.

Resident Evil 6 is an ambitious game with a lot going for it on paper. It offers a huge amount of content, multiple intersecting campaigns, and brings back several fan favorite characters. The idea of converging storylines is genuinely interesting, and there are moments where that concept shines. However, despite all of this, the game ultimately feels frustrating to play and lacks the defining spark that made earlier entries so memorable.

One of the biggest issues is the overuse of quick time events (QTEs). While QTEs have existed in the series before, most notably in Resident Evil 4, they were used sparingly and helped enhance tension. In Resident Evil 6, they are constant and intrusive, frequently interrupting gameplay rather than complementing it.

The shift toward action is another major sticking point. Resident Evil has always blended action with horror, but previous entries balanced this with pacing, resource management, and atmosphere. RE6 leans heavily into nonstop explosions and cinematic set pieces, losing much of the survival horror identity in the process. It feels more like a spectacle driven shooter than a tense, strategic experience.

Combat and progression also feel weaker compared to earlier titles. While RE4’s gameplay loop worked because of tight encounter design and impactful weapons, RE6’s gunplay lacks weight, and the skill point system does not feel particularly rewarding. Encounters often come across as chaotic rather than carefully designed, which makes repetition more noticeable and less engaging.

Although the game boasts variety through its multiple campaigns and mechanics, that variety comes at the cost of polish. Instead of excelling in one area, RE6 tries to be a horror game, action shooter, and cinematic experience all at once and ends up spreading itself too thin.

The story does not do much to elevate things either. Leon’s campaign starts off confusing and underwhelming, Chris’s arc retreads familiar ground from previous games, and Jake, while improving later, is initially one of the more grating characters in the series.

Finally, the camera and controls contribute to a broader issue. The game frequently takes control away from the player. Between forced walking sections, cinematic camera shifts, and constant QTE interruptions, it often feels like the game is playing itself rather than letting the player stay fully engaged.

Overall, I'm not criticizing RE6 for being different. I'm genuinely disappointed that it uses successful elements from previous games and pushes them to the point where the formula no longer works.

The negativity around this game is seriously overblown. I expected it to be a total mess, but honestly, it’s not.

I played through it solo, and it’s actually good. There are lots of big, cinematic moments, plus varied campaigns with their own bosses. Whether you’re surviving in a city during an outbreak as Leon or dealing with military-style bioterrorism as Chris, the vibes and perspectives feel completely different.

The story is at least on par with other entries in the series - basically a 90s-style action movie. I’d even say in some ways it’s better and more expanded thanks to the bigger budget. Although the plot is quite simple,  it is more confusing and complex than usual. I consider this a plus, but unfortunately for many fans even this small touch seems caused brain pain.

There are downsides though. The biggest one, in my opinion, is filler corridors and fights. Sometimes you just run forward, fight 2–3 enemies, then keep running. That can get a bit boring. For an example In Sherry's campaign where you need to find 3 memory cards and then go back to the very beginning, this is just stupid and you need to cut that segment out completely.
I’d say these moments make up about 20–30% across all campaigns. If you play in co-op, it’s probably less noticeable.

Another minor issue is some janky mechanics and questionable game design decisions that can get you killed in dumb ways. Like locked door-opening cutscenes or prompts telling you to press a button while enemies are still attacking and the game doesn’t pause. The new Max Payne–style movement is cool, but the hit stagger where you get knocked to the ground feels pretty bad.

Overall, I liked the game and have positive impression. It really feels like a rollercoaster packed with cinematic set pieces. I love the Re series and it was a joy to watch on such a large scale of action.

I also don’t think it’s a downside that the game leans heavily into action. That doesn’t contradict the Resident Evil formula or universe at all. The game doesn’t have to be a classic survival horror. The gameplay in Resident Evil 4 and 5 is more polished, but they lean more toward action than horror, and they’re among the best games in the series.

Going in, my expectations were low because of all the hate I saw, but this game absolutely deserves its place as a mainline entry in the series.

It is hard to decide what to say about this one. Resident Evil 6 is likely the most hated title of the franchise and I see where those opinions come from. In comparison to all the past titles RE6 was packed with lots of action... too much action for the likes of many (me included).

Gameplaywise this game is more focused on fighting hordes of C-Virus infected people instead of focusing on puzzles, horror and a bit of action like in the past. To be honest you could say the same thing about RE5 but that title had a way better story in my opinion and wasnt filled with that much over the top action and lots of quick time events like RE6.

Storywise I must say that this game has its up and downs. You play 4 different campaigns where each of the 4 follows the scenario of different characters, the stories of these 4 groups sometimes link up and you have to play an already once played level from a different perspective. But despite that all the four campaigns vary in their playstyle. Chris Redfields campaign has got its military aspects with missions like evacuating hostages whilest fighting hordes of zombies and a pretty action focused campaign. On the other hands Jakes campaign for example has more stealth elements where you hide from a big enemy or escape from a lab. And then there is Leons campaign which contained more puzzles but also way too much over the top action and a pretty weird final boss which I didnt really enjoyed as it (again) was just way too packed with crazy elements which in comparison to other Resident Evil titles felt out of place.

The good thing about this game is, that you can enjoy it together with a friend in Co-Op Mode which I was a big fan of as I played the entire game so far with a friend. I believe that If I had to play this game in singleplayer I´d most likely wouldnt have finished the first 3 campaigns. But being able to play this title with a friend ensures moments of laughter and a few hours of fun.

In conclusion if you think about playing RE6 with a friend then hell yeah, give it a shot.
But if you think about playing this game in singleplayer I´d go with a big hell nahhh.

I don't even mind its departure from its horror origins, the series embracing action to this extend makes sense, if you follow its trajectory; RE has always leaned into contemporary film tropes and you can track this evolution with the times, it's actually interesting.

The problem is that it's SO BORING. If RE5 suffered from its multiplayer component by not accounting for the lack of a human partner during campaign, RE6 is straight up designed like a multiplayer game. The way the levels are laid out, the constant arena fights until a door or something opens, the buddy system; the whole thing is just multiplayer to its very core. Which is probably fine if you're playing with someone else, but in single player, it is such a droning experience. 

On top of that, the core mechanics still maintain a needless stiffness, instead of fully embracing the new action-oriented design and between this and the inexcusably low FOV, half the time you can't tell what the hell is going on around you. 

I didn't play far enough to really have an opinion on the story, but I did get to see Leon acting like an idiot in the beginning of his story, canonically a decade and a half since his first assignment at the RPD, trying to reason with a zombie, then wanting to save two random people that were getting munched by other zombies, only to turn around and warn his companion she shouldn't hesitate to take these things down. Oh my God. This game might just be some hot ass. What isn't there to complain about? I'll start with the positives. Multiplayer game + bad game = a fun time with a friend. It's always a good time if you're playing with the right person, no matter how bad the game might be. Leon is also still pretty Leon in this game so that's another plus. Characters' finishers are zombies were actually really cool and fun to execute. The general uncoordinated chaos can be fun at times and, oh yeah, you can toss a sentient hand into a microwave and blow it up.

But other than those things, this game is just a hot piece of garbage in so many ways. I'm not even sure where to start, but I begin with the inventory since that's typically the first thing people experience in this game. I'm not really sure what they were thinking with the inventory system in this game but it actually blows huge ♥♥♥♥♥. It's confusing, doesn't really make a whole lot of sense, navigating it is a pain in the ass, crafting sucks, switching weapons sucks, the inventory is just a huge mess compared to literally every other resident evil game.
The second part of this game I couldn't stand was the button layout. Another game where you should probably play on controller because on PC, this is a button mapping hell. So. Many. Actions. There is actually an ungodly amount of abilities and actions you have to map onto your mouse and keyboard, something you will likely end up doing because a lot of the keybinds have to be the most questionable keybinds I have ever seen in video games. In the first mission, I spent maybe about 30 minutes trying to figure out where and how I was going to rebind buttons in order to make the game a smoother experience.
Next, the movement. People love the movement when you really start getting into it, but me personally, I could definitely live without stumbling on every dead body, stopping in my tracks when a graze a wall, and stumbling whenever my partner performed any actions. And sorry player two, if you don't like the placement of the camera angle and want to change it, that ♥♥♥♥ is going to go right back where it was before after opening a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ door with your teammate. I can see the movement being insane and maybe even fun if you really get to know it, but for me without quite playing enough to get familiar with diving, crawling, dodging, jumping, sliding, and everything you can think of, it was overwhelming and annoying.
Next order of business, action. In the positives I mentioned the chaos can be fun at times, but again, that's only really fun if you're playing with a friend so you can laugh at the game together. If you aren't playing with someone, may God have mercy on your soul. The action in this is the videogame equivalent of a terrible fast and furious movie. ♥♥♥♥ just be happening and, oh yeah, if you can't peak 10 seconds into the future, there is an endless slew of unreactable events like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ train plowing through you at full speed that will literally repeatedly instakill you until you memorize when it comes out and where. I mean, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hilarious the first couple of times, but it starts to get old REAL FAST.
Not even sure if this is the final complaint but to keep it short and simple, the story is, uh... something I guess. There were definitely things that were going on and honestly the best part of the story was when Leon and Chris run into each other. But other then that, things were definitely happening, which leads into the next complaint.
Being player two sucks. For some reason, being player two at times really just blows. You have a super awkward camera angle that you can't really get rid of permanently, (for Leon's campaign) your story relevance is questionable, and there are important story moments where you have NOTHING TO DO. Multiple times, player two is locked to essentially standing around and playing cheerleader for player one, watching from a distance and practically doing nothing.

There are A LOT of things I'd say about this game in a negative light but, at the end of the day, I did have fun playing it with my friend, if it wasn't mentally straining at times. Somehow, this game lacks all the personality and janky fun Resident Evil 5 had and swapped it out for bland uncoordinated chaos and extremely questionable decisions with game mechanics. I know I probably sound like a hater after all of that and not recommending this game, but for me personally, I wouldn't really recommend this game to none Resident Evil fans or Resident Evil fans. There are just too many problems that plague this game and I can only imagine what else is in store for the other campaigns, which I do plan to play and then edit my review after in the future. This game had its moments, but not many.

The first campaign with Leon is the weakest out of the four story campaigns. Introducing new gameplay controls and mechanics through the weakest campaign does not set the game on a positive start along with being slow and very cutscene heavy. Once gone through the differnent stories, the plot starts to make better sense and players will discover and appreciate a deep control system that allows for a lot of different character movement abilites like sliding, jumping backwards, rolling, shooting prone and different excellent cqc moves and countering abilites. On PC this is further hampered with a cumbersome default key bindings but once learnt the combat shows its quality. 

This is still a very action oriented, the most action oriented mainline RE game, focusing on trying to constantly deliver hollywood action set pieces with so many qtes that it becomes annoying. Chris's campaign story wise while cliched and predictable is strong due to the character arcs in their journey. Jake and Sherry's campaign was the most fun, interesting and just the right amount of length without feeling like too much padding. Ada's campaign was the shortest but also straight to the story points, retreading and covering all previous campaigns to fill out the missing plot mysteries which was fun with her unique crossbow. The Mercernies mode is also great fun with the expanded combat and movement range.

The graphics, environments and visual design are great and well done and Capcom's impressive
MT Framework engine delivers these great visuals that still look impressive today. The graphics engine restricted to only Capcom titles and aside from lacking benefits in open world titles is probably the best game engine before it's successor the new RE engine. Better than unreal and with scalable visuals and performance all the way to mobile and handhelds. Not just visually but being able to incorporate a very adept, fluid, dynamic freeform standalone movement,physics and combat mechanics.

Aside from the cumbersome default key bindings the pc port also suffers from high mouse sensitivty when aiming which can be adjusted to remedy but not found in the mouse settings but in the camera setting. It also has a narrow default FOV which also can be adjusted to make the experience better. Overall a good fun RE game but also being so action oriented and hollywood like, makes it also the least traditional RE game in the series. At time of release it deserved the critiscms for being so drastically action heavy and being a qte fest but playing this entry now, getting past the weak early content and while still the least RE like game, it is actually a very fun entertaining game with great co-op functionality. 

On its own a great game that manages to deliver four different story campaigns, each telling a different impactful character story with the right chemistry between characters, with differing gameplay, all intertwined into one main story is an impressive feat.

It's been years, and I STILL cite this game as a masterclass in game design.

There's a whole lot you could nitpick about the game, and a lot of that is warranted, sure.
But what is most impressive is that it is functionally one game, and also four games, at the same time.
You get 4 in 1: horror, puzzle, action, and stealth.
It's all the same mechanics in each, they just change the layouts, stats, supplies, theming, and other ancillary bits.
The totality of changes that AREN'T the main mechanics result in wildly different experiences between each scenario, all with the same core mechanics.

As to whether you'll enjoy playing it? Eh. I've enjoyed it with friends.
But, we're all game devs in the industry, so it's really the design of it all that fascinates us most.
Take that for what you will, but damn this game is impressive.

Mixed bag which I'll recommend with the hefty caveat of it being for fans of Action Horror only. What you're actually getting with RE6 is a number of 'Campaigns' that each focus on a different two characters (except, notably, Ada's, which is single-player only) with the ability to co-op. The stories sometimes intersect with each other and are meant to create one big overarching narrative with each Campaign having its own primary antagonist. Gameplay is /very/ action-based, and you'll have a full arsenal of weaponry nearly from the very beginning of each campaign.

That's the problem, though. No one campaign gets enough time to really develop. In the end everything feels weirdly disjointed, and its obvious that developing these campaigns took vital development time away from refining the mechanics. It would honest have been way better to have had one big campaign, and then release one or two more as DLCs down the line. Instead they released a bunch of 'Modes' for a multiplayer no-one ever used.

It might also have done better if it were more transparent about what the game actually is: Action Horror. There isn't a trace of 'Survival' here. Ammo is plentiful, you are required to mow down hordes to progress, and puzzles are highly simplified. In my opinion, ditching the co-op would have been better as well, as RE5 taught us that it /really/ doesn't work well in these kinds of games. At least the AI bots get an infinite-ammo handgun so they don't eat up resources like Shiva does.

I'm glad they seem to have learned their lesson with subsequent games. 7, 8. and Requiem are much improved experiences for those seeking actual Survival Horror, and RE4 Remake is absolutely awesome if you want more Action Horror.

Played on Steam Deck.

Performance & Compatibility:
Runs great on Deck. I was getting around 60 FPS with decent settings, and it can go higher if you push power limits. You can also lock it to 30–40 FPS for better battery life. Controls, UI, and overall compatibility are solid—no real issues here. This is easily one of the smoother Resident Evil titles on the Deck.

The Good:

Huge amount of content (multiple campaigns)
Fun combat if you like action-heavy gameplay
Great in co-op (honestly where it shines most)
Frequently very cheap on sale

The Bad:

Barely feels like a survival horror game
Over-the-top action and messy pacing
Story is all over the place
Too many QTEs and some clunky mechanics
AI partner can be frustrating solo

Why the “Mixed / Mostly Positive” Reviews:
This game is very divided because it’s not what many people expect from Resident Evil. Instead of slow horror, it leans heavily into fast, explosive action. If you go in expecting something like RE4 or the classic games, you’ll probably be disappointed. If you treat it as a co-op action shooter, it’s actually pretty fun.

Verdict:
On Steam Deck, performance is excellent—but the game itself is hit or miss depending on your expectations. Worth picking up on sale, especially if you have someone to play with.

S-tier action game. Should've been advertised as a spinoff action game called "Resident Evil: Apocalypse" and it would've been adored. I was surprised by the amount of combat mechanics. Examples:

1. Three different kinds of stuns that enable you to do different things.
- Headshot stun leads into a powerful melee takedown that usually kills.
- Regular stun that leads into a melee that knocks down enemies.
- Powerful stun that leads into a coup de grâce melee takedown that kills 100% of the time.

2. Multiple ways to perform the previously mentioned stuns.
- Quickshot, slide, sprint melee attack - all cause regular stun. If you perform it to an already stunned enemy, you will cause a powerful stun.
- Regular attacks only cause a regular stun.
- Headshot stuns are self-explanatory.
- Flashbangs, as well as incendiary grenades and cryo rounds can stun enemies, though I can't recall what kind of melee takedown they lead to.

The stuff I mentioned here mostly applies to regular enemies. Some enemies can get strong-stunned by a regular melee attack. Some enemies have weapons and you can kill them by doing any kind of stun and doing a melee takedown, where your character uses the enemy's weapon to kill them. There are also parries. When an enemy is about to hit you, you can perform a counter-attack which either kills them or stuns them. Depends on the enemy.

3. When it comes to dodging, you can:
- Crouch; roll forward, left or right; or jump backwards.
- When you do so, you can hold right-click, which makes your character stay prone and you can shoot from this position.
- While prone, you can roll left and right to dodge more attacks. You can hold forward to slowly crawl, or back to crawl backwards, but you can't shoot while doing that.
- If you hold a direction while prone and stop aiming, your character will have a unique animation for getting up and starting to run in the direction you're holding, giving you another opportunity to dodge.
- When you roll forward, you can dive further forward and quickly turn 180° and shoot from prone.

This is an actually great 3rd person action shooter that would've influenced the genre had it been advertised correctly. For 5€ it is a steal. Just the story mode alone took me easily around 40 hours the first time I played (I beat the game before I bought it) and then you also have Mercenaries that is often considered as one of the best ones in the franchise and after giving it a few hours, I will say it is very fun. Haven't tried the other online modes so not sure if you will get players on those.

Something to not forget, you can play through the whole story with another player at the same time (online or split-screen). The game has 4 stories that all intersect at points, but the last 4th story was originally solo only, so the co-op experience won't be as good for player #2 there, since it got added later after everything was already made for solo only. IF you only want to play solo, then unlike in RE5, you can choose which of the 2 characters to play (except for story #4). I recommend choosing the character who's story it is named after for your first playthrough (Leon for Leon's story, Chris for Chris' story, etc.). Each character has unique melee animations and different loadouts to keep things fresh.

Overall, possibly one of my most favorite action games. Well worth even the non-discounted price.

I'm going to be straightforward and honest with you.
This game sucks. This game is bad. This game is dumb, long, stupid, annoying, and just flat out boring. 
However, this is the best game I have ever played in my entire life, for the SOLE reason on how stupid it is. If you're able to trudge through an atrocious attempt at a Resident Evil game, you will have moments that will make you laugh like there is no tomorrow.
The story is not that good. It feels rushed, or at least, told in a 'not so effective' way. Some, if not most, cutscenes feel useless and like it was designed just to pad out the run time. Which makes no sense, since there are 4 campaigns. Each with five chapters.
The plotlines of each campaign, at most points, are just annoying, like you're doing chores more than playing the game. At most, you're there for the gunplay against the creatures and stuff, not actually learning or playing the story. That's how it was for me after the second campaign I completed.
It feels rushed, and not at the same time, and I dislike that.
But, there will also be moments where you will want to let this game burn in a fire caused by its own horrific actions. It took an extreme amount of effort to continue playing this game, and the only reason was because someone else was there to experience the sanity.
There was a moment in the Ada campaign (which by the way was only meant for singleplayer, but also allowed multiplayer, the second player is never mentioned, they disappear in cutscenes, and CANNOT advance the story, only Ada can) where there was this one animation that would play if you fail any of the 5 QTE's in Chapter 3. I apologize if this review has a lot of repeating words. The game is that bad. There isn't much to say about it. I'm at least surprised that it runs fine. That's honestly the only thing good for it. (Played with mouse & keyboard on PC; no idea what might be different when playing with a controller and/or on console)

Woof...where to start with this one?

First and foremost, this is very much a third-person action shooter rather than a survival horror game.  Sure, you still have limited ammo and resources, but there's essentially no "creeping through dark/creepy spaces hoping nothing horrible attacks you"; instead you're basically just moving between a series of shooting galleries.

Second, RE6 is an absolute masterclass in awful UX design.
• Shared keybindings that make no sense.  "R" is pick up items...and reload...oh, and sometimes it's "interact".  Space is sometimes interact, sometimes "dash" (a.k.a. sprint), and sometimes "reset camera to default position".
• No map; instead you get a "route guide" button that you hold and it puts a giant arrow on screen directing you to your current objective, which simultaneously manages to be annoying, immersion breaking, and not all that useful.
• Multiple keybinds for the same action, but some can't be remapped and are weirdly convoluted.  For example, "roll left" can be done with "Z" (can be remapped), or with "right-mouse button + 'A' + Space" (can't be remapped).
• 2 is one of the default keybindings for crouch.  Yes, you read that right, the number 2 is crouch. (But so is "right mouse button + Space"!)  3 is the default for "roll forward", but "jump back" defaults to "X"
• Using skills is bound to the function keys because the number keys are bound to weird ♥♥♥♥ (as mentioned above), so unless you rebind, you're having to take your fingers entirely off the movement keys in order to use a skill.
• The menu for changing settings is presented within in-game devices, like a cell phone, and the game doesn't pause while you're in the menu.
• You can pause the game with the Pause key, but not during a cutscene, and you can't access any settings or menus when paused.
• In some menus/interfaces, you use WASD to move through the choices, in others, you use the arrow keys, in others you use the mouse wheel
• You can use Caps Lock to switch "hands", which just moves the camera to be off the left or right shoulder of your character, but sometimes the game just switches hands automatically after interacting with something for no apparent reason, so if you have a preferred side, you're constantly having to switch it back.

Finally, the actual gameplay is full of little annoyances.
• You move with an absurd amount of momentum, so unlike a real actual human, you can't just change direction immediately when walking; you have a freaking turn radius like a car.
• There are dead bodies that if you walk over them you will stumble...Every. Single. Time. Apparently, learning to step over things is beyond your characters' mental capacity.
• If you're playing solo, your AI controlled partner will frequently stand in narrow hallways and doorways getting in the way of you moving through them.
• Your AI partner will also shoot and stagger enemies as you're trying to shoot them, messing up your headshots.  This happens A LOT.
• There are frequently regular zombies (i.e., not bosses or "special" enemies) that you shoot once, starting an animation (standing up from a person they were feeding on, for instance) and said zombie is entirely invulnerable until the animation finishes and only then can you continue to damage them.  Of course, not every zombie reaction animation is like this, so you're never quite sure whether you should keep shooting and potentially waste ammo on an enemy you can't hurt, or wait a bit, putting yourself at risk of attack since a number of zombies can lunge and/or sprint.

Also, you'd better love Quicktime Events, because you're going to get more QTEs in just the first 10 minutes of RE6 than there were in the entirety of RE5.

I think ultimately there could be a good game somewhere in here but it is certainly not the product they released. The Chris campaign is far & away the best one, followed by Leon, then Jake, then like 30 places down Ada. Every campaign could use with some time reduction, there are sections in here that just drag on forever, like the subway section at the start of Leon's campaign, or the car chase section in Chris's campaign, or the final bosses in every campaign that come back 8 different times for some reason (did they seriously have to do this for every single final boss???). I think with some tinkering & some dual protag switching, you could take Chris's & Leon's campaign & make a pretty decent campaign. Jake's starts out good but just gets worse as it goes on, & Ada's isn't much to talk about, especially not with the shoehorned coop where in the last mission your partner can't do nearly anything.

The combat is absolutely terrible, I don't know if I've experienced gunplay this bad before. Every gun is floaty, weightless, almost hard to differentiate from one another. The enemies show no impact or reaction to getting shot, it's honestly hard to tell if you're even doing damage half the time. The melees are super wonky, the targeting doesn't always work, I had plenty of times where I'm trying to do a melee to an enemy on the ground & I'm just high-kicking even though I'm making sure the prompt is on screen before doing anything. There's also stamina which just compounds how bad the melee combat feels, because you get a few attacks off & then can't do anything, & there's different stamina amounts for different characters as well which is a weird choice. I think this game would've been at least somewhat more tolerable if it was literally just RE5's combat again, but I guess you had to do this to get to 7 or something, whatever they say. 

The UI takes a bit to get used to, I suppose it's not super terrible, but it's certainly a stylistic choice, that's for sure. It also switches styles between campaigns which can throw you off. The heal system also isn't great, I'm glad they ditched this system for the rest of the mainline titles.

All in all this game is not overhated, if anything it's hated the perfect amount. Even in coop this is an experience that is fun maybe 20% of the time, & in certain campaigns that's being a bit generous. I would take 5 over this any day, coop or not.

If other Resident Evil games are fine vintage wines, then this one is a cask of Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
I'm not an RE purist or anything, but this game is such a mixed bag.
Aside from the great visuals (and incredible performance on Steam Deck), it really doesn't have much going for it.
The game seems to want to indulge old fans with returning characters and nods to moments from past games, while simultaneously abandoning everything that made those games great.
The classic horror elements from RE 0-3 are completely absent here. Make no mistake, this is not a horror game; this is an action game.
The over-the-shoulder camera from RE 4/5 are here, but it just doesn't work like it should. The game is constantly trying to pull your attention in multiple directions at once, and it makes for an often frustrating experience.
The inventory management is worse than ever. I don't expect a full attache case like we had in RE 4 (the game is too fast-paced to make that work), but you're constantly given way more ammo than you could possibly need, and I often found myself just leaving things behind because I had no more room to carry anything.
The story is all over the place, made worse by the fact that you'll need to play through 4 separate campaigns to get the full picture. These campaigns are filled with the most inane dialogue, campy character moments, and baffling design choices I've ever seen in an RE game.
Worst of all, and by a large margin, is that the game seems to have no interest in letting you actually play it. Most of the actual interesting set pieces are just cutscenes with a heap of QTEs. If you absolutely must play this one, you'll want to play co-op, because otherwise you'll just be standing around waiting for your AI teammate to run around in some unseen hallways until they hit some unseen switch. 
If you play solo, be sure to go in with tempered expectations. If you're looking to experience more classic RE goodness, this isn't it. You're going to be getting a generic zombie shooter that wants to be John Woo's Stranglehold, and it unfortunately falls flat on its face time and time again.

RE6 is a hard game to review. I think it's one of those 'Bit Off More Then They Can Chew' situations, as the game is incredibly ambitious. It basically tries to tell one story from the POV of 7 characters. And when it does that right, RE6 can actually be very fun, in co-op or solo. However, those moments are few and far between, unfortunately. Majority of the game, similar to RE5, is just enemy spam. At the end of the 20 hour campaign, you're probably going to end up with around 3000 kills. Enemy spam aside, the game mostly relies on it's characters to do the heavy lifting and keep you hooked. I feel like that works for the most part, not because the writing for the said characters is necessarily amazing, but mostly because of the talent voicing them. I mean, Troy Baker? Laura Bailey? Matt Mercer? It's very hard to make me uninterested in characters voiced by those three. Regardless, point is, RE6 is a mixed bag. At it's worst, RE6 is a slog to get through, and at it's best, it's an engaging story about characters, new and old, that we all like or even love. I personally prefer RE6 over RE5, because at least RE6 tries to do something new, something risky and something grand. I believe RE6 would really benefit from a high budget Remake, as it has many good ideas, but not all of them were executed good here.

I’ve finished Leon’s campaign, and I can confidently say that this game is just as mediocre as Resident Evil 5, although slightly better overall.

There are numerous “eliminate all enemies” sections that quickly become repetitive, especially since they often feature the same two types of enemies. This lack of variety makes the gameplay feel stale much sooner than expected. Another major issue is the absence of a proper map, which can make navigation frustrating. Tho the game is very linear.

The six plus hours I spent playing felt significantly longer due to the pacing. I played the game in co-op with a poor soul (my friend), and I can say that we both enjoyed SOME parts of the experience, which definitely helped make it more tolerable.

The final boss fight feels unnecessarily stretched out, dragging on longer than it should. The quick-time events are a decent addition in theory, but their implementation is inconsistent—they are either heavily overused in certain sections or completely absent in others, with no real balance.

The inventory and healing systems are somewhat confusing and not very user-friendly at first, although they do become manageable over time. The skill system is a nice addition, but being limited to only three active skills is a drawback. Some skills clearly outperform others, making the system feel unbalanced. Additionally, upgrading them is very expensive, which encourages grinding enemies—but this often doesn’t feel worth the effort. It would have been more satisfying if weapon upgrades were included instead.

I would still recommend playing at least one campaign. While the game is an improvement over Resident Evil 5, it’s easy to see why it received so much criticism and is often considered a low point for the franchise. The level of hate it gets may be slightly exaggerated, but it is understandable.

Overall, for my 8th game in the franchise I enjoyed certain parts, but as a whole, the game feels very mediocre.

It may not be a good Resident Evil game, but it's still a decent game. It's honestly really fun, the high-octane gameplay is definitely the main highlight. This game ditches the survival horror aspect and leans hard into almost character action levels of gameplay, so much so you have to respect it. 

There's a wealth of content both in terms of the campaigns and side content. Of the main campaigns I'd say Leon's is the most "grounded", while Chris's is the most interesting. Jake's campaign is also fun on account of his cool & flashy melee. Ada's is probably my least favorite. The game does have meta progression through the skill system, which all provide different bonuses when equipped.

Mercenaries mode in this game is another beast. It's a ton of fun due to the depth and fluidity of the overall combat mechanics, and the really satisfying gunplay. There are 9 characters available to choose from. Most characters can also unlock alternate skins, which often have inventories/weapons unique to them. Do note that certain additional skins require signing up and linking to RE Net in order to earn them.

There's also a sort of "invasion" style gamemode. If set by the host when booting up a chapter, other players can join and play as one of the enemies and attempt to down the host. Pretty interesting concept, but it usually favors the host heavily as the enemies are much more restricted in terms of movement and attacks compared to the main characters.

There are some other PVP modes available, but I never really touched them.

All in all, while I wouldn't go as far as to say the game is super underrated, it's definitely way too overhated. Pick it up on sale and hop on with a friend for some dumb fun.

Quite possibly the worst entry in the main (numbered) RE canon by far, but there's a LOT of game for the pricetag here. I personally spent a good 30+ hours on the main campaign. Given I'm playing this game over 14 years after release at time of review (and not getting the benefit of the many bonus and coop modes) that's good value.

In short: this is over-the-top and silly fun, punctuated by quicktime events and vehicle chases as pure filler. While each chapter tries to weave characters in and out to build a larger story, the plot is sadly both thin and poorly delivered for such a lengthy game. The pacing feels really off, and I feel the devs would of benefitted from cutting or changing certain sections- focusing in on a handful of characters in more detail instead of hopping across the world every 5 mins.

Leon's chapter will appeal to many (city streets overrun with zombies and plenty of action packed setpieces are sure to please), and the character arcs of Jake & Sherry were actually well done, but suffered from the pacing issues mentioned above.

Final verdict: This Resident Evil was a victim of the action-shooter euphoria at the turn of the 2010's, and I'm pleased to see Capcom went back to survival horror after this entry. However, RE6 is worthy of a playthrough and there's lots to do here. Just don't take it too seriously.

I dont understand how so many people HATE this game. I believe it did a lot of the same things RE5 tried to do, but just... better? 

The way people talk about this game I was sure I was going to struggle through one "slog" of a campaign and then give up and never touch the game again, and honestly I almost did, Leons campaign is probably the worst of the 4 available. But by the time I was playing through Chris' campaign I was just having a lot of fun. RE6 leans harder into the action TPS genre than any other RE mainline title has before (or after, as of RE9) but I think it delivers a unique experience to the franchise and at its core the gameplay is very fun!

RE5 felt like it took every possible step backwards from RE4, this game instead takes several steps in a completely different direction, and executes on every thing it tries to do differently FAR better than RE5 did.

A lot of people criticize the story the most, and while it is probably one of, if not THE weakest of all the mainline games, the way its delivered is *very* cool. You basically play 4 different games, set during the same events, and every once in awhile the stories cross paths and help you figure out whats going on (even though there isnt really ever a "big reveal"). When I first heard that concept explained to me before playing I was worried that it was essentially going to rehash a bunch of locations over and over again, but no, 4 different campaigns, with small segments shared between them, but (most of the time) played completely differently.

 -Leons is probably the closest to RE5 (or 4 I guess), and also probably the worst in its execution, its not that bad but the first like 30 minutes is spent slow walking through buildings and I feel that completely kills any potential replay value. Helena is also a glup-♥♥♥♥♥♥ tier character, just a big nothingburger.

 -Chris' is very action-oriented, with barely any survival-horror elements left in it, but I felt overall it was more cohesive with what the game was going for tonally. I feel like many would argue that Piers could be seen on the same tier as Helena, but I think he served a bigger purpose in developing Chris as a character than Helena did for Leon.

 -Jakes is probably my favorite campaign, as I felt it struck the perfect middle ground between Leons and Chris' in execution, and I really liked the character dynamic between Jake and Sherry. It also felt very much like an homage to RE3 in how its main villain is basically a Nemesis sent after Jake.

 -Ada's was kind of whatever, but it was short and I liked the whole thing more than Leon's because it was set up more like Chris and Jake's campaigns.

I also think the environment and overall concept of this game is way more interesting than RE5, which I felt was an absolute slog because everything was a different shade of grey or brown and most if it was run down villages or temples (Wesker was cool but totally underutilized). This game instead tackles the idea of how chaotic a bioterrorist attack on a major city would be in a Post-Raccoon City RE universe, where most of our cast has undergone the training to be the "action heros" they are portrayed as.

I really like this game, and while I would only recommend it to someone planning on marathoning the entire RE franchise, I struggle to recommend RE5 to anyone ever, that game ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ blows!

Even though RE5 is a lot older, it felt like the mechanics were way better on KnM, in comparison to RE6. The QTEs were just horrendous. There were so many sections were they added a QTE mechanic for absolutely no reason, which just destroyed your gaming experience. Why am I running from a crashing helicopter like in a sloppy hollywood action movie? The fact that you need to use the poorly designed dash-mechanic for that, while basically just running in a straight line, is very questionable. Don't get me started on the camera movement while you dash.....Also... the dodge-mechanic, crawl-mechanic, roll-mechanic etc, etc.......Burn it....

Item management was a catastrophy. The game wouldn't pause when you try to mix herbs, which you couldn't just click on and mix them, but you had to press 20 different buttons just to do that, same with discarding an item. Speaking of pause, the ESC-button was you opening some kind of menu on that weird phone, but the game would not pause, as it was binded to a whole nother key called pause for some reason. It made no sense for "Pause game" to be on any other keybind than ESC.

The story was a mess, girl... There would be some cutscenes, here and there, for you to then be thrown into a room with a million enemies spawning, on normal mode, by the way, and for them to then continue with a cutscene. It felt like you couldn't care less about the story at that point, because of the way the executed this, and I'm saying this as a person who is very lore-and story focused whenever I play. 

Jake and Sherry's storyline seemed like it would be super interesting, which it was to an extent, however, their campaign, like all the others' were a mess when it came to the story. It felt like there was no red thread floating through the story which otherwise wouldv'e made you feel hooked to it. Loved Sherry's and Jake's chemistry. It's sad that they haven't decided to explore and use Jake's character further, in other installments, as, after all, his bloodline has had a huge impact on the story.

Of course Leon and Helena's campaign seemed interesting to a start, but they also just spawned enemies until kingdom come, without any purpose, whatsover. It was like playing mercenaries but with a little story slop thrown in, here and there. It was a little tolerable (barely) because who doesn't like watching and playing as Leon S.(exy) Kennedy. God, his look in this game was so gorgeous, with his little facial hair, hunter-eyes and that side-bang of his.

I really liked Piers' character. The subordinate and captain relationship between him and Chris, as well as their chemistry as brethren, was kind of cute. But as always with RE6, it felt like you almost couldn't care less because of how the story was exectued. 

The worst campaign has got to be Ada. They did her so wrong. It was so boring, and the whole storyline with her and that clone felt like it was pulled from their asses. I couldn't wait to be over and done with her campaign as soon as I started the first chapter. Just spawning masses of enemies, cutscene slop, masses of enemies.... repeat...It was yawn-worthy.

All in all, they tried to do way too much with this game.
