The moment Resident Evil looked at horror, shrugged, and said “what if explosions”
I did not like Resident Evil 6. Not in a “this isn’t for me” way. More in a “how did we get here” kind of way. This game feels less like survival horror and more like four different action movies arguing inside the same Blu ray disc.
Earlier Resident Evil games were about tension. Limited ammo. Creeping dread. Carefully opening doors while mentally preparing for disaster. Resident Evil 6 replaces all of that with unlimited sprinting, roundhouse kicks, sliding tackles, and explosions that happen so often you stop questioning them entirely.
Instead of feeling hunted, you feel like you accidentally joined a Michael Bay internship. Zombies are no longer scary. They are obstacles between set pieces. Horror takes a backseat while action drives the bus directly through a wall.
The game proudly offers multiple campaigns featuring different characters, which sounds cool until you realize they are all happening at the same time, intersecting randomly, and somehow still not explaining anything.
You play as Leon S. Kennedy (with Helena Harper), Chris Redfield (with Piers Nivans), Jake Muller (with Sherry Birkin), and Ada Wong each in their own campaign that overlaps events but never actually helps you understand what is going on. Characters appear, disappear, fight you, help you, and vanish again with no context. It feels like watching a TV show by shuffling all the episodes.
The plot is an absolute mess. There are bio weapons, global outbreaks, secret organizations, personal vendettas, clones, family drama, and at least one moment where you stop and ask, “Wait, why am I here?” The game does not answer. It just starts another explosion.
Levels constantly shift tone. One minute you are fighting zombies. Next it is gun wielding enemies. Then it is a vehicle section. Then a boss fight. Then a cutscene that pretends you know what just happened. The pacing never settles, which makes it hard to care.
The mixed campaigns are supposed to create a big interconnected story, but instead they fragment it. Playing one campaign alone feels incomplete. Playing all of them feels exhausting. Either way, the story never fully clicks.

Final Verdict 🧟
Resident Evil 6 is a loud, chaotic action game wearing a Resident Evil name tag. It abandons the horror roots, replaces tension with spectacle, and delivers a plot so confusing that finishing it feels more like endurance training than enjoyment.

Playing Resident Evil 6 on Steam/PC was my second playthrough of all of the four campaigns, and I actually touched Mercenaries this time. I will admit that I strongly disliked RE6 the first time I played it, but I decided to grab it on sale on Steam not only to build the franchise in my PC library, but because I genuinely wanted to give 5 and 6 another go with keyboard and mouse, which I preferred over my initial experiences on a controller. So, I ended up liking RE5 a bit more than I originally did after I played through it again on PC, but RE6?

Sorry, this is still the worst mainline entry in the series, and I ended up hating it more this time around. RE6 throughout its four campaigns tries to capture different tones and emphasize different gameplay elements as the four campaigns try embracing elements of the franchise that were present at that point. What the end result is is a complete mess in narrative, gameplay, and design choices. To give RE6 some credit, the melee system is fun to use when you actually have stamina and set it all up. I ended up taking most enemies out by shooting them in the head or right arm to stun, then delivering the melee follow-up to finish them off. The gunplay itself also isn't too terrible, but that's all I can really praise regarding the gameplay. 

All of these campaigns are just a slog to get through and are way too linear. I mean, RE4 and RE5 were pretty linear, too, but those campaigns and those chapters didn't feel egregiously long or tedious and had much better pacing. RE6 is just "walk to the literal marker on your screen" and do whatever it is you need to do, which could be killing enemies until something happens, finding certain items, triggering some stupid scripted event or chase sequence... you get the picture. It's extremely boring to navigate these environments when you're mostly following a straight path and there isn't a lot to explore around you. 

And oh boy, does RE6 love its scripted events, QTEs, and chase sequences. I generally didn't have too much of a problem on a controller doing the chase sequences, but this was hell on mouse and keyboard. The forced camera angles and the way the controls work during these sequences SUCK. I died many times in some of these sequences because these really just don't work well on keyboard. When trying to run forward while holding space (the button to run), there were numerous instances where it would instead drop me off the side I just climbed up, resulting in me losing time and dying in numerous cases -- because the controls don't work with the fixed camera angles very well. It was very frustrating when literally holding forward and space just to see my character go the entire opposite direction. 

The last thing I'll comment on is the story and the overall narrative. It's dumb. Very dumb. I love cheese and camp in my Resident Evil, but I can sum the overall events of the four campaigns as "dude simps so much for Ada Wong that he ruins a woman's life and she ultimately tries to destroy the world with the C-Virus." Obviously, the campaigns add more depth and detail, and I do have to say that I appreciated the depth of Chris' character in this game; however, the overall storyline is just really stupid and laughable when you think that all of this happened because a powerful elite simped for Ada Wong so hard.

Firstly just want to say its not as bad as I've heard people say.

(non-spoilered, but still very biased)

That being said, its not phenomenal, BUT the plot is really good imo. I'm a sucker for plots that show it from different character POVs, and this does exactly that. I love that it did, and that each campaign felt like it was a true piece of the puzzle, rather than a means to an end. Seeing all these characters interact was a treat, even if it was just for small moments most times. Plus, seeing the same parts from different POVs lends to a really good depth to the story in my eyes.

As for the campaigns, Leons was for sure the most Resident Evil™ feeling campaign, from zombies to inexplicable labs in random places, to insane ruins that have no business being where they are. It was great as the first campaign, but it does also lend to sort of lessening the others for me as they don't hit as much as that one does for the traditional RE feel. That being said, Ada's was probably my favorite overall, as it was a perfect capstone to the story if played fourth, but I think Jakes was the most "fun". Chris's campaign... we don't talk about his campaign.

For the gameplay, as is the same with my feelings with 5, I'm not a fan of the inventory system, but my biggest irk is how often the game chooses to do a 5 second cutscene for something the player could have done, or a 5 second playable area only to go right back into a cutscene. That, and how often there are doors that require you AND your companion to open them. It feels in some campaigns (esp chris's I feel) that you cant go more than five feet before you get hit by a door asking you to wait for your companion. It really does lower the flow of the game in my eyes, but it could be worse. 

That being said, its not a bad game in any way, and is the natural successor to 5 in my eyes, as it seemed they were already veering down this path from that game. Its very action-y, but still manages to still have the underlying Resident Evil soul underneath it all somehow. I see why they pivoted to 7 how they did, but I still think this game truly isn't bad, just not as good as others. Still, play it and see for yourself!

The infamous [b][i]Resident Evil 6[/i][/b] - very cinematic and action-focused, with documents only available as unlockable extras.
[i]Is it one of the best entries in the series?[/i] - No.
[i]Is it still overall fun and worth experiencing at least once?[/i] - Yes.
(Plus, it's probably fun playing in co-op, if you have a friend to play with. I only played solo.)

[b]What I enjoyed:[/b]
[list]
    [*] [u]Structure:[/u] Having the story told through multiple campaigns from different perspectives/with different protagonists - occasionally overlapping -, shedding more and more light onto what's going on as you progress, is quite interesting IMO.
    [*] [u]Setting/environments[/u]
    [*] [u]Melee combat:[/u] Overall fun and gives you more agency.
    [*] [u]Companion:[/u] Unlike in some other RE games, the AI of your companion isn't so bad (when playing offline/single player mode). They pretty much allways help you out if needed (unless physically unable) and you rarely need to worry about them dying. They do their job just fine.
[/list]

[b]What I didn't enjoy:[/b]
[list]
    [*] [u]QTEs:[/u] All campaigns, but especially Leon's has a great amount of QTEs. The intention is probably to make the gameplay more intense, keep you on the edge, but for me it was more frustrating when a sudden prompt shows up and you die because you missed the timing or pressed the wrong button.
    [*] [u]Controls/user interface:[/u] Honestly, not a fan of the new UI (that isn't even explained and looks differently in each campaign), R for pickup and combining, F for first aid spray and grenades, G for weapons, how you have to put herbs into containers etc.
    [*] [u]Vehicle segments:[/u] What could be fun action sequences, trying to escape or chasing after a car, often turned into frustration. Maybe it's a skill issue, but IMO it's too easy to hit an obstacle or lose the target if you don't know the strat/course. The somewhat janky controls don't help either.
    [*] [u][spoiler](Nearly) unkillable[/spoiler] enemies:[/u] Every campaign has them, and at some point they just become a real pain in the butt...
[/list]

I decided to pick this version up on sale, and my god... even after all these years and coming back to this game, it is still by far one of the worst entries in the franchise.

And it's a real shame too because there are ideas here that could have been good:

- manually executed melee attacks
- sliding, ducking, diving, rolling
- skillsets 

Good stuff, but painfully misused. 

[h2]Melee System[/h2]
The melee attacks were the bread and butter of Resident Evil 5. You wanted to dispatch nearly all enemies in that game using a melee. It was THE thing about the game.
So, in RE6, they decided to foolishly gimp you by giving you a stamina meter...
Why???? Why give me the power to execute melees all I want, but then limit my ability to do so? I want to be kicking the crap out the zombies all day, but uh oh! Leon's exhausted... got to rest a bit. Dumb. I get they don't want the player to feel overpowered, but when I can't use a basic melee attack for fear of draining stamina, it just disrupts the flow.

[h2]QTE Abundance[/h2]
The focus on QTEs went absolutely bananas here. The four campaigns are filled with them, but the cardinal sin is making them part of the combat: counter attacks. 
When a zombie is about to attack you, you have a very short window of time to press a QTE that issues a counter melee attack. Sounds cool, and when you pull it off, it does look cool. 
The problem is that the window, much like a lot of games that try to do these mechanics, is extremely inconsistent. You have to be a certain distance from the enemy. You can't press it too early. If you do, you just do a melee attack make yourself open to attack. It's just messy. 
RE5's combat, while it does have some clunky tank-controlness to it, works way smoother than this inconsistent mess. When a QTE prompt pops up in that game, you are guaranteed to avoid the attack and get i-frames if you press the buttons. 
In RE6, you could roll, dive, and what-not to your heart's content, but whether or not you actually have i-frames is a coin flip. 
I honestly don't know how Capcom managed to take literally none of the good parts of RE5 and bring them here. 

[h2]AI Partner and Inventory Management[/h2]
If you hated Sheva in RE5, well, now you have an AI companion that can only die in scripted events - completely rendering them pointless to the overall context of the game. You can't even use them as a pack mule to store items - they are just a constant presence. 

And the whole managing your inventory thing - a staple of the RE franchise - it's gone. Each character has a set amount of weapons they get throughout their campaigns and there is no upgrade system like in 4 or 5. Remember how cool it was to try out different weapons? Well, that was just too much fun, because the only amount of customization you get now is the Skill System.

[h2]Skill System[/h2]
Yikes... this is seriously one of the worst Skill Systems I have seen in any game. 
First problem: there are a whole bunch of skills, yet you can only equip three. Yeah - Three! I could understand that if the number of skills available was only like 15 or something, but there's way more than that. 
And even worse, in the Mercenaries mode, you can only equip one.
So, with that rigid limit on the skills, you would think that the Skills available to pick would be something really awesome right? Like turn all your bullets into incendiary or acid rounds? Maybe make your melee attacks infused with the powers of Zeus and lighting strike any zombie you hit? Cool stuff, right? 

No... you get lame stuff like Ammo Drop Increase. Lone Wolf. Make Herbs heal two blocks instead of one. Laaaaaaaaaame.

Just so much potential that was simply not utilized here. It demonstrates a stunning lack of creativity and a distinct ignorance of the games that came before. 

[h2]The Campaigns[/h2]
It's no secret that this game was rushed, but my god... it shows way too hard. 

Four campaigns - already a bad idea, but somehow they managed to make it worse by making them some of the most snore-inducing campaigns ever. You will not care at all about any of the events going on. Many people say that Leon's is the best, but honestly, I'd say none of them are good. They offer pretty much the same experience in each one - putting up with game's inconsistent combat and QTE overload. They try to vary things up by adding in some vehicle segments, but the game's basic combat is serviceable at best, so it's hardly any better on a vehicle. There's a lot of walky-talky segments - in fact, for first time players, there is a non-skippable tutorial segment as soon as you start the game that does a good job at showcasing how bad this game is gonna be: walky-talky segments, QTEs, annoying inventory usage, srcipted set pieces, and just general clunk-a-dunk gameplay.

[h2]The Mercenaries[/h2]
When the game's mechanics work in your favor, it does give you that feeling of "Wow. That was cool." 
Trouble is - those moments are way too few and far between and require a lot of investment from the player to even set up in the first place. 

In the Mercenaries Mode, the goal is to take down all enemies as fast as you can with as many melee attacks as you can. The more enemies killed with melee attacks, the more time you get. And they do incentivise you to use certain melees (counters provide +10 seconds as opposed to just the 5 you get from a normal melee kill. Coup-de-graces give +7). Setting up a coup-de-grace is not fun though as it often requires a combination of a slide, melee, quickshot just for one damn melee kill! 
And the countering, like I said earlier, if you aren't standing in the right spot and don't get that timing down, good luck. 
Can it be cool when it works? Oh yeah. 
Is it fun getting it to work. No. 

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
I do not recommend it to anyone even at its reduced price point. It is truly one of the biggest examples of how not to make a mainline entry in an otherwise successful franchise.

Here we go, the big bad dreaded Resident Evil 6, the game that almost derailed this behemoth of a franchise and set Capcom on a panic course correction that led them to return to their roots in horror, the game that most fans point to as the worst example of what the franchise has to offer. Did it live up to its hype as a dumpster fire of a game? To my pleasant surprise, no. Now, don’t get me wrong there are a lot of issues here, which I’ll get on shortly, and sure enough when measure up against other entries in the series it fails to reach their heights, but for all it’s flaws I gotta say RE6, much like RE4 did when it came out, had a vision of it’s own and carved it’s own identity and I respect it a lot for that.

Let’s start talking about the tone, in 5 we were way past caring about horror and barring a pleasant creepy surprise on Ada’s campaign, horror feels like a distant memory, instead we get a full on jump the shark every five minutes action game, that to its detriment takes itself way too seriously for most of it’s runtime. I genuinely believe that if this game had taken a goofier approach to it’s presentation like RE4 did it could have pull it off for more fans but sadly most of the stories feels like a soap opera with constant plot twist and reveals and an interconnectivity within it’s 4 main plots that feels sadly half bake. As such, half of the time in the story for most campaigns is both sets of companion characters staring intensely into each other while yapping a lot, it gets boring quickly especially since so many events into the campaigns overlap so you mostly know what to expect. The other half is where these game shines, and I know nothing about what I’ll mention feels resident evil but dammit I respect the boldness on display here. 

On the first 15 minutes in the tutorial, you go from slow crawling to get a herb to heal to then jumping to a helicopter while escaping a huge explosion having to pilot said helicopter while your partner fights of a zombie behind you and then “safely” crashed the chopper to your destination, it’s absolutely shameless balls to the wall action and I can’t help but love it. This sequence in the tutorial perfectly sets the tone for most of the gameplay sections that don’t consist of the regular loop of gunning down enemies while getting the key items and unlike in 5 where I felt most of such inclusions where there because those where the trends of the time, here I have to commend the variety and exaggerated scope of most of these sequences, like I said they most certainly don’t feel resident evil but they do feel awesome in their own right.

Since we’re talking story I should talk about it’s structure, you have 4 main campaigns that of Leon, Chris, Jake and Ada, all 4 of them with a different feel, slight gameplay modifications and somewhat interwoven plots as while they all cooperate at several points in the story, however each character is doing their own thing so you, as the player, are expected to play through all of them to get the whole picture. Here is another big aspect in which I feel this game dropped the ball, by having each character have a completely separate tone, gameplay style, and assorted enemy types, they ensure variety at the cost of depth. In previous entries when you had different protagonist embarking on different paths, they shared the same gameplay style and looped and differ in their choice of equipment and maybe a few stats, so Capcom could ensure that the core gameplay loop was great. 

Here Leon is the one that gets the classic RE experience with having to roam around in creepy little abandoned building gunning down mostly familiar enemy types. Chris has a straight up COD campaign, I feel like if the enemies didn’t mutate when shot you could easily forget you’re playing an RE game 80% of enemies on his campaign wield so you better get used to the cover mechanics which have improved since 5 but not by much. Jakes campaign feels like Chris’ but with a sprinkling of Nemesis which is a welcomed addition to spice things up and Ada’s feels like Metal Gear at times. While the gameplay variety is all over the place, all approaches feel sadly undercooked as each campaign is different and short enough that you don’t quite get truly used to its style before you have to adapt again and they are long enough that Capcom couldn’t give them enough love to realize their vision for a truly different feel that actually merit playing all campaigns gameplay wise. The plot itself is serviceable enough but you get enough unresolved ambiguity at the end of each campaign that it can be frustrating to wait 20 hours to get the answers you would normally get much faster in other entries.

Gone are the gold and pesetas of yesteryear here, as now instead of having the pretense of purchasing stuff the game introduces a set of skills with a weird RPG-like mechanic where you can 3 equipped at a time and you collect chess pieces throughout the levels that give you the skill point you need to buy and upgrade them. Words cannot describe how much I abhor this mechanic. First of all, it’s impossible to have a steady growth throughout a playthrough as upgrades scale dramatically with each level so you are going to need to find a hell of a lot of chess pieces to fully upgrade a skill which can take more than 1 campaign’s worth of points. Upgrading weapons actually felt like a fully reasonable progression scale as it’s natural to understand and carry it through different playthroughs and allows the are to have an economy which expands the settings worldbuilding, it doesn’t feel natural that the abilities I leveled with Leon carry over to Chris and vice versa. And lastly but certainly not least, it’s incredibly annoying to be waiting to see what drops after breaking a box or killing an enemy when you’re low on ammo and herbs and finding a freaking chess piece instead.

I can’t comment on the coop as I played this in singleplayer, but the companion AI gave a lot less of a headache, they always prioritize puzzles when they had to, not once did one die on me unless I failed a QTE and felt much more like a helping hand instead of another concern to manage.

So, after reproaching it so thoroughly would I recommend it? If you’re a fan of pure survival horror and not action games, not really, I feel like you’d be bored quite quickly and could just watch a recap of the story on YouTube, believe me it would take a lot less time than trying to piece together the story on a regular playthrough of the 4 campaigns. However, if you like pure dumb fun, this game is certainly for you, pick a conservative difficulty and enjoy all the hype moments and aura this game has to offer. Just beware of one thing, this game for some reason does NOT like to install properly, I had an issue on Leon Chapter 2 that had gave me an infinite loading screen when going to the chapel after the cutscene forcing me to replay the graveyard bit about 7 times before I dug around in some forums and try to just reinstall the games and it work wonderfully afterwards (keep in mind I had installed the game like a week prior so is not like a had it for years on my drive) and the problems seems to be persistent across all ports of the game, so if it happens once just try it and save yourself the headache later.

Side note, WHY DOES EVERY CHARACTER HERE ARCH THEIR BACKS ALL THE TIME? I feel like the real outbreak going on here is that of the scoliosis-virus.

This is easily among the top 5 worst games I've played. It's horrible both as a game and an entry in the Resident Evil series. Don't listen to people coping saying "uhh this isn't survival horror but it's still good". It's just an endless stream of very bad repetitive tasks followed by useless minigames alongside an endless stream of action. If you don't have a friend, don't even think of spending a single second. Even with a friend, this was extremely unbearable, I just wanted to finish it for completeness sake going through the games. Here is a more in-depth review of why this game sucks:

- The UI is the worst I've seen across many games. For every character, they showcased another course on how to make a UI that looks like ♥♥♥♥.

- Campaigns are bad streams of endless action, especially Chris' campaign has to be the worst thing I've played. You are endlessly ganked by Malphite clones and lizards. If you enjoy shooting blindly and watched through all entries in the Fast and Furious series, you'll love it. 

- This game is not horror, it's a comedy at best. Literally closing my eyes in a dark room would be more dread inducing than playing through this game multiple times. The only dread is induced when I see another group of enemies rushing towards me and transforming into grasshoppers, spiders, flies etc. that use machine guns, as I'm reminded of how bad the game is. 

- Technically, the game / the port sucks badly. Playing with an Xbox one controller in Chris' driving sequence with Piers, I just couldn't drive the car at full speed. I legit thought I was the problem for 20 minutes, only to stumble into an old GameFAQs entry stating that for some reason the controller input when driving doesn't accelerate the car fully, so I had to grab my mouse and do it with that and it fixed it. Literally untested. I am sure they didn't play through the game once when testing, if they did they would've noticed it sucks big time.

Overall, avoid unless you really want the story and have a friend who is willing to torture themselves just so you can learn the story. Just watch / read the story somewhere else and you won't miss out even a tiny bit of anything.

TLDR: if you're 1) playing this singleplayer, 2) are there purely for the story, and 3) do not enjoy action gameplay, i would not reccomend buying this game. get this game on sale. this game is best when you play with a friend - the co-op is one of re6's best features IMO. if you play this with a friend, be warned that ada's campaign is not co-op friendly despite it being an avaliable feature. agent cannot interact with doors or help complete puzzles. 

people give this game a bad rep for being a terrible resident evil game, and i understand why. it's not that the game is completely terrible, but its because its honestly more action horror rather than your standard survival horror game that you would expect for the resident evil series.

as someone who enjoys action, i found the combat in this game to be extremely enjoyable and fun. theres a bunch of small mechanics and combos that you can do which are very fun to learn. later in campaigns, you'll find that the combat becomes repetitve and boring however, since there's many scenes where campaigns overlap (i.e - there is a scene in ada's campaign that overlaps with a scene in leon/helena's campaign, which both my friend and i found boring and long).

the story was mid. the campaigns overlap with each other, with is cool, but i found that many of the campaigns felt unfinished despite the fact that each one had 4-5 chapters each, and that each campaign was supposed to build off one another. even after finishing the game to its entirety, my friend and i were still confused on the main reasons and motives of one of the major antagonists. the game gives you only crumbs about carla despite the plot revolving around her, which made it hard to connect with the story. the only campaign that felt fully satisfactory to me was leon and helena's campaign, where the end credit scene and the final chapter felt complete enough. but the other campaigns have flaws in their story and their endings. 

in particular, i have two major gripes with ada's campaign and jake/sherry's campaign.
spoilers for ada's campaign: [spoiler]one massive gripe i have is that in the end credit scene of ada's campaign, we don't get a credit scene with her in it. instead, we get jake. my friend and i found this absolutely ridiculous, because jake already has an entire campaign to himself and already has an end credit scene with sherry. despite her campaign, we still know so little about ada story-wise, so having an end credit scene that doesn't have any implications of what she's doing after the events of re6 is a slap to the face to anyone remotely interested in her character beyond her ties with leon. we also get very little interaction between carla and ada which is disappointing because from the very first campaign, the story invites you to be interested in carla, her motiviations, and the relationship she may have with ada. in ada's campaign, which is supposed to tie everything together, you still don't really understand anything about either of them.[/spoiler] 
the co-op in ada's campaign is terrible, too. but it makes sense because the co-op was added after backlash, but it is a terrible experience for the person who plays agent. he (agent) is never aknolwedged by ada, cannot help with puzzles, cannot open doors, is often soft-locked out of battle areas if ada goes ahead of him or is behind him, and randomly goes invisible during cutscenes or teleports whenever ada uses her grapple.
spoilers for jake/sherry's campaign: [spoiler]their campaign was actually very enjoyable. their dynamic which each other was cute, and i liked their back and forths. however, the way the campaign starts is extremely weird. you're lead to believe at first that they have a pre-established relationship, only for sherry to reveal that they've only just met. later on, there is a scene where they are kidnapped and experimented on for 6 straight months due to the fact they both have blood that can help with the virus. we NEVER get any mention about how they felt, how they were treated, or if they were traumatized from this experience. i feel like this is an extremely missed opportunity for them to bond and understand each other, because they both are understood as "cures" to the virus. the story also never explores sherry's powers in regenerating, despite being hinted at. their dynamic has so much potential, but the story never fleshes out their characters or relationship in a natural way. it is extremely disappointing.[/spoiler]

As someone that just got into Resident Evil a few months ago and has been playing the games in order I've been wondering why so many people say this is the worst game in the series, but I just completed 4 chapters of Leon's campaign and I completely understand why so many people think this game is horrible. 

For starters, this game hopped on the same trend of many other games in the early 2010's of forcing unwanted online features onto players and since the game is meant to be played online you can't pause the game. Even when you choose to play offline the game still doesn't allow you to pause. As an adult with other things to do, I don't always have the time to glue my butt to a chair for 60-90 minutes uninterrupted just to complete 1 chapter of the game. I also dislike how drastically different the UI and controls are to previous games in the series.

One last thing is that the story is all over the place, especially in the cutscenes. The cutscenes in chapter 4 of Leon's campaign specifically, the dialogue went by super fast with no pauses between sentences that it almost sounded like the voice actors for the different characters were speaking over each other while sharing 1 microphone. I also just feel like the story isn't well thought out and at times it comes across like someone's sloppily written fanfic where they include all of their favorite characters and add in their own made up characters that feel like self-inserts. 

Maybe this review was a bit harsh and once again I'm not done with the game yet so maybe I'll give an update when I'm done with all 4 campaigns

UPDATE: I just finished the game and I have some more thoughts to add and the rest of the review will be marked for spoilers. [spoiler] I feel a bit more validated in my original thoughts toward this game, mostly in regards to there being too many characters in such a short 5 chapter story. Honestly this game should really only revolve around Ada, Sherry, and Jake. I feel like have so many characters could work if there was only 1 main campaign that switched perspectives per chapter, rather than 4 separate campaigns happening at the same time. However, I feel the game should've only revolved around Ada, Sherry, and Jake because they're the only characters that feel relevant to the plot. Helena and Piers are sloppily written and don't get enough background or character development in 5 chapters for me as a player to care about them, and Leon and Chris both feel thrown in to the story purely for fanservice because they're the most popular characters in the series. Whereas Ada has a history with Simmons, Sherry works for him, and Jake has antibodies for the C-virus that Simmons created, making the 3 of them relevant to the plot and the antagonist. 

Other than my gripes with the story I noticed many technical issues with the game, especially in Ada's campaign. In Chapter 3 Ada's fight on top of the bus with the chainsaw mutant was bugged out and she kept dying instantly as the fight started and the only was for me to be able to do the fight correctly was to restart the entire chapter because the checkpoint saved right before the death animation started, meaning the game was stuck in a death loop if I restarted from the checkpoint. Additionally, the final boss fight in her story was bugged and whenever her, Leon, or Simmons would say a line of dialogue it would cutoff and immediately the next transition scene in the fight would play. 

I know this game has a cult following amongst many older resident evil fans, but after I had such a bad experience with this game I feel like anyone who likes this must be blinded by nostalgia. Or in the case of Piers, they only like the characters because of made up fanon and not what's actually in the game. This game is like Resident Evil's equivalent of DMC2 and I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone.  [/spoiler]

Additionally, for Ada fans out there, I think this game shows more about her. It shows how she’s not a completely bad person. She may be morally grey, but throughout her story you’ll see her helping others, not only Leon.

I started my gameplay with Ada’s playthrough, so it was fun to see how other playthroughs fill in the gaps.  You can start like I did, or play Ada’s segment as last — summarizing all other playthroughs while adding something more about Ada. I really loved the way the stories are all connected in some way.

What else? Some positives — I love the melees in this game. I had fun with those, especially during Ada’s story (there’s something about her movements that makes me screammm)

The game may have its downs, but it’s really fun to play coop. I’d recommend you to play it if you are a big RE fan, as it still fills in the plot about the characters.

The characters and the combat system are well thought-out as to give characters their perfect movesets in combat, and well-fitting weapon loadouts in the mercenaries mode (or other applicable bonus modes)

This game gets a bad rap but it's not a bad game. It deserves it's reputation as it is far and away the most non-Resident Evil game despite having a ton of the original characters and being a numbered entry in the franchise. To be clear, this game did not lose Capcom money, in fact it sold very well when it initially released but had less sales and more criticism than RE: 5 which showed Capcom that there were issues which allowed the franchise to get back on track with the more horror based RE: Revelations 1 & 2 and eventually RE:7 and beyond. For these reasons we may have this game to thank for the RE franchise being more alive now than ever.

I said this was not a bad game and it's true. It's not. In fact with the right approach this could easily be one of the most fun single player/co-op action shooters I've ever played. There are 4 campaigns each with characters that have distinct playstyles and gear with lots of replayability and a massive variety in enemies and bosses. Not to mention it's DLC's with other arcade like modes. The voice acting is overly dramatic but good and still carries some of the campy RE vibe.  Far and away the best part of the game for me is some of the dodge/roll mechanics. While it may take some time to master, with some practice you get to a point where you can feel like John Wick in a mutant zombie apocolypse. You can can dodge roll in all directions and end up in posistion akin to to Tom Cruise in the movie "Collateral" where you're on your back, blasting away with your handgun as enemies try to get to you. 

Has the game aged? 

Yes, while impressive for it's time, the game definitely looks like its from the 7th generation era with the ai being perhaps it's most glaring issue, but in fairness, the companion ai was considered poor even when it first released over 12 years ago. I have never encountered any game breaking bugs. 

Do I wish the game didn't exist? 

Of course not. It's fun and I have good times with it. Thank goodness it does exist for the future of the series sake. 

Do I wish the game had not been a numbered entry in the series? 

Yes. It would have been better as some other one off with maybe one or two mainline characters. Making this a numbered entry kinda messes with the story in a way that  makes you want to retcon the scope of what it affected. 

Is it still a horror game?

Yes? Technically? It's definitely more like an action game with horror moments or elements. It's the least scary of the franchise but I still wouldn't play it around little kids.

Do I still play it today? 

Heck. Yes. As a gamer and as a fan of the series it's a worthwhile game but even if you're not a fan of the series it's fun. Especially if you have a friend that you've been playing action coop titles with as it makes the game better and can lead to some hilarious and genuinely fun mindless moments. It's top tier coop stuff.

Overall, It's a real hoot when you accept the game for what it is which is a playable Hollywood B-movie action film. Whether you're new to the series, a series veteran or are just looking for an action game, I recommend it but mentally distance this experience from the rest of the franchise to avoid messing with your expectations for the other titles as they are for most part very different.

For starters, this game is really long because of the four different campaigns you have to finish before you understand the whole plot. This is not a bad thing if you enjoy the franchise itself rather than a specific playstyle. However, if you play this game because you like a specific playstyle, then you might be disappointed. The four different campaigns feature also different sub-genres. For example, Leon's campaign leans more toward horror and puzzles; Chris's storyline focuses more on action while Ada's campaign combines espionage and puzzles. Finishing a campaign whose playstyle is not up your alley might be a struggle. What I really love about this game though is the intertwining storyline from the four different campaigns. I enjoy the connection between the characters' choices and how each choice influences one another. For me, it is hard to choose the best campaign as I love all the campaigns; however, if I have to choose one, I would pick Ada's campaign. Each chapter has different strategies and playstyles. For instance, in chapter 2, you have to solve some puzzles. After that, in chapter 3, you have an option to accomplish the chapter without being noticed (That is why I described it as espionage). All in all, I love the game and what it offers within the horror/action genre.

The problem with doing something incredibly different in nearly every entry of a game series is simple: at some point, you're going to faceplant. I won't do the whole "here's my experience with each campaign and my rating out of 5" rigmarole since I'm too exhausted for that, but I'll concede that some campaigns stand heads and shoulders above others. Chris' and Jake's are busy action romps that howl with adrenaline and ludicrous violence, multiple stages of fighting increasingly fleshy monsters that rival 5's in grotesqueness. I like the visuals and action for the most part, but I feel like the UI and game systems are a step down from its predecessor. No upgrades, no item passing or sharing... the discussions I'd have with my friend about how to use our nine slots are long gone, dissipated totally when we realized how single-player-centric the whole thing was. Scrolling inventory isn't fun, managing tablets is a lateral move that doesn't change much, and on the whole it just feels... weaker. Resident Evil 5 was about partners, and the gameplay reflected that. 6 is four messy scenarios trying to fit together in one bowl like some kind of foul soup, leading to a lot of clutter... which is... reflected in the gameplay? There’s a lot of experimentation that simply doesn’t work, especially the locked-camera scenes where you need to sprint away from a threat like a Crash Bandicoot game. Great work, Capcom. I got to chapter 3 of Ada’s campaign before I had my fill. So long, RE6.

i know this opinion alone is enough to send certain people into a full-body meltdown, and honestly, that’s half the fun. resident evil 4 is treated like sacred text, like it personally invented video games and cured hunger. but playing resident evil 6 so far has been more enjoyable, more exciting, and way less interested in forcing me to bow to nostalgia.

resident evil 6 is pure, unfiltered chaos and it owns it. explosions are nonstop. set pieces are absurd. characters are dramatic in the most over-the-top action movie way possible. i don’t want subtle survival horror every five seconds - i want leon diving through windows while the world is actively collapsing, and re6 delivers that without a shred of shame.

meanwhile, resident evil 4 fans will swear the game is flawless while leon slowly pivots like a broken shopping cart every time you aim. incredible stuff. stop to shoot, stop to move, stop to exist. but resident evil 6 actually lets you play the game. you can move, shoot, slide, roll, punch, kick, and suplex your way through absolute madness. it feels alive. it feels modern. it feels like it actually wants you to touch the controller.

and the scope is ridiculous in the best way. multiple campaigns, different tones, constant momentum. resident evil 6 feels like capcom said “what if we just went completely off the rails” and committed to it fully. it’s excessive. it’s messy. it’s loud. it’s dramatic. and it’s way more fun than people are willing to admit.

is resident evil 4 iconic? sure. is it untouchable perfection that must never be questioned? absolutely not. resident evil 6 may not be subtle, but it’s confident, bombastic, and actually respects my time instead of demanding reverence.

so yes, resident evil 6 is better than resident evil 4 so far. if that makes you mad, that sounds like a personal problem.

Resident Evil 6 takes a two steps forward but one step back when it was first released in 2016. This title has to be one of the longer entries in the series where you play a total of four different campaigns about five-six hours long: Leon and Helena, Chris and Piers, Sherry and Jake, and final fourth solo character with an optional partner character. Like its predecessor, you are accompanied by another player or a computer AI as you traverse through obstacles together. This time however each player may equip a skill that can boost attack power, play supportive roles or have other effects.

Players have full movement control and can strafe while shooting which is a vast improvement on its predecessor's gameplay. The game is still very great looking and the character acting is solid. All characters can melee at will and can heal each other very quickly. And like before the cutscenes are good and carry the regret theme very well. You also have the option to switch between the default crosshair or the laser pointer AND you can change your character's viewpoint between right-handed and left-handed. Just like the previous game the post-game The Mercenaries mode is a ton of fun especially with its new movement system but enemies are much harder by comparison and plays a banger rave-like theme.

The biggest problem this time around isn't its story but rather its pacing jumping between random points in the story that fail to tell one cohesive story. The music in this game is somewhat forgettable. There are a lot of infuriating fatal quick-time-event prompts that will have you restarting certain battles. In fact there are more than a handful of instant-death traps that can make the game feel unfair at times. The antagonists are not as entertaining compared this time around. If you play this game solo your computer companion cannot be killed in combat except with a few gameplay events, but they don't really harm enemies either so they feel pointless to have around.

For better or worse the game becomes a full-on action game with some disturbing themes that play into the horror genre, but you won't feel underpowered at any time thanks to its abundance of ammo and currency. As an innovative first, several points in your campaign playthrough will connect you with other player sessions whether you join forces to take down a strong boss or compete in a race to your objectives though I don't know if most player will enjoy this feature due to the lower player base as of 2025. It's an old game. Unlike the previous games, you can only manually reload your currently equipped weapon on the field as opposed to the inventory menu, and weapons cannot be upgraded.

Resident Evil 6 was very ambitious with its stories and its gameplay, but painful level design and its confusing story timeline makes the experience feel more annoying than delightful. Despite all of my complaints it is still a solid co-op game that rewards those that master its gameplay. This game will not satisfy survivor-horror fans, but it can attract those looking for a darker story that is full of action and a great combat loop.

[b][u]UI:[/u][/b]
The UI sucks and is horribly obtuse to navigate. Each campaign's UI aesthetic is different, which would be cool if they didn't all look absolutely awful. You can upgrade and equip skills with up to 8 customizable presets, as if [i]anybody[/i] would ever care to strategize about equipable skills that hard. I’ve beaten this game more times than I can count. I even climbed the Mercenaries leaderboards once. I adored it on the Xbox 360, bought it again for the Xbox One, again for the One X, then grabbed it on PS3 and PS4, and now here I am on Steam like a mad fool repeating the ritual. I can’t stay away from this thing.

Let’s get something out of the way. If you want horror, the classic creeping dread is gone. But if you loved RE4 and RE5, then RE6 is everything you were secretly craving. The action is wild, the combat dances around you, the slides are smooth as silk, and the movement system feels better than most modern shooters. You can weave i-frames into your attacks to shrug off damage if you time it right. Even if you think the story is goofy, the Mercenaries mode alone is worth the twenty bucks. If it’s on sale, even better. This is one of the best versions of Mercenaries ever made.

The story is the weakest link, but it carries that early 2000s Capcom charm. Stylized American action heroes doing things so ridiculous they make Tom Cruise break out in jealous sweat. You get four full campaigns, each following different characters through the same global disaster from different angles. In RE5 the co-op sometimes felt bolted on. Here it feels like the game was built around it. Harder difficulties turn the intensity up until the screen feels like it’s trying to burn through your eyes. Horror is gone, but what replaces it is chaos, spectacle, and a surprisingly dense mountain of content. Co-op is practically required, and when it clicks it becomes one of the best cooperative action games ever made.

I’ll be real with you. When the game first launched, I hated it. But over time it became the Resident Evil I return to more than any other. I’ve played them all, and this is the one that stuck its claws the deepest. I can’t go back to RE4 and RE5 after sinking time into this masterclass in over the top action. It feels like Devil May Cry and RE5 had a beautifully unhinged child, which makes sense since Devil May Cry originally evolved out of RE2. This is still one of the highest selling RE titles ever, and the reason is simple. If you silence the constant chanting for horror and just enjoy what this game is trying to be, it’s brilliant.

Here are some features worth highlighting. Four lengthy campaigns with intersecting storylines. Drop in and drop out co-op. A movement system that lets you dive, slide, roll, shoot prone, and pull off melee counters. A skill system that lets you customize your playstyle. Mercenaries mode with some of the best maps and flow the series has ever offered. Unique enemy types for each campaign. A global scale story that ties the characters together. Weapon variety that rewards aggressive play. And one of the most fluid third person combat systems Capcom has ever made.

If you want a horror game, it isn’t here.
If you want adrenaline, spectacle, action, and pure mechanical satisfaction, this is one of the best. Let yourself enjoy it. It deserves it.

The nadir point of the main [b]Resident Evil[/b] series? Quite likely.

One thing I couldn't get past back when it was new, and much less I can nowadays, is how much worse than [b]RE5[/b] this game looks. The production effort is very evident at times, especially in animations, but it all looks so muddy and sometimes even outright undefined, like the high number of assets they had to produce led them to sacrifice the level of detail. Not like it wouldn't be the sole case of quantity over quality here.

They made the control scheme a bit more convenient, and the AI of the partner character is not a hindrance anymore, but the flow of the game is constantly broken by small QTEs and short and long cutscenes, and an apparent necessity for every setpiece to feel "climactic", which ultimately leads to just exhaustion. While Leon and Helena's campaign has, at least, some atmospheric moments meant to evoke the feeling of Leon's earlier adventures (but in its latter part, it's got some of the most ridiculous bosses ever), the other two don't quite manage that, with Chris and Piers' especially feeling like some wannabe [b]Call of Duty[/b]. I mean, those have got zombie modes, no?

It's a long game, but how worth all that content is, when it's so clunky and at times even outright unpleasant to play, and occasionally even to look at, all strung together with a story that is so over the top but wants to be taken seriously at the same time?

[b]RE6[/b] is an ambitious project, especially evident by how the narratives of the four campaigns intertwine with each other, but the same ambition has led to it trying to be everything and excelling at nothing. Fortunately, after this, someone at Capcom realized they had to refocus and look into a smaller scale.

EDIT: There is a complex movement system to be learned here. Once you have mastered it, you will really enjoy the game. Unfortunately, they do not teach you that.

[i]Resident Evil 6[/i] is a remarkable entry in the franchise that boldly expands the series into high-octane action while still delivering the tension, atmosphere, and survival horror roots that fans cherish. It is an ambitious, cinematic experience that offers multiple interconnected campaigns, each with its own characters, story, and perspective — creating a vast, engaging world full of intrigue, danger, and memorable encounters.

The game lets you step into the shoes of multiple protagonists, including Leon S. Kennedy, Chris Redfield, Jake Muller, and Ada Wong, each with unique gameplay styles and missions. Leon’s campaign focuses on tactical survival, blending classic horror elements with intense combat. Chris delivers raw, explosive action, perfect for players who enjoy heavy firepower and adrenaline-pumping sequences. Jake’s story mixes speed, mobility, and over-the-top encounters, while Ada provides a stealth-focused, narrative-driven experience. The diversity of campaigns ensures that no two playthroughs feel the same, keeping the game fresh and engaging from start to finish.

The world of [i]Resident Evil 6[/i] is massive and varied. From eerily abandoned city streets to sweltering jungles, secret laboratories, and infected urban centers, each environment is rich with detail and atmosphere. The game balances horror and spectacle, creating moments of pure terror alongside epic, cinematic set pieces that feel like playable action movies. Environmental design reinforces both tension and excitement, with careful lighting, weather effects, and sound design enhancing the immersion at every turn.

Combat is a highlight, offering fast-paced, dynamic encounters with hordes of infected, grotesque bosses, and intelligent human enemies. Each campaign introduces new enemy types, encouraging players to adapt strategies, use environmental hazards, and make tactical choices. The blend of melee, firearms, and explosive devices keeps encounters varied and satisfying. The co-op functionality adds a new layer of strategy, making teamwork and coordination both rewarding and fun.

[i]Resident Evil 6[/i] also excels in storytelling. While the game is larger in scale and more cinematic than previous entries, it maintains the series’ signature tension and drama. The intertwining campaigns gradually reveal the scope of a global biohazard crisis, highlighting personal stakes, moral dilemmas, and high-octane survival moments. Character development is strong, especially as the game explores familiar faces like Leon and Chris alongside new protagonists, giving players a deep connection to the narrative.

Technical presentation is impressive. The game’s detailed environments, smooth animations, realistic character models, and cinematic camera work create a highly immersive experience. The sound design, including ambient effects, tense musical cues, and the chilling growls of infected enemies, heightens both excitement and fear, fully complementing the action-heavy gameplay.

[i]Resident Evil 6[/i] is not just an action-horror game; it’s an ambitious, multifaceted adventure that pushes the franchise in new directions while retaining the essence of survival horror. Its multiple campaigns, cinematic presentation, fast-paced combat, and memorable moments combine into a complete, thrilling experience that caters to both longtime fans and newcomers alike.

A must-play for anyone who enjoys cinematic action, fast-paced survival horror, and a sprawling story full of suspense, thrills, and unforgettable encounters — [i]Resident Evil 6[/i] delivers a bold, action-packed adventure that is both thrilling and unforgettable.

Don't buy this game thinking it will be more RE5, because that's what I did and oh boy was I wrong...

This game... I'm not sure if Capcom ever finished it, to be honest; It feels so "raw" and unpolished it's crazy to think that somebody play-tested this and said "yeah, this is good". What happened here, seriously? Does anybody know? My only guess is that they were in a real rush to push out the next mainline entry for some reason, but the end product is a good moral lesson on how good things take time.

I won't bore you with how this game feels nothing like a Resident Evil game because if you've played Resident Evil 4 and 5 you should be used to this franchise's action game phase by now, and yes; It definitely does feel like some summer blockbuster shlock that Michael Bay would direct, complete with cheesy dialogue and one-liners that make you roll your eyes so hard you could count every wrinkle in your brain. I hope you're not attached to any of this universe's characters because RE6 turns them into unlikeable one-note stereotypes and misogynists.

The graphics? Let's talk about the graphics: The phrase "this looks like a PS2 game" is often misused in my opinion, because a lot of the big budget games on that platform looked pretty damn good. So when I say "RE6 looks like a PS2 game", I should clarify that it specifically looks like a *bad* PS2 game; Ugly texture seams, low poly character models, weird shader effects that make some objects appear extraordinarily shiny... You can stumble upon random 3D objects that emit light bloom as if they're christmas decorations... A ton of world objects aren't scaled properly, so be prepared to find huge chairs and toilets.

Sure; Graphics aren't everything, but RE6's visual presentation is a huge step back compared to 5, which still holds up pretty well in the graphics department.

The controls? Complete ass, no question. Movement direction is controlled by both the mouse and the WASD keys, so your character movement always feels imprecise and squirrelly. I'd much rather take RE5s tank controls over this, because even after 46 hours of playing I never feel 100% like I know what I'm doing. Even worse is that the game loves to start cutscenes seemingly at random, and give you control back when the camera is at a different angle that changes where your character moves; This happens *so* many times, yet you will never be prepared for it and it will cause a significant amount of your deaths.

I've read some of the more recent reviews say that they enjoy the controls and how "fast paced" it is, but I'm not sure what these people are smoking...

How about the music? Sure, music hasn't always been on the forefront of the franchise, but it has definitely been memorable and helped build the game's iconic atmosphere and suspense. Here, it sounds like a generic royalty free orchestra soundtrack; It almost never feels appropriate and at worst will make you hunt for the mute / volume button. Same goes for the sound effects: Prepare to hear a whole library of familiar sounding stock sounds. I was half expecting to hear a Wilhelm Scream.

The story is... Bad. It's just not good. It's basically an attempt at turning Resident Evil into a story that spans the globe, but it only limits us to a handful of locations, and besides a change of scenery you'll be fighting essentially the same three or four small groups of enemies over and over again but with different "skins". I will say that the concept of intersecting storylines is novel and an interesting idea conceptually, but Capcom did not pull it off well here and most of the story intersections and how they relate to one another introduce plotholes more than anything else. At no point does the writing ever feel like a fully realized Resident Evil game; It teeters on bad fan-fiction.

Would I recommend it? Steam reviews only allow for positive and negative reviews, so it's hard to provide a nuanced opinion sometimes, but I think it depends mostly on your tolerance of bad games and if you have somebody to play it with. If you're someone who enjoys the occasional bad media (i.e. The Room or Birdemic) and you have a friend who does too, then I think RE6 can be a blast. I know I was laughing almost every other cutscene, for sure. That being said, I don't think you'll get much enjoyment out of playing this by yourself.

Before I begin, though I am giving critiques, no I do not think RE6 is unplayable or not worth your time, I actually think it is quite fun! But here we go!

RE6 is not the traditional resident evil experience, not by a long shot. It is an action game through and through, despite Capcom's best efforts to make each campaign a "different" experience. Leon's campaign is probably the closest we get to "horror". Unfortunately, they also do not do a great job at linking each campaign together into one cohesive story. This is not aided by the fact that the story as a whole has a lot going on that is not well-explained even within the self-contained campaigns. I'll go into each campaign without spoiling, just what I think of each.

Leon/Helena- Like I said, this one is probably the closest to "horror" and is the best as a self-contained story. It doesn't largely intersect with Chris and Jake's campaigns outside of the major events where you play all together and maybe this is for the best. It has some good moments, Leon and Helena are good characters that work well together and the story is really not bad. Their gameplay sections are pretty alright as well imo. 

Chris/Piers- This campaign, in my opinion, has the best story in terms of character arcs. I won't go into too much detail because even though this game is old, I don't want to spoil. Chris has a good and sad character arc, and Piers is a perfect character to pair him with for this purpose. I was not a huge fan of the gameplay in this campaign if only because it is the action-heaviest one, with plenty of explosions and angry yelling. However, I think the drama and character makes up for it. The way it plays into the larger narrative is fine too, though I'm not going to applaud the overarching story of this game. 

Jake/Sherry- This is my personal favorite campaign. Jake's story is just as interesting as Chris's and again Sherry is a perfect partner to pair him with because of their chemistry and parallels. There is a stalker enemy throughout this campaign that feels like a Mr. X callback and this is pretty cool. Overall, I have similar things to say about gameplay/the overall story because that is a constant throughout all campaigns. 

Ada- You would think her campaign would tie up the loose ends and help us understand the story the best. This is not the case. I feel like the only reason I understand anything about this game is because of files and sources outside of it. This is not how you tell any story. I don't mind Ada's campaign, there are some good puzzles and her combat is pretty fun. It's just the story that brings it down for me. 

Ultimately, and kind of a TLDR- RE6 is not an irredeemable game. What it lacks in story and horror it makes up for in fun gameplay (including some pretty good melee and counterattacks that I have fun with, as well as a good co-op experience), and character stories. It's major weakness is unfortunately the narrative it is trying to tell regarding the C-Virus. It's character stories for Chris, Jake and his dad and their parallels between Piers and Sherry are actually very gripping in my opinion. It's just the outer-story that is weak, leaving Leon, Helena, and especially Ada (the center of this game's story) left with little to do. Overall, however, I think this game gets far too much hate and there is very much something to enjoy in it :)

Resident Evil 6 surprised the hell out of me — in the BEST way. I don’t care what the haters say… this game is GOATED if you actually play and enjoy the story.

First, let me talk about the storylines. Bro… FOUR campaigns?? Leon, Chris, Jake (yeah Wesker’s son—tough dude), and my MOMMY, QUEEN, GODDESS Ada Wong. The fact that each campaign connects and forms one giant story is crazy. It feels like watching an entire Resident Evil universe unfold in front of you.

Leon’s campaign? Beautiful mix of horror and action.
Chris’s campaign? Military action heartbreak.
Jake’s campaign? The next generation stepping into the chaos.
Ada’s campaign? Bro… peak cinema. She just walks in, saves the day, acts mysterious, disappears, and looks GORGEOUS doing it.

I’ve supervised Leon and Ada’s story since RE2, followed them again in RE4 Remake, and now seeing their dynamic continue in RE6… DAMN. The chemistry is insane. Their relationship is that legendary “I save you, you save me, but we're still complicated as hell” type of story. I LOVE IT.

And Ada in RE6?
Bruh.
The outfit, the attitude, the voice, the moves — CHEF’S. KISS.
Capcom knew exactly what they were doing. Every cutscene with her? I stopped breathing. That’s MY secret campaign.

Gameplay?
Fire.
Smooth movement, sick melee combos, cinematic moments, and the fact that you can play the whole thing with co-op makes it even better. Not many RE games give you FOUR full campaigns that interlock so perfectly.

People can hate all they want, but RE6 is ambitious, crazy fun, and full of iconic moments. If you love Leon, Chris, Jake, or especially ADA WONG (my personal religion), this game is a must-play.

11/10 — I didn’t survive the C-Virus, I survived ADA WONG’S BEAUTY.

Resident Evil 6 is a game that tries to do too much at once, and ends up losing the identity that defined the series. The constant shift in tone and gameplay between campaigns makes the experience feel inconsistent and unfocused, often leaning more toward loud action than tense survival horror. The pacing frequently suffers, overwhelmed by explosions, quick-time events, and set pieces that leave little room for atmosphere or suspense. That said, there are some positives. The game offers a large amount of content, with multiple campaigns and co-op support that can be enjoyable with a friend. Some character moments still land, and at times the combat can be entertaining when it slows down long enough to breathe. Visually, the game holds up decently, and the soundtrack and sound design are solid. However, these strengths aren’t enough to outweigh the feeling that Resident Evil 6 lost track of what made the franchise unique. It’s a bold experiment with scale and ambition, but one that traded identity and coherence for spectacle.

[h1]RE6: A Mutation Nobody Asked For[/h1]

[i]Blending action and survival horror, Resident Evil 6 promises to be the dramatic horror experience of 2013.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Resident Evil 6 sees the world under attack from a new bioweapon called the C-Virus. Leon Kennedy must stop a conspiracy after the President is infected, while Chris Redfield battles mutated soldiers in China and confronts his own shaken resolve. Jake Muller, who is mysteriously immune, teams up with Sherry Birkin to protect a potential cure. In the shadows, Ada Wong uncovers a plot by Neo-Umbrella and a doppelgänger enemy spreading the virus.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil 6 shifts the series further into third-person action, prioritizing fast-paced gunplay and cinematic set pieces over traditional survival horror. Its story unfolds across four interwoven campaigns starring Leon S. Kennedy (DSO), Chris Redfield (BSAA), mercenary Jake Muller, and spy Ada Wong. In Leon, Chris, and Jake’s campaigns, players can choose either the main character or their partner (Helena Harper, Piers Nivans, or Sherry Birkin), with the alternate role filled by AI or a second player locally or online. Ada’s campaign is designed for solo play but also supports optional co-op with a non-canonical character known simply as Agent.

Each campaign delivers a distinct gameplay style with its own strengths and vulnerabilities. Resident Evil 6 expands the series’ mechanics with full-directional dodging, sliding, and the ability to shoot while sprinting. Quick-time events still appear during high-intensity sequences.

Co-op remains a central feature, supporting up to four players in specific crossover encounters where storylines intersect, such as when Leon and Helena cross paths with Jake and Sherry. However, most of the campaign is tailored to two-player co-op, similar to Resident Evil 5. In certain enemy-invasion sections, up to two additional players can also jump in to control hostile creatures.

Health management has been reworked. You convert herbs into tablets and consume them individually to restore health. Downed players rely on partners for revival or risk restarting from the last checkpoint. Enemies drop skill points that can be spent on permanent upgrades, from increased weapon power to more frequent ammo drops. Only three upgrades can be equipped at once, but they apply across all characters and campaigns. Players can even remove AI support entirely using the Lone Wolf option. Melee-focused combat is governed by a stamina bar that drains when executing physical attacks or using the Quick Shot ability, which instantly aims for enemy weak points.

Beyond the campaign, two additional modes offer more action. The fan-favorite Mercenaries challenges players to defeat waves of enemies against a countdown timer, while the PC-exclusive No Mercy variant ramps up the chaos with up to 300 enemies on screen and optional cameos from the Left 4 Dead 2 cast.

Agent Hunt flips the script by allowing you to invade other campaigns as enemy creatures, though this mode unlocks only after completing the three primary storylines. The longer you survive in a target session, the more points you earn.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
The main enemies include traditional zombies and the newly introduced J’avo. Unlike zombies, J’avo can communicate, use weapons, and heal themselves. They can also undergo various mutations that enhance their combat abilities, with the mutation type often depending on where they’re injured. In total, there are 15 different J’avo mutations in the game.

There are several boss encounters throughout the game, most of which rely on identifying and targeting clearly exposed weak points while dodging large, telegraphed attacks. Some bosses feature unique mechanics tied to their design. For example, the Lepotitsa emits a toxic gas that can instantly transform nearby civilians into zombies, adding pressure to take it down quickly before the situation escalates.

[h2]Environment[/h2]
The game takes place across multiple global locations, including Tall Oaks, USA; the war-torn Eastern European state of Edonia; and the Chinese city of Lanshiang. The environments are diverse, ranging from chaotic city streets and subways to cemeteries, mines, collapsed buildings, laboratories, and more. Level design is entirely linear, emphasizing fast-paced action and cover-based combat rather than exploration. Areas are not interconnected, and puzzles are few and straightforward, offering little challenge beyond the combat encounters.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
One standout enemy is the Lepotitsa—a genuinely unsettling B.O.W. Its towering, lanky frame is covered in pale yellow-green flesh, with disturbingly long, pointed fingers. The most revolting feature is its swollen torso, riddled with bulbous pores that pulsate and release a bright blue toxic gas. It’s one of the few moments in the game where the creature design actually manages to evoke discomfort and horror, and I just did not want to look at it.

Weapons feature punchy, responsive sound design that enhances the feel of combat, giving each shot a satisfying sense of power and feedback. Enemies also benefit from distinct audio cues, helping you anticipate incoming threats and react accordingly.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
Grenade handling is clunky: after throwing one, your character automatically switches back to a weapon, and you must re-equip grenades to throw another.

You can’t choose which weapons to carry, nor can you store any, as there’s no item box or inventory management between chapters.

Keybindings are awful. Reload/Pick Up is automatically set to R. You can change the keybindings of course, but you can't split them up. Imagine standing on some items while in a firefight where you want to reload, but the character prioritizes picking up items instead. Crouch is set to 2, Z is used for Roll/Dodge left, C for right, 3 for forward, X for jumping backwards. You can also sprint, slide, lay on your back, roll around while on the ground and even shoot while prone. They stuffed this game with so many unnecessary combat features it’s crazy. Rebinding keys is frustrating because there are so many actions—it's unclear where or how to assign them all.

The inventory is a disaster. It’s ugly and confusing. You have all your items in something called Item Slot. Herbs need to be moved from here into your Tablet Case to be able to be used. The keybinding for healing yourself with herbs or reviving your partner is set to 1. Weapon and item inventories are separate, with weapons switched via mouse scroll and items via F.

If you run over corpses your character starts stumbling around and losing balance. I don't understand what the point of this is—completely idiotic and very annoying.

Aiming is somewhat frustrating. While there’s a crosshair, it mainly serves to indicate the general area of impact. Inside the crosshair, a moving laser dot shows where the bullet will actually land, but the dot sways noticeably, making precise shots difficult. Very awkward!

In Chris’s campaign, enemies use firearms, and getting shot knocks you to the ground, forcing you to manually stand back up. It can happen repeatedly, and it quickly becomes frustrating.

Headshoting zombies sometimes make their heads roll off of their bodies and look ridiculous.

The partner AI is terrible.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Resident Evil 6 feels more like a generic shooter than a true survival-horror experience. It introduces numerous combat mechanics that feel unnecessary and stray far from the series’ roots. While the game does feature some interesting enemies, visually impressive set pieces, and a moderately engaging story, these positives are overshadowed by its many flaws. The weapons are serviceable, but the inventory system is one of the worst I’ve encountered in a game. Expect a bad RE experience!

Resident Evil 6 — Reviewed by Albert Wesker

Ah… Resident Evil 6.

The so-called “evolution” of the series — a chaotic cocktail of explosions, melodrama, and misplaced ambition. I had the misfortune of observing this entry from… beyond the grave, as they say. Even death, it seems, cannot protect me from disappointment.

Let’s begin with the elephant in the bioweapon lab: scale.
Capcom decided that bigger must mean better. Multiple campaigns! Four protagonists! Global outbreaks! Helicopters! Motorcycles! Tanks! As if the franchise were compensating for a lack of identity with an overdose of spectacle.
But what resulted was not evolution… it was mutation without control.

Leon S. Kennedy returns, of course — older, moodier, still suffering from that heroic complex that keeps him alive purely by narrative convenience. His campaign at least attempts to remember what survival horror feels like — shadows, slow pacing, tension. For a moment, I felt hope… and then the game threw me into a car chase and reminded me that subtlety is dead.

Chris Redfield, my old rival — now a grizzled, guilt-ridden soldier drowning in melodrama. Watching him struggle with “the weight of his past” would almost be touching… if I hadn’t spent years watching him solve every problem by punching it into dust. He fights bioweapons the way a caveman fights thunder — with blind rage and protein shakes.

And then there’s Jake Muller. My progeny. My so-called “son.”
How… quaint.
The boy has potential — strength, reflexes, regenerative ability — but no vision. No purpose. He’s what happens when superior genetics are squandered by morality. If he truly is my genetic legacy, then I am deeply offended by the result.

Sherry Birkin returns as well — all grown up, still clinging to the same government that ruined her childhood. Humans never learn.

The C-Virus itself is a grotesque attempt at innovation. A hybrid strain combining the worst traits of everything that came before — much like the game surrounding it. The transformations are impressive, yes, but without direction. A virus with no philosophy… a sin I could never commit.

Mechanically, the game feels like it’s having an identity crisis. One moment, it’s a horror title. The next, an action movie. Then a co-op shooter. Then a soap opera about redemption and loss. It’s less Resident Evil and more Resident Everything.
You can roll, slide, melee, dual-wield, quick-shot — it’s like watching Umbrella scientists throw every experiment into the same tank and hoping for brilliance through chaos.

Even the enemies seem confused. Zombies with guns. J’avo with jetpacks. Mutations that transform mid-fight just to remind you that “something is happening,” even when nothing meaningful is.

Visually, of course, it’s impressive — Capcom never fails there. The production values are superb. But presentation cannot mask lack of focus. You can wrap a T-Virus sample in gold foil, but it’s still a contagion.

My verdict:
A bloated monstrosity of ambition and ego — a game that tried to be all things and became nothing. There are sparks of brilliance buried beneath the rubble, but they’re smothered by noise, excess, and self-importance.

4.5 out of 10.

Resident Evil 6 is Capcom's attempt to make the series something more than just horror. The game features four campaigns with different characters, gameplay styles, and storylines. From the relatively dark story with Leon to the military action movie with Chris, everything looks grand, but not always balanced. The game tries to be everything at once, which sometimes causes it to lose focus.

The game is primarily aimed at fans of dynamic action: lots of shooting, spectacular scenes, QTEs, and constant changes in pace. However, the atmosphere of the classic parts is almost absent — there is little horror, resources are almost unlimited, and there is no fear of enemies. It's more of an adventure action game than a survival horror game.

Among the main drawbacks, it is worth mentioning the rather awkward controls — the characters sometimes move “woodenly,” and the camera behaves unpredictably in tight spaces or during dynamic scenes. Confusion often arises in combat due to poor camera angles. Also annoying are the excess of QTEs, the ill-conceived design of some levels, and the feeling of “oversaturation” with action, which can become tiresome towards the end.

Ultimately, this is a project for enthusiasts. As a spectacular zombie action game with dynamic gameplay, it can provide dozens of hours of entertainment, especially in co-op mode. However, from the perspective of the series, it is one of the least recognizable installments, which has almost completely abandoned its horror roots.
