This game is underrated, but perhaps justifiably so; gamers expecting a horror game went into Resident Evil 6 to face inevitable disappointment.

This is not a horror game. It has zombies. And weird abominations. And violence. But there is no doubt in my mind that this is an action-heavy third-person shooter with a whole lot of cinematic ridiculousness. And that's... honestly fine. It's just that it's a far cry from what many people expect from the series, hence the hurt feelings and somewhat mixed reception.

Resident Evil 6 represents the summit of the hybrid ranged-melee combat system that the dev team has been working on since back in Resident Evil 4. The basic loop is shoot enemy -> close in while they stagger -> use melee finisher. While it sounds simple, it's actually a surprisingly robust system with a lot of variety; depending on where you shoot an enemy to stagger them, where you stand in relation to them before using your melee, and more, you have access to a plethora of melee finishers. It's quite fun experimenting to see how stylishly you can bring down infected, and the fact that you save ammo by killing opponents efficiently with melee attacks means that this system isn't just for show, either.

On top of this you have lots of crazy options in play, none of which are necessary to beat the game, but many of which will benefit you quite a lot. You can perform a slide, which allows you to shoot while evading, plant a remote bomb on the ground while sliding, and transition into a prone position to hide behind cover. You can fire snap shots without aiming, which is useful when you want to get an enemy off you quickly and don't have time to stare down your sights. You can perform a quick recovery after taking damage to avoid being knocked down. You can perform a powerful melee counterattack right before an enemy attacks you, negating all incoming damage. You can animation-cancel slow-reloading weapons to fire them at higher speeds.

Suffice it to say RE6 has a lot of tech, and if you bother to learn it, you'll begin to feel like a bona-fide badass.

That said, it's not by any means a perfect game. There are four campaigns total, and they all feel a bit different from one another. One campaign might be a bit more suspenseful, with few enemies and resources, but lots of darkness and surprise attacks. Another might be all action, with easy access to powerful weaponry and waves of enemies bearing down on you. Some of these moments are awesome, and others fall flat. There are places where I got lost for an inordinate amount of time, trying to find the next objective, and became a bit frustrated. But these moments were not too common, and for the most part, RE6 does a reasonable job keeping the player engaged.

The primary reason I recommend this game, though, is the co-op. If you have a friend who's willing to play through the campaign with you, you will most likely have a great experience. RE6 is one of those rare games that actually emphasizes the cooperative aspect of co-op play by giving each character different strengths and giving the players slightly different roles. Every character is capable of shooting up zombies well enough, but those moments where the players have to come together to solve a little environmental puzzle by vaulting one person up onto a high platform (as just one example) add some much-needed variety to the gameplay. They also serve as a powerful reminder that you have an ally by your side at all times, which is important, because teamwork really does work wonders when you're faced down with overwhelming numbers or some of the scarier enemies in the game.

Is might not be a veteran's idea of the ideal Resident Evil game, but RE6 sure has the potential to be fun as hell if you're willing to give it a chance.

You pick a character you will play their story and you have no other choice than the follow the directions given to you. Which sounds boring but for a co-op game this is the only way the game will work and I am afraid this is the reason for some of the negative reviews.

Still I had a wonderful time playing this game Solo and Co-op and as you can see by my hours played even after finishing the game I still come back to it once in a while since the replayability of the game and the graphics hold up great.
After finishing the story mode there are multiple other multiplayer modes that are more arcade based if you are looking for a quick 10/20 minutes of fun playtime.

At the moment the game is heavily discounted, if you are reading this and there is still a discount available I highly recommend trying it out.

If you take a look at my profile you'll see I'm a big RE fan, though most of my playtime is in Playstation consoles (played the series since the PS1). I love RE. However, I simply cannot recommend this game. As a RE fan, or even as a normal gamer, it doesn't matter. RE6 is just...bad. I don't even know where to begin since pretty much all of it is quite flawed but I'll try my best to give this some structure and explain why I don't think anyone should get this game *except maybe coop players starved for games*

First off, this game isn't entirely without merit. It tries some new things to varying degrees of success. For example, the movement. This game handles differently to 4 and 5. 4 feels kind of floaty to control and 5 feels more grounded. 6 would be the next step in this evolution. For example, they made it possible for you to run into objects and physically "crash" on them or trip over bodies. While I think this is neat and adds to immersion, it can also become pretty annoying quite fast. So I consider this change more of a side grade rather than positive or negative. On that same note, lots of new actions were added like sliding around or dodge rolling, which allow you to maneuver way more than ever before. They're not entirely flawless and can feel pretty janky, but hey at least they work most of the time and serve their purpose.

Now, what about the mechanics/aspects that are indeed negative? Well... I have to talk about the UI first, who in their right mind thought that making the interface for each character different was gonna be cool? It's not, and it can be jarring if you're constantly switching between campaigns and characters but that's the smallest issue of all. It's the actual icons and the inventory itself that are absolutely terrible and one of my major gripes with this game. RE5 had a very simple but very intuitive and fast inventory, as well as potential for higher level play with it. RE6 on the other hand has a very cluttered inventory that is visually unappealing and too distracting. 5's inventory was more ergonomically designed, allowing you for quicker inputs whereas 6's feels clunky and sluggish. It's just a step back unfortunately.

Now here's another issue that is more of a bunch of systems with 1 common flaw: the camera. The camera in this game can be pretty unruly. To point some of these instances, take dashing for example. When you dash in this game, you pretty much can't move the camera at all. Why? Because doing so will make reset its position for no reason, try looking down or up while dashing and it'll start the rebound process. Which is especially aggravating when going up some steps or anything that involves changing elevation (because those make it bounce naturally already). Dashing by itself already feels bad considering there's severe understeer but with this annoying camera "feature", it gets really annoying. Another time when the camera can royally screw you over is when the game decides to show you "this event is happening, look at it!". So what does the game do? It takes total control of the camera over you, often times mid fight! So there you are trying to make sense of what's happening while getting your centre of attention elsewhere, often times not even on the enemies you're supposed to be fighting. What's even funnier is that aiming during these forced cameras makes it return to normal, but only while aiming. Games taking control away from you in such an intrusive and random way is a problem that in this day and age shouldn't be a thing, but it seems like this focus on "cinematic pieces" rather than actual gameplay and player input are even more common now. There's even some instances where you're viewing a cutscene and immediately after it's over you've been grabbed or attacked by an enemy that wasn't even there before. Don't know if that's a bug but it's certainly annoying, especially when playing in the higher difficulties where your health gets deleted by these cheap moves. Also speaking of these, there's plenty of times where the game autoaims for you after opening a door or watching the characters interact. Why? Does the game think players are too stupid to ADS for themselves? Sometimes there's no immediate threat yet the game still aims for you for a couple of seconds (without letting you do anything else).

Lets take cover shooting, since it's also affected by this in a sense. In this game you take cover automatically *sometimes*. Other times it doesn't. I have no idea what makes it apply auto cover since in previous games, there would be context sensitive button prompts to take cover, which makes sense and isn't intrusive or disrupting to the gameplay. But this game doesn't have such logic (RE6 even has those prompts, yet it still included an autocover!). It feels poorly implemented like most of the game, and it just pains me to see and experience considering all they had to do was keep the mechanics the same as previous games. To add insult to injury, I had times where my laser and the dot were lined up on enemies while shooting from cover...then as I fire I notice I'm actually hitting the cover. One time, this hitbox was literally on thin air. I had a clear shot, yet pieces of rubble fell from an invisible extension of a wall rather than blood pouring from the enemy's bullet wounds. Did they even playtest this game?

I guess they didn't because the game is buggy. During Jake's campaign, there's a section where you get chased by a tank. Yet the second the cutscene ends you get squished. No matter which keys or direction of thumbstick you use, you die. Probably because you don't get any input at all, the moment the cutscene ends you die. Look it up if you don't believe me, hell the friend I was playing with even stayed behind on purpose without pressing anything yet I still got killed. We tried many things but what ultimately fixed it was restarting the game, reloading that checkpoint with reversed roles as host and (oddly enough) moving left instead of away from the tank. And no, just pressing left wasn't the solution since I tried that before we restarted the game and I still instadied. We had to quit, reload and switch as well as press something that doesn't even make sense just to get past it. Also had instances where some context sensitive actions don't even show up, causing more resets. Maybe this PC version is buggier but that's still no excuse.

Now to end on a positive, I have to say the melee system is actually pretty fun. And overpowered! Honestly, you're better off using melee attacks than guns most of the time. Guns feel like they tickle enemies whereas melee staggers them and lets you finish them in one combo quite often. Probably dependent on difficulties (we played on Veteran) but this just highlights yet another problem with the game. Guns feel less viable than melee, on a third person shooter lol. As a related side note, there's many sections in the game where the whole camera/world shake tremendously and it makes precise aiming unnecessarily more annoying. The worst is when you're trying to snipe during these, because scope sway is already quite high so it's a nightmare.

This didn't even touch on the absolutely nonsensical story, or how Michael Bay-ish the game is where things explode for literally no reason every 10 seconds, or how each chapter long overstays its welcome and ends up feeling repetitive and tedious (the gimmicks that would be cool if they lasted 5 minutes, instead last triple that). I wanted to focus more on the gameplay side of things because I can't stress this enough, the game just doesn't feel good to control or play. It had some neat ideas, but it bit way more than it could chew and instead of delivering a fun, tight experience like most other games in the series it ended up a mess in every single aspect. I played this when it came out way back and didn't really enjoy it. Now that I got it again and tried giving it another shot, it feels even worse.

For a game that the community has dubbed "the franchise killer" this is a shockingly solid game.

Let's get the boring stuff out of the way: Yes this is as far removed from original Resident Evil mechanics as you can get. No this game isn't even remotely scary and no this game isn't going to win any awards or beat out the old, beloved games that we all know and adore.

Got it all out? Great let's keep moving.

This game has an incredible amount of content and passion put into it. 4 long and complex campaigns with a star roster of Resident Evil characters ranging from Leon to Chris to Sherry and even Ada, all while throwing in some new faces that helps spice things up.

The game is just a joy to play with it's incredible combat and varied enemy types. While the game is far removed from it's survival horror roots it is still very much Resident Evil. It has all the insanity that you come to expect from a title in this genre what with it's grotesque monster designs, wild explosive weapons and out of this world insane cutscenes and stunts that will make you go "How the ♥♥♥♥ is any of these characters still alive and breathing!?"

It was the same deal in Resident Evil 5 and it was the same deal in Resident Evil 4. Even in 4 which, to many, is considered the best entry to the series has some really insane and wacky stuff you wouldn't see from it's Playstation 1 origins.

The series soon came around with Resident Evil 7 and it's return to survival horror but even that entry has some insanity thrown into the mix.

What I'm trying to get at here is that it's unfair to say that Resident Evil 6 is a bad game because it's more action oriented compared to it's predecessors because even the older games had that same flair of crazy action horror. Resident Evil 6 just steps it up a notch by throwing in some fun combat and shooting mechanics that leaves you curious how far you can stretch it's mechanics for the joy of taking down monsters in an almost Devil May Cry like fashion.

The story itself is also fairly deep and you can tell Capcom was passionate about creating a complex and intertwining story. At key moments in the 4 campaigns the characters collide and it's fun to explore the different campaigns perspectives for the overall narrative and how it all ties together at the end.

Finally it's coop allows you to experience this joy ride alongside a friend while you laugh at it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazyness. It will never live up to it's predecessors but it doesn't have to. Resident Evil 6 stands on it's own and if you can accept that it's not a survival horror then you got a really great Resident Evil worthy experience on your hands.

Oh and give Mercenary mode a try while you're at it. I'd argue it's the best entry of Mercenary we have seen in the franchise so far.

The Resident Evil series is knowingly a long-running franchise and it's still relevant due to the way it keeps reinventing itself, often to controversial results.

One of these reinventions was the series actionized escalation, which started becomeing evident in RE4 and reached its apex here in Resident Evil 6, before critical mass'ing and returning to its pure horror roots in RE7.

Resident Evil 6 is divided into 4 scenarios, each with different characters, parallel stories that connect and different playstyles.
- Leon and Helena have a more classically-bent, RE4 inspired campaign facing mostly zombies.
- Chris and Piers have a very actionized story facing against the more intelligent J'avos, infected "half-zombies".
- Jake and Sherry also follow an action-heavy story that has elements of a Mr. X / Nemesis like entity thoughout the plot.
- Ada goes back to a more puzzle-focused campaign that is reminiscent of older titles.

All in all, I really enjoyed this game. The action scenes, plot and sheer impressive moments are incredible, and voice acting is top-notch delivered by greats such as Matthew Mercer, Laura Bailey, Roger C. Smith and Troy Baker.

It may not be the best one in the series and too actionized for fans of the classical survival-horror titles, but RE6 is a very fine all action game with horror aesthetics.

[b]Disclaimer [/b]: Although it says I've played over 36 hours of this game, there's a chunk of it that was just spent with me AFK. This review was also posted as of finishing the campaigns of Leon (veteran & professional difficulty), Chris (veteran difficulty), and Jake (veteran difficulty). I just started Ada's campaign on veteran and I'm almost frustrated enough to uninstall rather than finish it.

[b]Pros:[/b]
+ Four separate campaigns, each with several difficulty levels, that provide plenty of play time, provided you're not frustrated by the cons that I'll be mentioning below.
+ Leon's campaign is very reminiscent of older Resident Evil games, since you've got traditional RE zombies in there. The nostalgia kinda falls off once the action and story just get ridiculous, like [spoiler] fighting the big bad of Leon's campaign who transforms into a zombie centaur,  then a zombie dinosaur, and then a Godzilla-sized zombie fly. [/spoiler] The early parts of his campaign do have a nice horror feel to it, though. I definitely enjoyed that.
+ Somewhat decent AI partner if you decide to play single-player. It's not great, but not terrible either.
+ Wide selection of weapons to use, ranging from pistols to shotties, automatics, explosives, and more.
+ Skill system that encourages replaying the game to unlock more skills.

[b]Cons:[/b]
- The camera angles can be a worse enemy than bosses or even regular enemies and turns even mundane fights into a struggle; it feels like they took the worst parts of the original RE camera angles and slapped it onto RE4's over-the-shoulder tank controls, so suddenly switching from over-the-shoulder to fixed camera angles throws off your direction/movement flow. It's janky as hell.
- Very limited inventory space; it's hard to hold more than one stack of each ammo and throwable type together with herbs and first aid sprays.
- Too many quick-time events. It's easy to tell that the game isn't modern at all based on the sheer number of QTEs the game throws at you. It's also incredibly frustrating when failing a QTE just instantly results in a mild case of death. Combined with the janky controls and bad camera angles, it's sometimes already a challenge just to start the QTE, then a horror story when you actually have to punch in all those QTEs once they've started.
- The camera angles are just so bad.
- Story-wise, [spoiler] the whole background can be summed up as "guy gets too horny for some woman in red and starts a bioterrorism crisis." [/spoiler] The RE franchise's story is generally cheesy, but this one's less cheesy and more just bad. It even gets to the point that the big bad goes on a full mustache-twirling let-me-tell-you-what-evil-things-I've-done monologue at some point.
- Dying multiple times to a forced POV/camera angle switch isn't fun at all.
- Not a fan of how hitting Esc to open the menu in single-player mode doesn't pause the game at all. You have to press the dedicated pause button to do that, and you can't access the menu to change up any settings while the game's paused. When a zone was too dark and I needed to brighten it up a bit, I had to raise the brightness while hiding behind cover, only to get killed by an ambush.
- The game isn't well-optimized for PC. I'm a bit over the minimum requirements and running everything on the lowest graphics settings, yet I'm seeing sudden framerate drops on occasion that turn it into a slideshow or just outright freeze the screen for a moment and result in me dying/failing the objective. The same goes for cutscenes; most of them end up have desynchronized audio and video, with the cutscene stuttering for a moment and the audio lagging behind once it resumes.
- Did I mention how much I dislike or even outright hate the forced camera angles?
- Considering how long ago this game was released, I didn't have any expectations for online multiplayer. Tried it out anyway and it's pretty much dead. If you're really looking for a proper multiplayer experience with this, bring a friend along with you. Public lobbies/matchmaking isn't happening here.
- Speaking of multiplayer, game modes like Siege are locked behind DLC. On top of buying the game, you gotta pay for that feature too.
- To whoever decided to put forced camera angles and janky tank controls together, who hurt you so badly that you had to take it out on everyone who decided to play this game? After playing this, I'm glad camera angles and controls got overhauled for the Resident Evil 2 remake.

Not since the Wii eras shovelware have I experienced a game this poor. I was dead set on playing all of the RE games, but I can't stand a game which makes me feel physically ill after a 1 hour session.

This is where the series finally took the jump in the chaotic, filthy cesspit of over-the-top, dumb action, taking all of the bad things that characterizes what I like to call the "AI Trilogy": RE4-5-6, three games in which you're stuck with a dumb AI companion that hinders more than it helps you. Now, I agree that RE4 was a good turn for the series and it has its iconic moments but it set a very bad trend for the series with a focus on action that doesn't always work right. I enjoyed RE4 because it tried something new while keeping some of the classic DNA. It did just enough to be fun without being ridiculously frustrating. RE5 was an annnoying but decent experience with its moments and I respect the bold decision to make a RE game set during daytime. RE6, though, was an exercise in frustration with a pacing that's constantly crippled by scripted events and QTEs. 

RE6 tried to be that epic blockbusters that brings well-known heroes of the RE universe in an epic multi-layered fight to save the world, much like most Hollywood action movies with shared universes. In Capcom's mind, it meant explosions and self-destruct sequences, tense chase scenes and incredibly tough bosses who only drag the fight on for the sake of spectacle. You could argue it would work for an actual action movie but even so, a good action movie doesn't drag things for too long. And RE6 likes to overstay its welcome with pathetic attempts at padding with QTEs you barely have any time to react to and that kills you instantly. These doesn't serve the game at all, it's just an half-assed attempt to keep players on their toes, not because of surprise attacks from monsters but because at aty time the game might plop you in front of the jaws of some annoying trap that will immediately kill you should you fail to press the buttons quick enough.

This game should be called "RE6: Wigglesticks" because wiggling the joystick and mashing buttons is what you do the most often in this game, wheter it's to shake off an enemy or avoiding a cheap death trap. QTE to avoid a blade sticking out of the wall, QTE to not get your head stuck in a grinder because of a monster popping out of nowhere, QTE for this, QTE for that. Even combat has QTEs to kill or push a zombie who grabbed you, this I could forgive more easily, but the rest are just scripted ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that just slow the game.

And you have four bad campaigns to get through, three of which must be completed to unlock the fourth one and they're all mostly forgettable. Leon's campaign is supposed to be the most "survival horror" of the four but this is where you get most of the annoying QTEs and insta-kill traps. Chris' campaign turns the game into a cover-shooter with most setpieces being shooting gallery that has you fight gun-toting terrorists that can mutate into half-monster creatures. And Jake's campaign is the most laughable of all, it puts you up against a gimmicky monstrosity called the Ustanak, who's basically a discount Nemesis. Between uninspired boss fights and chase scenes, you have a dumb stealth section in which you have to avoid some kind of insects who warns the Ustanak of your presence and you get insta-killed if you don't hide before he gets you. Finally, you get Ada's campaign, which is a subpar attempt at stealth, putting you in tight corridors where you have to takedown enemies to avoid alerting everyone around and getting overwhelmed. These four campaigns are easily the weakest part of the game and they're a proof that quantity over quality is no way to make a memorable experience.

As for the story well, it makes no sense, as expected. With each new game since RE4, the series jumped the shark to ridiculous extent. Here you have a virus that has little to no explanation and only seems to infect anyone who doesn't wear plot armor and the games enjoyes cliché'd tropes way too much, like the big tough hero Chris turning in an alcoholic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because his men died during a mission or Helena trying to reason with a too-far-gone, mutated sister or the bad guy Simmons going on about bringing order to the world through viral warfare. The game is shock-full of bad clichés and predictable twists without even the slightest attempt at surprising the player. If this was a bad Hollywood action movie, nobody would bat an eye but unfortunately, this is a bad action movie you have to PLAY.

Sadly, the most fun I've had with the game is its Mercenaries mode, in which the game's combat truly shines. Unlike the main campaigns, here you actually need to use all kinds of combat moves and strategies to stay on top since you can't rely on an AI partner to save your butt once you go down. You can use slides, tackles and follow-ups to bring enmies down and you have to prioritizes threats to avoid taking an attack that can damage you hard or worse, insta-kill you. You can unlock characters and costumes through playing the mode and it'll keep you busy in a much more satisfying way that the campaign ever will. To be honest, Mercenaries should have been the whole game; a spin-off title with heavy focus on action, pulling monsters and stages from the entire RE universe, a bit like Mercenaries 3D on 3DS did but with much better technology and more content. 

And this might be the reason I would recommend getting this game on sale for a low-low price because the best part of RE6 is an extra mode where the action focus actually works. But even so, there are other action games that might scratch that shooting gallery itch a lot more for the price, even though, in my opinion, the "shoot-enemy > Follow-up attack" of post-4 Resident Evil games is so satisfying. If you really want to get this, keep your expectations very, very low for the campaigns and don't expect anything groundbreaking for the Mercenaries mode. As far as Resident Evil games go, its overall mediocrity is only outdone by the likes of Operation Raccoon City and Revelations 2.

Resident Evil 6 Review

Racoon seems like a walk in the part…

Some key points that this game offers:

1.	Four different campaigns
2.	Co-op play
3.	New C-Virus
4.	New enemy types
5.	Mercenary mode
6.	Skill point system

Gameplay & Controls:

Less Horror Survival, unfortunately, but a whole lot more Action has been packed into RE6.
The game handles and plays pretty smoothly, they upgraded the game controls immensely, we no longer have the Tank controls we have come to love and hate over the years. Now we can shoot and move as we go about our way. Adding to the heavily updated controls is sprinting, dashing, and combat role in any direction. Dash and slide your way towards victory, or take a heroic stand armed with all new melee moves and lay the hurting down on the new hordes that are bent on devouring you.

The game is more action shooter oriented now, there is also a feature where you can take cover against objects and even change the shoulder view of your character, however, as fun as the game is here, it lacks a lot that any shooter should have. With RE6 a lot of the RE essence is lost and abandoned, however, the new mechanics there is fun to be had, but it’s nothing special or spectacular.

The game features four campaigns, starting with Leon and his partner Helena caught in the middle of a conspiracy and a new Zombie Outbreak. There is Chris and his partner Piers who is taking on the new C-Virus type zombies. Then we have Jake and Sherry who are in all kinds of trouble and last but not least we have Ada in her own solo campaign. Each story arch is unique with unique gameplay and occurrences but they all tie into each other towards the end. 

You can choose which character to play within his arch, and each character has some unique weapons, for example, Helena has the Hydra shotgun and Piers with the Anti-Material Rifle. Each campaign has its own theme and atmosphere, Leon and Ada’s are the only ones that have some real survival horror in them, Chris’s campaign is more running and shooting which was quite a let-down. Jake and Sherry’s campaign are a bit of a confusing mess, never knowing what’s really going on. 
The inventory screen has been updated as well, it’s larger and you can carry more items, however, but at the cost of the item box. There is no longer a box where you can store additional items or weapons. Each character has all their weapons and items on them. The shop is also no longer present and you can’t upgrade weapons either. 

However, the new skill point system makes up for that. As you play and complete levels you earn skill points, enemies also drop skill points. As you progress through the game you unlock skills that you can purchase and upgrade. These range from increased weapon damage, to picking up more ammo or increased damage against an enemy type. There are a variety of skills that can be purchased and some that can also be upgraded. Unlimited ammo can also be acquired once all the campaigns have been completed. 

Graphics:

One of the things they got very right! The game is absolutely beautiful! From Leon’s leather jacket shiny reflection with the water dripping from it to Ada’s pants showing all her curves as she crawls through those ventilation shafts. The game's lighting adds shadows and has gotten a massive upgrade from RE5.

The game's rendering is incredible, there is so much detail, you often forget to shoot because you got distracted by the beauty that RE6 offers. Every level has been beautifully designed to offer us a visual marvel as you fight for our lives in them. 

Character models are on par with the rest of the visuals. Facial features and expressions are simply amazing. The zombies and other creatures have never looked better than they do now. So much detail and so much in terms of appearance! Everything looks absolutely great. 

Sounds:

As always, a great game isn’t great without a fantastic soundtrack. RE6 has that and it really enhances the overall quality of the game. Coupled with the fabulous background music you are set for an excellent experience.

Whether you are skulking around a frozen mountain top or swimming for your life to get away from a shark, you can be sure that the music is there to back it all up and hype up the occurrence to ensure your adrenaline is pumping. 

Voice over artists did an amazing job here bringing their characters to life. Scripts are great every now and then, but what really makes them stand out is that they tie in facial expressions that accompany them. 

Replayability:

RE games are all about replaying them. RE6 is no different, we have four campaigns waiting on us and when we complete them, then the fun only begins. Upgrade and buy skills to take the game on on a higher difficulty and earn some more skill points to buy some more… Infinity ammo doesn’t come cheap!

Mercenary mode is also back so we have that going for us and then there is already talk of more competitive modes coming soon.

MGR Gaming’s Conclusions:
Spoilers Ahead:

RE6 is fun and great in its own right. It just strayed too far off from what Resident Evil was initially about. Leon and Ada’s campaigns were great, with Ada’s offering quite the challenge being solo and that, but it was a true survival experience. Leon’s wasn’t too far off either. It was dark, it had its scary moments and for a moment it felt like Re again. Chris’s was mostly running and shooting, it was fun but it lacked many shooter mechanics, but it didn’t feel like a RE game at all.

Jakes was an utter mess, as fun as it was, it never really went anywhere, it really felt like Chris and Jake’s campaigns tied in with what we did with Leon and Ada. The experience just wasn’t as fun or entertaining as I would have wanted it to be and I am a massive Chris Redfield fan. He’s my go to zombie slayer, and this was a rather sad disappointment to see and play him here when we had what we did in RE5.

The new mechanics are rather great, they give us a massive improvement in manoeuvrability and a tactical advantage in every fight. I love it, I loved dashing forward propping up, and then round house kicking a zombie seeing three of them take flight. It is quite the experience, but it’s also what makes the game less survival horror and more action oriented, so it did come at a cost.

The story line is brilliant, the conspiracy, the double enemies, and the plot behind the plot. It was very well written and executed beautifully. It took completing most of the game to actually know and understand what was really going on. The different campaigns don’t play off all in the time, some a few months behind the others, so at first, it seems confusing, but the deeper you get the more you realize how well this was implemented. 

As much as I wanted to love this game, I just don’t. Unfortunately, it’s more a Zombie shooter than a resident evil title and that’s what hurts the most here. I agree that all games must evolve and what they started with RE4 was amazing, but they changed it so much that it no longer feels like a Resident Evil game and that is too much…

This game is perhaps one of the most poorly thought out and executed games I have ever played. Capcom has zero idea of who their audience was for this one. They have combined all of the worst parts of all the previous games into a bloated monstrosity. 

The controls are abysmal. The UI and inventory management are the most unintuitive systems I have ever used. The game actively fights you at every turn to merely try to walk along and try to enjoy yourself. It constantly interrupts the action to draw your attention to the thousandth building on fire while you slowly amble along while things are trying to kill you. During one fight there were 4 cutscenes that took control away from you in the span of 20 seconds. It switches to fixed camera angles abruptly but doesn't compensate for the current inputs so you are left spinning in circles or facing the wrong way during difficult or timed encounters. The biggest sin of this game is how much control it takes away from the player. It is more frustrating than enjoyable. RE6 can be used as a guide of what not to do in a game for almost every single design choice.

There is almost no puzzle solving or exploration of any sort in Leon and Chris's campaign (disclaimer: I haven't played the other two yet). You pick up all these weapons that you can barely use because you can't carry much ammo at all and the tablet system for healing is absolutely ridiculous. There is no combining or examining items in the inventory. It feels like they wanted to make an action movie and completely forgot what fans like about the series. None of the weapons feel satisfying to use since non-basic enemies are extreme bullet sponges. I will say the visualization of headshot damage on basic zombies is good.

The writing is atrocious even for the usually cheesy dialogue of the series. The characters are completely out of character and make the worst possible decision at every opportunity. They constantly lament their comrades/civilians who were killed but are causing large scale devastation and collateral damage. Resident Evil 5 looks like a masterpiece next to this game.

The quick time events are perhaps the most annoying ones I have ever encountered in a game. They add nothing. You could be walking down a hallway with a bunch of bodies on the floor. You can't shoot the enemies ahead of time and instead you have to let them grab you and mash buttons while they damage you.

This game completely jumps the shark. There are a bunch of giant, towering enemies that just have no place in the universe. We've switched back to a virus after the parasite in 4 and 5. The virus is airborne yet the characters walk through virus clouds constantly without any effects except when the story makes it dangerous. I'd gladly punch 10 boulders over the stupid set pieces in this game.

I'm happy that Capcom found its way after this complete pile of garbage with 7. A soft reboot was the only way to fix this travesty. I sincerely hope that whoever thought this game was fun and in a state to be released    no longer works in game development.

RE6 has got a bad rap, being savaged pretty hard by both the games media and fans alike at the time of its release. Like all contentious media, it’s had something of a renaissance of defenders in recent years, who claim that it isn’t an awful game at all, merely a poor Resident Evil game. The claim is that its mechanics are poorly explained and understood, and that once mastered there’s an awesome action game hiding underneath. 

Well, for once I’m going to have to join the journalists in laying in the boot. Resident Evil 6 is bad. Resident Evil 6 is staggeringly bad, in that particular, magical way that only comes about when you have a project with too much money, a terrible concept and boneheaded direction. It’s badness is so core to its design that I believe it is entirely unsalvageable.

The issues start with the whole idea of the game – that you have four separate campaigns, each with differing playstyles and focus. Leon has the survival horror campaign. So far so good. Chris’ story is more of a military shooter, newcomer Jake has an Uncharted style adventure (wait, what?) and Ada gets a spy/stealth campaign. Out of these, you may have noticed that only one actually makes any sense for even an action focused RE game, and even if they were all meticulous, tightly designed experiences (spoilers – they’re not) they’re so different that it would be almost impossible to create something cohesive.

While I’m making it sound like the game starts promisingly and tails off (and reviews largely praise Leon’s section), in truth the wheels come off almost immediately. RE6 tries it’s best to craft a tense, moody atmosphere as you make your way through an abandoned university. It then immediately undoes this the moment combat begins and you start suplexing and roundhousing zombies with wild abandon. Sure, you had context sensitive melee options in RE4 and 5 (and they were silly there), but here there’s a dedicated melee button with a stamina meter and everything. RE6 seems to realise that maybe the horror angle isn’t working, and attempts to inject some atmosphere by making the whole game so dark that you can’t see a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing.

It only goes downhill from here. Remember the majini with guns near the end of RE5? Do you remember how those were the worst parts of the game, with a barely functional cover system and controls that just weren’t up to the task of avoiding gunfire? Well now you have a whole campaign of this ♥♥♥♥, and somehow they made the cover system an actual liability. This came out in 2012! How do you screw up a cover system six years after Gears of War? Most of the time it was so unintuitive and inconsistent that it was easier just to stand in the open and take the hits.

The rest of the controls and interface are just as awful. RE4 and 5 definitely had some clunky controls, but the games were designed around those limitations. Now you have a lot more freedom, but the controls are skittish and imprecise, though you can now move and aim which is a welcome change. And the inventory is just bafflingly bad. RE4 had the awesome attaché case, that was simplified for the co-op focus in RE5 (which was much less fun, but somewhat understandable and there were some improvements like much easier weapon switching). RE6 gives you a million guns, and you need to go through them one at a time to find the one you want. RE5 allowed you to set them on the D pad, and this worked absolutely fine – why change this? There’s also the herb system – now you have to combine them before use, to put them in a medicine case which you can use to fill up your health blocks one at a time. Why? The herb system was intuitive and functional, and basically unchanged in the 16 years Resident Evil had been a thing.

But really, it’s the level and encounter design where the wasting virus afflicting the whole game really takes hold. RE6’s inability to decide on what type of game it is means that none of the systems have had the time or focus they need and they all come off as sloppy and amateurish. You have cover shooting. You have driving (with several types of dreadful vehicle). You have QTEs. You have a melee combo system. You have barely functional stealth. You are wrenched from setpiece to exhausting setpiece, with no downtime or pace breakers. Even the core combat manages to make killing enemies as annoying as possible. In RE4 and 5, sometimes killing an enemy would mean the Ganado/Majini would pop out of the neck and try to give you a faceful of parasitic wing wong. Here the enemies mutate when shot in any body location most of the time, making all enemies tedious sponges. This is exacerbated by the lack of ammo, particularly in Chris’ campaign. It seems like a sick joke to turn RE into a cover shooter, then neglect to give you ammo. Both RE4 and RE5 expected you to play carefully and tactically, but RE6 is just too hectic and far too often you’re forced into using the ludicrous melee system while trying to avoid snipers.

The bosses really do represent the worst of RE6’s sins, and they are basically all a confusing chore to fight. As an example, in Ada’s campaign you have to fight a mutant chainsaw boss. The instructions are “kill the mutant chainsaw boss”. Of course what you in fact should do is avoid the boss for two minutes so that a scripted cutscene plays, and he’s basically invincible despite your weapons appearing to damage him. You have fought and damaged this guy before in previous campaigns. All the bosses are like this – you mostly have no idea whether you’re damaging them, whether it’s a scripted sequence or whether a random QTE will kill you instantly. 

As a last feeble kick into this well beaten horse, the story in RE6 is of course bollocks. It got a lot of flak in reviews, but in truth it’s honestly no better or worse than the laughable efforts in previous games. The voice acting is a step up, but the writing is leaden and self-serious which makes it easy to mock. The problem is that RE6 seem to think you’re very invested, and subjects you to endless, sometimes unskippable cutscenes. They’re terrible, of course, but are honestly welcome relief from actually playing the thing. 

So is there anything I actually enjoyed in RE6? Well yes, but it basically amounts to “laughing at it with a friend”. On your own it’s a miserable, frustrating experience that there is zero chance I would have finished. With a buddy you boggle at the terrible design together, the videogame equivalent of getting pizza, beer and jeering at Troll 2. As a warning Ada’s campaign (meant to be played last) can technically be played co-op, but was clearly not designed for it (player two gets to be “some guy” and can’t interact with the world at all, and co-op was added after the fact as a throwaway zero-effort update).

Probably RE6’s biggest achievement is it’s colossal failure. Without RE6’s critical and commercial mauling, we likely never would have got the recent Resident Evil renaissance. It was clear that the Hollywood blockbuster RE was a dead end, and it was time to return to the slower, horror focused roots of the series and for that at least RE6 feels like a necessary failure.

As somebody who is not a long-time Resident Evil fan, I´m comfortable to make the following statement, after finishing RE 2 Remastered and finishing RE 6 Chapter 1:
Resident Evil is... evolving.
Like Assassin´s Creed, they are taking out the boring stuff and leaving only what really matters. (in AC, I never liked to lose a mission merely by being spotted; they took that away and it got so much better - my opinion)
In RE 2 Remastered, there was a lot of secrets, hidden things, annoying puzzles, a humongous amount of backtracking. So, more often than not, I was forced to look into the internet for walkthroughs, hints, etc. The remastered game was gorgeous to look at, but the hindrances and time-consuming little tasks and mini-quests took away from the experience.
And this is the word: experience.
Resident Evil 6 is waaay more straighforward. You have somewhere to go, you know the general direction you must go,  you have to free yourself from grappling zombies by means of manageable quicktime events, deal with zombies by shooting them (of course) or barehanded beat them, open doors, jump fences, climb stairs... nothing too fancy or mysterious. Even when a key is needed to open a door, the key is nearby. 
So you must just... go on, and keep going.
So you can really focus on and feel the experience of fighting for your life in a zombie hellish mayhem, a dark, confusing, chaotic, flaming nightmare, beautifully rendered, as the story progresses at every checkpoint. This games really provides you the experience of being in a zombie apocalypse. Nothing more, nothing less.

To start this off this was the last of all of the mainline Resident Evil games I played. Many of the games in the series are up there with some of my favourite games of all time. I came into this game expecting a game in the vein of Resident Evil 5 but attempting to cater more to the action crowd with a bit more of an action centric game. It was much worse than what I came to expect. I went in with middling expectations and came out having played a game that I can easily list with the worst games I've ever played.

Cons:
- Playing the same segments multiple times to pad out content because "two characters were there"
- Weapon accuracy is all over the place due to the erratic laser pointers
- The movement controls. Getting characters to accurately move to where you want to go is so much harder than it should be and makes for a frustrating experience trying to interact with things.
- The map design is occasionally so unreadable there had to be a button to point the player in the right direction.
- Almost everything in the game stun locks you constantly taking control away from the player 24/7 which is incredibly frustrating.
- Almost the entire game is non stop action with tedious enemies that weren't fun to fight without any breaks.
- A lot of the story threads in the game went nowhere and there were some laughably bad moments thrown in there. Chris' story was somewhat interesting but the military focus lead to the majority of the gameplay feeling incredibly generic and tedious.
- The coop. It might as well not exist. If you need to do something in coop it usually involves both players doing the same puzzle individually or being an assistant to killing enemies. (In the 4th campaign your coop partner can't even interact with the world)
- The inventory system. Seeing as the game made the effort of streamlining it out I'm not sure why it still exists just to mix herbs. Having it there just to have to fumble with the single row inventory during the hectic combat scenes does not work well.
- Constant quick time events for everything you do doesn't make for engaging game play. The analogue wobble ones are just ridiculous.
- The in game menu's were a bit of a mess mainly due to the fact all of the options were only icons so many of the options require you to scan over them to know what they are.
- The camera is thrown to different locations quite often making playing those sections even more difficult along with the dodgy movement systems. A lot of the times they'll just get you killed.
- The game occasionally changes the aiming methods of your character from keeping the crosshair in the centre to moving the crosshair around the screen. Why?
- Everything that made Resident Evil what it was is gone in this game.

Pros:
- There are a few decent story cut scenes.
- There were a couple of basic puzzles in two of the campaigns which were alright.
- The attempt at interweaving story lines was an interesting idea and  it was cool to see an alternate story line playing in the background of a few segments.
- The character models look pretty good graphically for the time it came out.
- The dive mechanic is pretty fun.
- It can be so ridiculous at times that it can crack you up

This game is a huge disappointment.

The main story is split up into multiple campaigns for several pairs of characters, they each have a distinct style of gameplay but none of them allow you to enjoy this core gameplay for any stretch of time due to how handhold-y and linear the story is.
Resident Evil 6's story is very poorly paced, dragging along while never really giving any sense of tension or excitement, even when compared to Resident Evil 5's story which could be considered fairly simplistic manages to be more engaging than this. While the two games before it made some use of QTE button prompts within some cutscenes, this game forces them on you excessively during both cutscenes and during normal gameplay.

Many of the primary locations featured in the story give off the vibe of the back streets in a GTA game that the developers never chose to stage any missions, where the windows are flat jpegs and there's zero atmosphere, interactivity, or hidden detail.  Each campaign is very linear, despite the length at which new rooms are blasted through and left behind to be forgotten forever, the experience still feels as though it lasts a hundred years.
The inventory management has been simplified to a linear list of weapons and items, with a different counter being visible for the number of heals available. My only guess as to why this change would be deemed necessary is that it allows for multiple D-Pad taps in one direction to provide you with complete control over your inventory, while this allows you to switch your gear around while staying in the action, the same advantages are provided by RE5's 3x3 square grid inventory which allowed for both numpad support and D-Pad.
Rather than implementing something similar to the upgrade system from RE4 and RE5 which was well liked, players now have to choose three perks to bring into each story mission, which feels very shallow by comparison as you might expect.

The new flashy movement techniques and attacks that the player can pull off such as sliding on the while firing two weapons,  rolling around on the ground, or grabbing enemy weapons mid-swing give the combat a feel that is very distinct from the rest of the series, maybe character action fans would appreciate it in the context of this mode.

Unlike its predecessor, The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt doesn't exactly come screaming off the starting line. Compared to The Witcher 2, where you're immediately plunged headlong into a sexy story of intrigue and betrayal, this main quest can seem mundane, even perfunctory at times. But each time I stepped off the well-beaten path to blaze my own trail, it turned into a wild, open, exhilarating fantasy roleplaying experience, rife with opportunities to make use of its excellent combat. Even after over 100 hours with The Witcher 3, it still tempts me to press on – there’s so much more I want to learn, and hunt.


The Witcher 3 is as dense and deep as the other two games in the series in terms of RPG mechanics, and the overwhelmingly massive open-world environment has at once made that depth more intimidating, and in the long run, more rewarding. It’s difficult to express just how huge and open this world is: verdant, rolling fields liberally dotted with swaying foliage of every shape and size fill the space between loosely connected, ramshackle townships where people struggle to scrape by. A full day/night cycle and dynamic weather pull it all together, cementing The Witcher 3’s landscape as one of the most authentic-feeling open worlds I’ve ever seen. A handy minimap points you where you want to go, which might seem like a crutch, but honestly, without it, I’d have been hopelessly lost. That a world this size still feels so purposeful, and full of things to do is quite an achievement.

The one caveat on all that though, is the technical performance on the PS4 version I played for review. 30 frames per second was sometimes too much to ask, transitions between The Witcher 3’s two main maps are just a bit too long, and minor glitches do pop up from time to time. None of it ever impacted gameplay in any meaningful way, thought it did compromise the beauty of the experience ever so slightly.

This new open-world map obviously has ramifications for the structure of the story, and though there are flashes of greatness, the main story is ultimately the least fulfilling part of The Witcher 3. You might call it another case of The Elder Scrolls Syndrome. Our tale begins as a multi-continent search for Geralt’s long-lost lover Yennifer, and Ciri, his surrogate daughter. My single biggest issue though, is that it never becomes much more: the overly long main story is essentially just Geralt running errands for people in exchange for information on Ciri’s whereabouts. It effectively maintains focus and momentum, but it feels more like a wild goose chase than an intriguing mystery to unravel, like the one we got in Assassins of Kings.

Thanks to lots of excellent dialogue and voice acting there is some emotional payoff along the way, but it’s mixed in with too much padding in the form of meaningless fetch quests and collectathons. Every time I felt like I was on the verge of an interesting revelation, I’d have to suddenly stop to escort a goat, or search for a lost, narcoleptic dwarf. Heck, even Geralt can barely hide his frustration with the constant parade of menial tasks at times.

It’s also worth noting that though you will get along fine without playing the first two games in the series, without the context provided by the Witcher novels, Ciri is more or less a complete stranger until the last quarter of the journey, which made it difficult to care about finding her as much as The Witcher 3 expected me to – especially given the slew of intriguing characters who are relegated to supportive background roles.


Thankfully, they all get chances to shine once you venture off the beaten path, and that’s where The Witcher 3 gets nearly everything incredibly right. Depending on your decisions in The Witcher 2 (which can be handily recreated via some dialogue early in the game), you’ll see lots of familiar faces returning to play a role in Geralt’s search, and once they have, they offer you a secondary line of quests that typically provide far more interesting scenarios to dabble in. Underground turf wars, assassination plots, love triangles, and unexpected alliances are all part of these optional romps. They’re all so meaty and full of rich story content that they feel like they should have been part of the main story.

The same can be said for a lot of the side quests you pick up in the field as well. Aside from the bevy of standard side-quests, monster lairs, and bandit camps generously littered about The Witcher 3’s gargantuan land mass, you also get a bunch of monster-hunting Witcher contracts to persue. Geralt's quarry ranges from ethereal wraiths that need to be made tangible before you can harm them, to Foglets who conceal themselves in thick smog, waiting for a chance to strike. The payoff here is twofold: in keeping with the lore, these represent your most reliable stream of income, which is refreshingly significant due to an appropriately stingy in-game economy.

The other upside is that, more often than not, these hunts and other side activities provide interesting insights into a land being destroyed by war, and the many forces that play a role in shaping it. Best of all, you’re one of those forces. It may not shift the main story’s conclusion in monumental ways, but I often returned to places I’d visited earlier to find that a seemingly small decision played out in a very big way. There is no morality meter, no paragon or renegade rating. In the grayscale world of The Witcher 3, there is only cause and effect; the decisions you make, both big and small, can legitimately change the world around you – far more so than most games that make similar claims.

Character progression and equipment choices are equally impactful. Relative to The Witcher 2, I found that Witcher 3’s RPG systems have been streamlined in some ways, and made more complex in others. In both cases though, the result is the same: a better experience. Simplifications to how you restock and use potions and oils makes them feel more practical and immediately useful, as you no longer need to meditate to do any of it. Sure, the old way was more in keeping with Witcher lore, but in a wide open world, it makes less sense to expect players to predict and prepare for everything they might come across in advance. On the flip side, there’s a wider variety of powerful, interesting potions than ever, including those that greatly enhance mounted combat, and others that restore health as you cast spells (or Signs as Witchers call them).


Speaking of Signs, they’ve been improved across the board with alternate casting modes, and a wider variety of upgrades, making them impactful in every fight. It’s actually entirely viable to build a sign-focused Geralt. I played him a lot like a Jedi actually, able to influence people’s minds in conversation, a powerful long range “force” push, and the ability to reflect crossbow bolts back to the sender (a returning ability that’s been made far more usable). The new skill system provides a good deal of flexibility while still rewarding players who want min/max for the best builds, and weapon and armor crafting is as deep and nuanced as ever, if not more so.

All of this shines through in The Witcher 3’s responsive, brutal real-time combat. Where combat in this series has up until this point felt vague and even a bit clunky, here it’s so fluid and satisfying that I walk around hoping for bandits to jump me just so I can repel their attacks with magical barriers, parry their blows with uncanny precision, and relieve them of life and/or limb with the occasional gory flourish. Game Mechanics & Ideas:

I would still say that RE5 inventory was better in a way though RE6 inventory does have some better things than RE5's inventory. 

Graphics: 
The graphics are very nice & detailed. They did NOT put a filter that removes away the true colours which is a good idea because they kind of made everything darker and balanced it with lightning visual effects. The visuals & mapping design is very creative & it can easily be said that they put in a lot of effort which is why you don't see a lot of RE6 modded stages simply because it won't be easy modding these type of stages. For me, I really liked it as it seemed to have a unique theme for the RE franchise. The glow, colour saturation, details, shadows, lighting, environments (Ground/Tunnels/Inside/outside/Houses/Sewage), are all PERFECTLY well made!

CONS:
- Game uses microphone & finding the option to disable it is very complicated for some people.
- Accessing the inventory can cause you to slow down or sometimes disable your character's movement.  
- Regular Mercenaries has too little enemies & it's very boring to play.

- The inventory for some of the characters in No Mercy Mercenaries is very badly put & it doesn't fit the style or theme of this game at all.

The game has several campaigns that all try to do something different and as a result they rarely succeed.
[list]
[*] Leon's campaign tries to recreate the "horror" feeling of the older games so of course the game is going to start with an action set piece with QTEs and explosions all over. After that the actual campaign felt a lot more like a third person Left 4 Dead than anything else. The gameplay just isn't tuned for this kind of atmosphere so as a result there never really is any tension and everything feels flat.

[*] Chris' campaign is an action shooter and it's probably what the game is the most competent at. Now that's where the "not a real Resident Evil game" thing probably comes from, most enemies will use machine guns and other kind of weaponry so it really feels like you're just fighting generic army dudes. This is also where people defending the game will tell you that "RE4 did it too" but anyone who played RE4 will tell you that the island (where gun wielding enemies appear) is the weakest part of this game. One thing I'll give the game credit for here is that the J'avo are actually interesting enemies, they basically develop mutations depending on where you shoot them so they might get a shield or jumping abilities when you fight them. Piers is also a really good character, it's a shame they decided to butcher Chris.

[*] [strike]Sherry's[/strike] Jake's campaign has you running away from discount Nemesis with stealth sequences and the worst vehicular sections of the game. They tried to put the focus on hand-to-hand combat in this one but the game still feels so clunky to play it's never really enjoyable.

[*] Ada's is a spy simulator, with puzzles reminiscent of the older games. Don't try to play that one on co-op or the second player will have to play as Ada's imaginary friend who can't do anything. This campaign tries tie the entire story together and at that point that will be the only reason you'll still be playing this.
[/list]

Now to come back to the whole "not a real Resident Evil game" thing, I do agree that it's not a good argument against the game. RE has changed so much through the years that what constitutes a "true RE game" is going to be different for everyone. That being said this game is obviously a lot more action focused than other titles (with Michael Bay explosions and the like).

My personal recommendation would be to just play 4, 5 or the Revelations titles if you want a good action oriented Resident Evil or something like Binary Domain if you're just looking for a good third person shooter and if you care about the story just watch a stream or something so you don't have to suffer through the gameplay yourself.

Let me get this straight: the amount of satisfaction you'll get directly depends on the expectations you set. If you are expecting a classic Resi1-3 survival-horror experience then you are going to be very disappointed. However, if you liked the more action-oriented Resi4 and 5 and you're into a more linear "Uncharted in the Resi universe" adventure then you'll have a lot of fun here!

First of all, the combat is quite fun and it's much faster than in previous titles. You can now move while aiming (omg, right?). But wait, there's more! A lot of people don't even notice this, but you can make all sorts of cool tricks and dodge-moves Max Payne/The Matrix-style. Run into an enemy and jump-kick him down! Dodge out of harm's way and continue shooting on the ground! It's all crazy, stylish fun!

As for the plot, I actually liked it. Again, it all depends on your expectations. You should never take the plot in a Resi game too seriously (this is Capcom, expect some cheese!). So, if you enjoy a B-move or an 80's/90's action movie, then you're likely to enjoy this game as well. And I really liked how the scenarios of all the characters interconnected throughout the four campaigns.

And last, but not least. If it wasn't for this game, then we wouldn't have Resi7 as we know it. The initial outcry and negative reception of the core fan-base to Capcom's attempt to broaden its user-base by taking it into a more action-driven direction were what later forced them to rethink their approach and take the series back to its Survival Horror roots.

And look at the reviews now! It's "mostly positive" on Steam! So, I guess, now it's a cult classic!

P.S. Capcom also fixed a lot of issues that plagued the initial release like adding FOV-sliders, camera/HUD customization, so they deserve some respect for at least listening.

After many years of ignoring this game and after some recent favorable reviews i've decided to give it a try. I cannot believe how bad Resident Evil 6 really is. Ever since 5 the series went through a big decline. Everything both reviewers and fans said back in 2012 still holds true, this game is HORRIBLE. Both RE 5 and Revelations were dissappointing in the sense that they weren't real RE games but at least those games were fun to play, Resident Evil 6 is a huge pile of ♥♥♥♥♥ of a game.

Before i get into the bad stuff here are some improvements. You've got zombies that act like zombies (sort of) in Leon's campaign, it also has some puzzles that were okay at best, your A.I. partner doesn't die nor depend on you to survive and the game actually feels different and not just another RE 4 reskin and yeah that's it.

RE 6 has 4 campaigns and each of them tries to please a different audience.

Leon = action horror
Chris = action military shooter
Jake = melee combat
Ada = stealth combat

The problem is that all of them suck and ends up with a game that pleases nobody. 

Now, as expected, the game is not scary, not in the slightest. It lacks atmosphere even in Leon's campaign which gets lots of praise for being somewhat horror-esque, in reality it's mostly jump scares and even those aren't scary because you never feel like you're in real danger because you're always with a partner behind you talking azz all the time. The game has horribly clunky controls, there's too many buttons and button combinations that perform different things and most of it is never explained because the game's tutorial sucks. The graphics and character models are all a huge downgrade when compared to RE 5, when it's dark everything looks fine but in bright areas the characters look like PS2 models even worse than what they looked like in RE 4 and the overal art direction looks bland, too dark and uninspired. 

You can run over bodies on the ground but doing so your character will perform this annoying trip animation which is just distracting for no reason. Also while running, the camera has difficulties staying center while turning left or right, which makes the game feel all wonky and floaty especially when fighting multiple zombies at once. Speaking of zombies they all look and feel the same, mostly because they all use the same similar looking models for each enemy type whereas in previous RE the enemy types had some variety in their designs. Also they all feel like sponges because you can shoot all you want but it never feels like your shots make any impact other then stunning them a bit. They just keep standing up so your only option is to shoot the head if you don't want to waste bullets. The QTE's in this game are worse than in RE 5 now you have to actually Time the quick time events or else you might die or take damage. They're not hard to perform they just takes longer.

RE 6 has way too many cutscenes that break the pace of the game, one moment you're playing and shooting zombies on the streets the next moment a cutscene interupts you showing a truck crashing through and then you're back at fighting the zombies who immediately attack not giving you a chance to avoid them. The game has so many cutscenes that it tries to be like one of Resident Evil's CGI movies, in fact, this game might have worked better as a movie if it did not have bad voice acting with minor lip syncing issues and not to mention, a horrible story, but all those things are exactly what it has to offer.

The inventory system is another downgrade now you have to slide left or right through a long list for weapons and up or down for grenades or healing items, very tedious. The upgrade system has been replaced with the skill system and the list of skills is just overwhelming not as fun as upgrading and customizing weapons. And last but not least... What is up with that damn logo? Seriously, is that "6" meant to be funny or is it meant to summarize the game as a whole? Like yeah playing this game feels like giving a Giraffe a blowjob... Yeah thanks Capcom,,,

This game is weird, it feels like a good game trapped inside a really bad one.
The campaign is absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, not because of the story, no that always sucked in RE games, but because it's just filled with the worst videogame tropes from the Xbox 360/PS3 era of games, i'm talking a billion QTE's, glorified cutscenes where you're forced to walk *veery slowly*, way too many explosions. And also a cover system for some reason? It also just has straight up bad levels, Jake's campaign especially, like the one where you have to get 3 who-gives-a-♥♥♥♥♥ in the middle of a snowstorm that is just terrible.
Superficially, the game looks good, unless you try to look close into any of the assets, which reveals some of the worst textures i've ever seen in a videogame.
The good part? Well the gameplay is actually very well done, the characters control really well and there's a lot of cool stuff you can do, and the game's melee moves are really satisfying, it really shows that the developers put a lot of effort into making the game play well, it probably controls the best out of any third person shooter i've played. But even that has its own problems, the worst one probably being the fact that the game doesn't teach you how to use any of its systems at all, which is why most reviews for the game at the time it came out said that the game controls poorly or that it gives way too little ammo to work with. That's not the reviewers being dumb or bad, that's just the game not caring at all to teach the player how to play it, so the player, left to its own devices, plays the game like a cover shooter, which is probably the least enjoyable way to play the game (if there even is a enjoyable way to play the game at all).
The second biggest problem with the gameplay is that context-sensitive prompts really suck, the most common problem derived by this is parkour-ing when you don't want to, you'll be runninng towards a direction when suddenly you get close to a table and the game decides to make your character slide over the table in the opposite direction you were going which happens because for some reason the developers thought i'd be a great idea to make the parkour button and run button the same. Another problem happens when you try to stomp an enemy when you're close to them, the game doesn't know what to do and moving an inch results in the prompt disappearing and you doing a melee move to nothing.
The third problem with the gameplay is that you never really take advantage of what you can do. The campaign does but that sucks so you're not playing that, you could play the multiplayer modes but who the ♥♥♥♥ is playing RE6 in the current decade, so your only option is The Mercenaries, which can be pretty fun, but at the end of the day gives you no reason to make proper use of the game's mechanics, since every zombie drops ammo which will make you drown in it, so there's no incentive to use the melee system. You could say that you'd use melee moves for points, which is cool and all but getting an S rank is already super easy, and there's 0 rewards for getting a rank above A.

Closing thoughts: Game plays well, but the game built around that is a bunch of cobbled together garbage filled with terrible gameplay tropes, *very* questionable design decisions, and a very depressing conclusion that such a well-made gameplay system will never be explored in another game again. Overall, don't buy this game, at best it will leave you bored at times and frustrated at others, at worst it will just make you sad.

Resident Evil 6 is kind of a disaster. Not in the fun, zombie apocalypse way, but in the devastating, box office bomb, franchise killer kind of way. It's definitely one of the more inexplicable games I've ever played. It's also a terrific example of how trying to cater to everyone can end up backfiring hard in the video game world.

I joke that compromises are when all sides agree that no one will be happy, and that attitude is sort of the entire thesis statement of Resident Evil 6. The game tries to bridge the gap with three very different campaign styles. You have the old-school, slow zombie, street level trek of too-old-for-this-crap Leon, the gun toting, hoorah, bromance military mission with ultra-swole Chris, and... whatever the hell they were going for with some new idiot named Jake.

Most jarring by far is the Chris campaign, in which sort-of zombies shoot... guns... at... you. Like I alluded to in my [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/crateboxer/recommended/21690/]Resident Evil 5 review[/url], the 360 era was jam packed with third person military shooters. It didn't have a ton of survival horrors. Why try to break into the flooded market of the former with the franchise that literally created the latter? It's like Capcom tried to release three and a half games on the budget of one. Like I said, inexplicable.

"Wait just one minute," you're probably thinking, "why is this review a thumbs up?" Well, I've said time and again, the question Steam asks is not "Is this a good game?" but rather "Would you recommend this game to others?" If it was the former, I would slam dunk this bad boy with a resounding "[b]NOPE[/b]" and call it a day. But for the latter?

I'm [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/crateboxer/recommended/304240/]an unabashed fan of the dumb, dense, over the top lore of the Resident Evil world[/url]. Resident Evil 6 is so dumb, so dense and so over the top I can't help but like it, at least a little. It's basically self-parody—it tries to be the most Resident Evil-ass Resident Evil game ever by taking every single silly trope from the last seven games and vomiting them all into one bizarre game.

If you like it when people shout about Umbrella and Bioweapons, if you like it when characters drop dumb one-liners during anime fight scenes, if you like fighting huge mutant former-scientist bosses—by the way, hey scientists? Injecting yourself with the bioweapon historically hasn't been a winning move in 20 years of Resident Evil lore.

I digress. Resident Evil 6 is not a great game by any stretch. It's buggy, poorly paced, clunky and downright nonsensical. But it's also a game built on all of the best/worst impulses of the entire Resident Evil canon, making it a weird form of parody fanservice for people like me who love the campy b-movie aspects.

I definitely understand why 7 was such a hard reset though.

RE6 is my first serious tango (more than a few minutes) with the Resident Evil franchise and I have to say I am impressed with this title. The game has aged well in both graphics and gameplay departments and it has loads of content and replay value. There are many Characters to use/learn (8 I think?) with their own pros and cons for different fighting styles, 4 Campaigns each with 5 Chapters (took me 1-2 hours a chapter while searching for extras sometimes), and even a host of mini games with both solo and coop modes that are wicked fun with time limits, highscores and additional unlocks/maps that remind me of more classic games but with a well-executed coat of fresh paint.

The "zombies" themselves are bioweapon victims that you must fight in an impressive range of variety types, shapes, sizes, abilities, and all sorts of other variants. Some foes are weak fodder as you'd expect, but there are quite a few unique bosses and mini-boss throughout the game's different modes - all are fun and engaging, constantly pushing the game's combat and intensity to the limit.

Playing Mercenaries has been a major highlight, both solo and with a friend. I think this mode functions as a cross between COD Zombies and L4D, but RE6 definitely brings it's own unique take to the zombie slaying such as an easy-to-use and surprisingly effective melee combat system better than most other titles in the genre. Naturally some characters are better at the hand-to-hand stuff than others, but all seem to be able to stand their ground so long as their stamina holds up.

Also I'd like to give a nod to the sleek and simple inventory use. Find plants to mix into healing doses (like other RE games) along with other grenades types and equipment. The inventory mechanics here aren't too complicated but it's just enough to break up the fight... literally, opening the inventory won't pause game so mixing herbs and switching equipment can be done mid-combat if need be. I think this makes for great gameplay (as an RPG fan) since it keeps your adrenaline up when you're in the midst of a horde instead of giving you a breath whenever you equip something or use a potion.

My only complaint: the occasionally weird or cheezy moments in the campaign stories. Some uninspired dialogue lines, a few over-the-top stunts... when I'm playing he walks 1 mph and struggles to climb over a small box, but in cutscenes he's leaping into helicopters and surviving falls from 40 ft, getting up no problem - these things took me out of the experience at times but many games suffer from this so it's understandable. Also, there are lots of well crafted and awesome moments that really overwhelm these smaller blips in the course of the full story.

Overall, I definitely recommend this game to anyone with a desire to kick and blast their way through impressively diverse and dangerous hoards of mutant adversaries.
