Ahh, Resident Evil, one of the most famous series in all of gaming, with so many different games in its history. The original tank based controlled puzzlers, the more action based and silly Resident Evil 4, the even more actiony Resident Evil 5. Now we have the First person horror game Resident Evil 7, which I hope to get to one day. And then there’s Resident Evil 6. This is… Resident Evil 6.

With over five million sales in one of the strongest franchises ever, yet called one of the worst in the series, I had to wonder if what I was hearing was true. Is Resident Evil 6 so bad, or did it not meet the high standards of the fans, who even disliked Resident Evil 5.

The fact is I enjoyed Resident Evil 5, it was not horror, and the co-op took away a lot of the fear from the game, but I enjoyed the story and had fun with the game as it was. So I wondered if the fans were wrong, maybe there was a successful game hidden in a game that a diehard fan had a hard time with.

The game doesn’t waste time and starts with a problem, and while this didn’t shade my impression of the game it’s still ominous. The game helps me set my brightness like it asked me to. It looked alright and then I entered the game. The first thing I noticed was how dark the world was. I adjusted the brightness up in the game (which doesn’t let you pause ever even if you’re playing alone, so this was done on the fly.) I kept adjusting it up until I was almost at maximum brightness. I went from around a 12 to a 23 out of 30 possible points.

Now when I got the brightness adjusted correctly I never touched it again, but it’s strange that the first thing the game instructs me on doing, is something they get so wrong that the next half hour is spent with me tweaking the setting until I feel right with it.

The game also starts with a very linear opening where Leon is with this woman named Helena, a new character. The game doesn’t even attempt to introduce her. Instead, Leon’s on a mission to learn how to use health in the game and take out minor enemies. It’s a good tutorial, but it’s also a tutorial that’s from the end of Leon’s story, rather than the beginning. In fact, it ends with a cliffhanger at the final bosses’ location. Why choose that scene? Why not introduce some characters first, or even place the scene at the beginning of the game? This won’t be the last time I question this game.

So there are four campaigns, and I took them in order. Each Campaign is different in tone and style. The first one involves Leon (who was the President’s secret service until the president turns into the zombie in the first scene, good job dude). He teams up with Helena and she tells him they have to go to the church. That’s all she pretty much says for a chapter, that they have to go to the church, and she can’t tell him why yet. She says this so much that I wondered why Leon didn’t point his gun at her and force her to give him some more information.

Yeah, the story here can be a bit of a problem. Now I’ll talk about the gameplay later, but the story is a mixture. Some of these characters have interesting stories, and some of them like Leon’s are just a reason to keep going on. There are good moments, but there are also some “reasons for gameplay” ideas in here also.

So I finished with Leon’s campaign, and then there’s Chris’ campaign. A campaign where Chris has a new backstory where he had a group of men, killed by something in his past. He’s teamed up with a fellow BSAA member Piers, and this is more of a dudebro story and campaign. In fact, Chris doesn’t see any true zombies but fights against J’avos, which are mercenaries who shoot back and can mutate into the same beasts as the zombies.

Well, they’re called J’avos, apparently, the game decided not to tell the player except for a single name drop for over two hours. The entire first chapter of Chris’ campaign is spent fighting unnamed enemies. At the beginning of the second chapter, there’s an explanation of what they are. I still don’t understand why that single paragraph talking about them couldn’t have been done at the beginning of the game to explain what you are fighting so it’s clear to the player.

With Chris’ new backstory (that will upset longtime fans of the series, but you haven’t seen anything yet), there’s an attempt to have a good story, but we come to the first real problem I have with the game.

When playing Leon’s story, Chris and Leon meet up, and Leon stops Chris from killing a specific person. This seems sane as Leon needs to arrest that person as she has intel. The problem is when you play Chris’ story, that scene makes absolutely no sense. Chris has every reason to kill the target, but more so, Piers, the guy who’s gone through everything that Chris has, gets a clean shot and never even attempts to take it, and I don’t see a reason for either one of them to accept what Leon says. In fact, Chris could say one line, and he should be able to change Leon’s mind.

It’s a constant problem with the story in this game. Characters are forced to cross over, but not only are you seeing the same scene twice, it makes less sense when you get the other side of the story.

So on to the third campaign, there is Jake Muller, who we find out might be immune to the C-virus because he’s the son of Albert Wesker. Except he didn’t really know his father. He learns about the story and Albert Wesker from his partner Sherry Birkin, so he doesn’t have the strongest bond with his father.

Yet, later on, he threatens Chris for “killing his dad”. Sigh… again, a single line from any of the people about who Albert Wesker really was may have helped explain it. It’s not that he was close with his father, he found out who his father was and then who killed him, and suddenly blames Chris.

The level of this storytelling is weak, but it matches the game. I think Capcom wanted a game where there was a feeling that you were getting four stories about four (or seven) interesting characters, and the idea could have worked, but the execution and more importantly the stories they chose to tell just don’t work well enough. Even the meshing of the story seems acceptable and then on a different playthrough you realize how poorly they are done.

There is a fourth campaign and it’s unlocked immediately in the current game, but I’ve heard it was once hidden as a surprise, so I won’t spoil who it’s about, but the storytelling there tries to be the most interesting, but unfortunately all the surprises from that story are already obvious because of the three campaigns before it. And the surprise of who it is becomes obvious due to you team up with this person at different points in the game.

The other side of this is that when Chris meets Leon you already know what’s going to happen because you saw Leon’s story. The same is true with any other combination of characters, so really when you start the game if you already have a favorite character, I highly recommend starting with that character so you can properly enjoy their story. I started with Leon and felt Leon got the best story, mostly because I hadn’t already seen spoilers about his character.

Resident Evil 6 is one-of-a-kind.  Over 200 developers specifically worked on this game, not counting live orchestras, motion and facial capture, full teams for multiple mechanics and minor details.  If I remember correctly at the time this was one of the most expensive games ever produced.  

It is an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Graphically all over the place.  Wide open snowy fields, crowded downtown alleys and streets, underground biological research facilities, abandoned east European villages, dungeons and churches, an aircraft carrier, caves.  You're never in the same place for more than two levels in a row, and it really doesn't look that bad.  Main character models are detailed enough and there's some interesting enemy variety (for the most part) at least until you start getting into zombie dinosaurs and "Mutated Derek".  No real complaints here until you realize that almost every segment of these levels is simultaneously too linear and completely cluttered for a free-form style of combat that is completely unusable because of it.

RE6's combat is it's main strength. The biggest problem is that it explains nothing at all.  Did you know taking cover regenerates your stamina almost immediately?  Neither did I for 50 hours.  It doesn't help that there's no clear indication as to what you can and can't take cover on, and that the system for taking cover is unreasonably complicated.  Clearly designed for a controller (the ideal way to play the game, don't even bother with M+KB because you'll be using almost the entirety of the alphabet), you must approach an object and pull the left trigger/right click, then you're locked in cover.  After that the only way to peek out and fire is by using the left stick/WASD in the direction you want to look out at, then use the right stick/mouse to aim, and right trigger/left click to fire.  The *only* reason to take cover in this game is to recover stamina, which is used for ridiculous actions.

Stamina is used for melee and takedowns.  There are contextual melee takedowns, takedowns to steal enemy weapons (and kill them with the weapon if you do a QTE), melee combos that take down multiple enemies contextually, you can stunlock/combo enemies infinitely if you time your hits right.  You can use a Quickshot (L+R trigger/mouse click) which immediately spins your character to the closest enemy with your chosen weapon and fires, stunning them and opening them for a melee takedown.  You can do this multiple times in a row while changing targets, you can do this playing as Jake and literally bounce off of enemies, you can do this as Chris and throw enemies at each other, you can do this as Leon and JUGGLE ENEMIES WITH DUAL PISTOLS LIKE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ DEVIL MAY CRY.  If it wasn't for the clunky cover system and the fact that the level design does not facilitate any of this RE6 would be considering a pretty damn good character action game.

I'm not a Resident Evil fanboy but I'm aware of most of the franchise and characters.  6 is clearly designed as fan service all the way through, which old characters clashing with new constantly.  The problem is that the story is played so straight-faced and so self-serious, with NONE of the previous RE's campy self-awareness, that you objectively can not take this thing serious.  It's so bad it's good, but bad in a good way.  It's a parody of every 7th gen trope smashed into a single package.  It's hard to take anything in this game seriously when you're doing literal midair noscope collateral headshots off cliffs with Chris Redfield, suplexing enemies as Jake, or juggling multiple enemies in midair as Leon.  

I could go on about how RE6 is the best example of "less is more" in a game.  The massive development budget combined with the absolutely insane amount of people who worked on the game obviously crushed any real chance of the unique mechanics being fully fleshed out.  Did I mention that there's like 9 different asymmetrical multiplayer modes?  How about Left 4 Dead 2 cameos?  There's an "Agent Hunt" mode which lets you INVADE OTHER PLAYER'S GAMES AS A REGULAR ENEMY.  Did you play RE1 and think "Wow, I wish I could play as the first zombie you encounter and kill Jill"?  Guess what, you can!  You can play as a slow moving zombie with it's own moveset, unique UI, miserably slow controls coupled with attack animations that take up to 10+ seconds to fully complete.  It's pretty fun jumping into someone else's coop match and killing them as the equivalent of a RE4 villager, and you gain ingame currency for doing so.

This game deserves to be played simply because we will never get another title like it.  It revels in itself, takes itself too seriously, and throws a fat middle finger to the concept of basic gaming mechanics.  What the hell were they thinking?  Buy this ♥♥♥♥ immediately.

Oh yeah, there's an achievement for playing 10/20/50 levels as a female character too.

[b] Introduction [/b]
Resident Evil 6 is a horror action shooter game set in a third person view where by fighting through waves of zombies you proceed further through the campaign to find out the truth behind the virus spreading.

[b] Gameplay & Story: 3/10 [/b]
The story is absolutely boring typical zombie stuff - a biological virus that quickly spreads in the city and everyone is becoming a zombie. Obviously, you are a special agent that survives absolutely everything and everyone like a hero from a marvel movie and try to find out, where the virus is coming from and how to stop it. The gameplay consists of only running, press 2-3 action buttons and shooting zombies. I would have still played it further and tried to finish this game, but sadly the constant crashes (file not found, kernel error, crash to desctops without any error messages) made it impossible to proceed further since I got set back due to checkpoints.

[b] Combat & Challenge : 3/10 [/b]
The combat is absolutely boring, besides some of the boss fights where you have at least some minor mechanics. Shoot zombies in the head or if they run at you into their legs, so they fall to the floor and you stomp on them. Basically the whole combat in a nutshell. Challenge? Almost none even on hardest difficulty.

[b] Graphic & Interface : 4/10 [/b]
The graphic was somewhat okay, especially regarding the characters. The areas contained sometimes a nice level of details, while others were absolutely blank and felt like just placeholders. The worst were the explosion and fire effects looking like from 2003 instead of 2013. 

[b] Progress & Mini-Games : 3/10 [/b]
The progress was made by just running throgh the levels and shooting zombies on the way. There are multiple campaigns in RE6 that  somewhat fulfill the story, but still feel like the same just with another character. The whole progress was ruined for me by the constant different crashes I was getting and clunky controls for keyboard/mouse users.

[b] Audio & Immersion : 4/10 [/b]
The audio was fine in this game with decent weapon sounds aswell nasty zombie noises. Some levels, especialy detailed ones gave a nice immersion, sadly it happened not that often and most of the game's feeling was broken by the retarded story and overkill on the powers of the main characters.

[b] Side-Notes [/b]
[list]
[*]This game offers mutiple campaigns that can be played in Co-op mode.
[*]This game contains steam achievements and trading cards.
[*]This game kept constantly crashing for me with different error messages. Sadly, no repair helped to fix the issues which made the progress every hard.
[/list]

[b] Summary [/b]
Resident Evil 6 could have been a quite nice representative of the RE series, sadly this one has terrible technical issues, is not suited for keyboard/mouse users, has absolute 0815 boring story about zombie virus spreading, heroes that can have rockets shot up their back holes and still survive absolutely everything without a scratch including helicopter crash, car explosion and tons more just by asking the partner "Are you OK?" and getting "Sure, im fine." as an answer.

The music sounds like the only art direction was "we wanted Hans Zimmer, but we could only afford you." Guns sound like spitballs. Enemies only have a handful of barks.

This makes it predictably easy for enemies to stun lock you. Fun!

The other addition is the ability to... Crawl. Yes, because when you're shooting zombies the most logical thing is to get on their level and let them climb all over you like they're golden retriever puppies. At least you get the world's funniest butt-scoot animation when you move with your gun drawn.

And don't get me started on the levels. I swear: most of the levels were designed in Tetris. There's the line hallway, the L shaped hallway, the square room; sometimes there's an on-rails shooter section in between! Everyone loves those! Resident Evil 6 does not make a very good first impression. 

Forcing players through the highly scripted prologue, players are first hit with what feels like awkward controls and detailed environments that feel more constricting in the areas you can traverse. 

Between this and Leon's campaign initially feeling off due to how the "zombie" enemies reacted to bullets (they just kind of melt in place which is not really satisfying when you're hitting them with a shotgun) and how enemies could potentially stun lock the player I was initially pretty sour on the game. 

My opinion improved greatly as I learned the intricacies that the game doesn't really spell out for you. From having greater mobility in being able to dodge and roll  while being able to attack from those positions and the deeper melee system that allowed me to bust out elbow drops and german suplexes based on what charater I was playing, I found myself having a great deal of fun. 

The story is typical hokey Resident Evil, although the Chris campaign tries to take itself too seriously at times, and is still pretty good at making me laugh at some of the more absurd elements.

While the game isn't helped by how confusing its campaigns and story timeline are laid out, some neat ideas were incorporated with the online crossover with other players in other campaigns.

Resident Evil 6 requires more of a commitment through a rough patch than the other games in the main series, but if you can get over the hump, you'll probably dig it a good deal.

Oh and then there's also Mercenaries which is great with the additional movement options.

This game is far from a flawless game, but it is an amazing game for sure. However, I must lay out certain warnings first

-This game does have messy controls. This means you won't be comfortable with it straight away like many other polished games, so if you are one of those people who can't stand anything below perfect controls (which I've seen too many), then consider yourself warned and save the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. However, I think the controls aren't that big of an issue as players get used to them, and the advantages far outweight the messy controls.

-This game is from capcom. It is going to have cheesy dialogue, char development, QTEs (qtes arent hard like re4 though) and cutscenes. If you are one of those people who compare everything to witcher 3 or think bioshock infinite is the greatest thing ever, you are gonna be disappointed, and probably should not buy the game, unlike the bearable messy controls.

On to the actual review, this game is absolutely phenomenal. It has so many flaws, but at the same time it is a beautiful game with so much charm that I can't find in other games. In today's era of gaming with everyone rushing to metacritic to check for the scores to evaluate the score, people have developed fetishes for perfection, and the aim to achieve literature-level writing and execution. It's hard to disagree with that because there are so many games that have set the standards ridiculously high. Furthermore, considering how most of the critics are biased from a western perspective of storytelling and execution, it is fair to give such low ratings to RE6, but also it paints an incomplete picture of what the game is. Thus, I will try to pinpoint the major features of the game.

+action gameplay can be very stylish and cinematic. The footage you can produce with your skills is simply breathtaking. Resident Evil 6 contains all of the above, and seemingly upset quite a few people in the process, but is it a bad game? Definitely not. While the survival horror series' sixth main installment is lacking quite a bit in the survival horror department, angering fans of older titles, it stands on its own as a fast paced action game, and a good one at that.

The base game comes with four campaigns, one from Leon S Kennedy and series newcomer Helena Harper's point of view, one from Chris Redfield and series newcomer Piers Nivans' point of view, one from Jake Muller (another newcomer) and Sherry Birkins' point of view, and a final campaign from Ada Wong's.

Each campaign is good, but Leon's stands above the rest, being the closest to the survival horror action of 4, and containing great setpieces that deliver action thrills while maintaining a little (only a little) atmosphere. Leon traverses an American town, it's large, imposing church, and eventually the backstreets of China, getting the most variety in locales. This seems like the obvious campaign to play first, and one fans wishing for survival horror may find enjoyment in too.

After Leon's campaign, Chris' and Sherry's are the two to play, and unfortunately for some, they focus much more on action and shooting than Leon's, with the new J'avo enemies replacing zombies as primary fodder. These J'avo function as soldiers, able to use guns and other weapons, and while some of the shootouts are great, the game too often makes the mistake of setting a vague objective and spawning endless J'avo until that objective is reached, making some sections a little monotonous, the worst of which being in Jake and Sherry's campaign. That being said, the C-Virus changes these campaigns a little as J'avo will react to damage in certain places with inspired mutations, and the odd full mutation can add more variety and excitement to the game. Ammo is scarce, but if the early chapters from these campaigns are played like survival horror games, players can easily amass a surplus for use in later levels.

The final campaign players should play is Ada's. It functions as an extra, and clears up many loose plot threads left dangling in the other three. If treated as a bonus for beating the game, it's easily enjoyed, and features some classic Resi puzzles.

The combat in the game is great. Unlike previous Resident Evil titles, you can now aim and move at the same time, making combat more fluid, and every character has access to a variety of melee moves. Leon, for example, can roundhouse kick, judo throw, and bulldog, though Jake seems to have stolen his head-popping suplex from 4. As in 4 and 5, shooting enemies in different parts of the body will elicit different reactions- the head will daze, the arm will turn them around, and the leg will often make them fall to the ground. Tougher enemies will play with this, especially in Leon's campaign, as heads may not always be the weak spot.

Bosses are of a high standard in all the campaigns, serving as many of the highlights of the game. The design is often inspired, as with that of the enemies, and while I won't spoil any of them here, they're often tense and exciting.

For fans of crazy action games, Resident Evil 6 is well worth your time, which makes sense as it comes from a company whose pedigree in combat is indisputed with games like Devil May Cry 3, Devil May Cry 4, Street Fighter 2, Street Fighter 4, and Asura's Wrath under their belt. For fans of survival horror, perhaps look elsewhere for scares, but try it for action anyway.

Catching up on Resident Evil cause why not.  This one takes a lot of notes from 5 and tries a few things different, some of which work.

The mission structure used since 4 and co-op focus since 5 return here.  This time around, instead of a single campaign, there are four campaigns, each consisting of 5 missions that are about 45-60 minutes long each.  They each tell a separate part of the story, though there are small parts that overlap, allowing for transient 4-player online segments and cutscene reuse.

Despite any implications otherwise, the four routes do not differ majorly in gameplay, relying heavily on action set pieces to carry the game forward, either through segments where you have to run/climb through a collapsing area, fight a boss, or help your partner.  Interspersed between these are exploration segments where you collect key items or ammo before continuing forward at your own pace.  Here are what felt like the notable differences to me, ordering the routes roughly from most to least action:

[list]
  [*]Chris/Piers: Heavy focus on mass combat and vehicle/turret segments.  Unlike other routes, damage is small and frequent, with emphasis placed on using cover to minimize damage rather than completely prevent it.  Medium-Heavy weapons and few but large boss fights.  You can probably consider this a contination of the RE5 style.
  [*]Leon/Helena: Focus on partner co-op and boss fights.  A lot more QTEs than other routes, probably the most set-piece-driven boss fights, and a simple puzzle or two.  Probably aiming for RE4 vibes, though it's more of a coat of paint on top of RE5.
  [*]Jake/Sherry: A variety pack.  Combat avoidance is emphasized early on, with even a couple stealth segments, but this is quickly dropped as the route moves on to heavier weapons and action set pieces driven by a recurring boss fight.  This one's hard to pin down, though being endlessly stalked by the same boss is reminiscent of RE3.
  [*]Ada: The only solo route.  The early missions are focused on stealth and there are a couple early Resident Evil-style puzzles that require thought and experimentation.  Again, these are largely forgotten as they're replaced with turret segments and automatic weapons as the missions wear on.  Few solo boss fights, though you assist in a fair amount.  Feels a bit like early Resident Evil before getting distracted.
[/list]

The emphasis on action set pieces is probably for the best though, because they're the most well-constructed part of the game due to being largely on rails.  The exploration/stealth/mass combat segments suffer due to a combination of the poor cover system and environments.  Trying to use cover for stealth or combat often fails due to the janky controls, guesswork on what counts as cover, or fighting with the camera, leading to unavoidable damage or discovery.  

Meanwhile, exploration is usually frustrating and confusing due to an overreliance on context-sensitive actions to proceed, too many small hallways again fighting with the camera, and invisible walls.  The game includes a "where-do-I-go" button that points an arrow to your objective, which is a lazy but mostly effective band-aid.  I would argue such a function deteriorates the inherent reward of exploration, but this has already been mostly hollowed out by the continuation of RE5's small co-op focused areas. 

On a positive note, the weapon/inventory system has taken a huge leap forward from RE5, with hotswapping between items and weapons simply using the D-pad, instead of having to open any menus.  They also fixed the horrible co-op AI in single-player, though they did so by making them mostly invincible and ignorable.  It's a bit goofy, but still preferable to the babysitting that was required in RE5.

A mixed bag, though this is pretty standard for Resident Evil.  It's not survival horror but it's pretty good when it's not pretending to be.  The story and visuals are nice, and there's a surprisingly high percentage of new content in each route, making them worth finishing.  If you found RE4/5 mostly enjoyable, you'll probably mostly like this too.  If you are looking for rewarding exploration or survival mechanics, look elsewhere, this is an action game.

As an action horror with a lot of content, Resident Evil 6 is pretty unique even for it's release. As a Resident Evil game however, it still kinda still is.

The four campaigns all follow the same story involving pandemic over the newly introduced C-Virus but with different motivations and objections. Leon's campaign is about stopping the creator Simmons, Chris' campaign is about revenge on Ada for killing his men, Jake's campaign involves him being the cure for the C-Virus and Ada's campaign is about uncovering the mystery behind her supposed actions of villainy. The story is nothing special or very good and does takes itself on the same level of seriousness as Resident Evil 5, but the acting and characters are well done and the cutscenes and lip-syncing is top notch. 
Gameplay is a pretty good evolution of the third person Resident Evil games when it comes to it's action. Once you wrap your head around the mechanics and gameplay, it's incredibly fun. It carries over the enemy stun mechanic and offers a lot of different combat opportunities especially with the amount of replay value. There a lot of QTEs but I believe you can switch it off in options. It really feels like you're in an over-the-top action film with monsters and works for some bizarre reason in video game standards. Don't get me wrong, it does have problems. The levels do take about an hour or less to finish depending on your speed and familiarity and if you finished a big set piece and want to take a break by turning it off you might replay it depending if you make it past a certain cutscene in the level and shows the typewriter save icon. There are some vehicle and turret sections in the game that are pretty medicore but still competent. 
The graphics while not very colourful are pretty good with great character models, visuals and a steady 60fps. Though their were some problems like framerate dips, one crash and sometimes the camera can change to a fixed perspective that can mess you up depending if you're not fully paying attention.

In conclusion, as an action game with survival horror elements it's pretty good and has hours of content and variety but as a Resident Evil game maybe look for something else if you want something a little more scary and horrifying.

If there were a rating for 'shrug', RE6 would get it. It's not BAD. There are many, many problems, but I don't actively regret finishing it.

There are a lot of QTEs, but they come in four categories: Wiggle the thumbsticks; press A a lot; alternate L and R; and tap X in the sweet spot. The only one you can realistically fail is X, and it's used sparingly. They add nothing to the game, but they rarely frustrate you.

The story is dumb, and the cutscenes are GLORIOUSLY stupid. It's like they filmed a six year old playing with GI Joes while the director shouted MORE EXPLOSIONS!

It is not a survival horror game, at all. It's a shooter, even moreso than previous installments. There's a button that points you toward the next objective. The few times there are 'puzzles', text on the screen tells you what to do. That's not really bad per se, as long as you aren't expecting classid RE.

When paths crossover, content is reused completely wholesale. Multiple characters go through the same segments. No clever twists, just do this same event in two campaigns. They're all laughably easy segments, it's just tedious and lazy.

The skill unlock system is lame. Nothing is better than 'more gun damage' and 'more ammo', other skills are just self-imposed handicaps.

Real issues:

It is designed solely for multiplayer. Playing solo, entire action sequences are spent sitting around watching while the AI runs through its QTEs. And the AI is inexcusably bad. They block your path, push you around while you're aiming, and like to go on adventures instead of pushing buttons when you need them. Somehow my AI partner died in a chase segment when they just had to run in a straight line.

The tutorial is terrible. Learn how to dodge roll, learn how stamina works, learn to execute downed enemies. I would never have known you could dodge if it hadn't happened accidentally halfway through the game.

Cheap deaths are way too prevalent. Sometimes you can dodge things with a QTE, then the next time you die instantly, because you were expected to avoid it a different way. 'Dead' zombies are invincible and uninteractable until they're scripted to grab you. Enemies can't hurt you during cutscenes, but they can surround you and wind up an attack. Sometimes your character just doesn't want to make a timed jump. Stupid things that shouldn't exist in a triple-A game.

If you liked RE5 and want more, get it during a heavy sale. If you want a super polished, engaging experience... no.

First things first, in fairness, whike I don't recommend the game at all, it isn't completely terrible in every way - It ran nice and smooth from the first time I started it up with no hassle, never crashed or locked up in my playtime, and the controls themselves are actually pretty good. It's got the foundation of a potentially very good game, but it's all ruined by the actual campaign. And as far as that problem goes, I don't even know where to start.

First, it's horribly linear, practically every door in the game is a point of no return. I know Resident Evil has never even been remotely open world, and that's totally fine, but this game is practically a rail shooter in terms of the amount of exploring you can do and choice you have. It's just go go go go, all the time. Often literally run-or-die, since the game absolutely loves long multi-stage boss fights where sometimes the only thing you can do is run for a while. Until the game suddenly expects you to fight the boss that is, with no room for error or time to question things. At which point you die and then succeed the second time thanks to now knowing what PRECISELY the game wants you to do at that spot, which is often not clear at all. Heck, even when you think you're in a boss fight, there's lots of times the boss won't actually take damage. And don't think that's only an occasional problem, because this is the most boss-fight-heavy RE game of them all. Which means that for me at least, they took what I generally consider the least fun parts of even the good RE games and drilled down on that. And then made the boss fights just plain worse too due to them being needlessly long and complex, pretty much every. single. one. of them has some sort of location-specific gimmick or invisible timer or something, it's never just a bigger than usual monster you need to shoot until it dies while not dying in the process. And the same goes for even common enemy encounters, far too often you're stuck in some survival holdout scenario where infinite monsters will show up, all that matters is waiting for somebody to open the door or whatever the gimmick is. It's like the scenario writer really wanted to write a movie instead of a game, because while these scenarios are certainly good spectacles, they are NOT fun to play. There's always some annoyance going on that requires QTEs to solve instead of just letting you fight monsters with the core mechanics, which is FAR more satisfying than climing collapsing pillars by mashing one botton fast enough. And even when you are fighting regular monsters, it feels off... Like, usually you can walk up to a downed zombie and just smash it, but every once in a while it'll flip out at the last second and grab you instead. Why? Who knows, it just happens sometimes, which is bad game design. It's fine to screw up because the player made a mistake, but stuff like zombies doing that quick bite is just plain random, there's no lesson to learn, no way to avoid it be doing better the next time. And so many other things enemies can do are similarly random, just suddenly busting out some move that will ruin whatever you're doing that usually works with no time to react. It's like this game took a good look at everything Resident Evil 4 did so very right, and chose to do them wrong. I suspect a lot of the problems are due to the design necessities of co-op and Agent Hunt modes, but considering I couldn't care less about them to put it mildly, they don't justify the costs one bit. This game may have better graphics and improved controls over RE4, but in every other regard, I'd gladly play RE4 yet again over the painful slog of getting through this game even once.

Oh, and yeah it's picky, but the characters didn't even look like Resident Evil characters. I can't quite put my finger on what, but there was something about the character design from the very first game through RE5 that tied it together that was also lost in this game. And the same goes for music, none of the music in this game felt like RE music. It wasn't bad or anything, just not RE-style. And the title music really makes me think of the Batman Arkham games for some reason. Anyway, this is all just scratching the surface of what I disliked about this game, but the main point is that it was often no fun whatsoever and the whole package just felt like Resident Evil in name only to me. Definitely a soulless entry to an otherwise good series that's not worth the time. Maybe some people will enjoy it, if you're super into co-op and gimmicky fancy spectacle cinematic third person shoters it's probably great, but it absolutely did not deliver the sort of single-player experience that I buy Resident Evil games for. Which at this point, would basically be RE4, minus babysitting Ashley, and with snappier controls. RE6 delivered the improved controls, but completely ruined everything else.

When I first bought this game I hated it with a passion. It was not because the horror elements were gone – I was already used to this by Resident Evil 4/5, games I liked for what they were, even though I have the most fond memories of RE1 and RE2. Of the newer RE games, "Revelations" is my favorite and atm I'm a real happy camper regarding RE HD remake. But my hate for RE6 was not because it left survival horror fans in the lurch, it was due to other things: 

1) The game starts off with an irritatingly long and superfluous prelude, which one has to trudge through before the real game starts – and even then, there’s not happening much in the first 20 minutes of Leon’s campaign (which Capcom meant us to play first). There’s way too much handholding - you can’t run, you can’t shoot etc until the game *finally* lets you. That section is obviously meant as a tutorial, but it comes across as longwinded and boring (especially after that prelude). And to top it off, it even utterly fails to give you an overview over and insights into the most important functions like sliding, taking cover, quick-shoot, counter, dodging etc.

2) Once Leon’s campaign picks up, for a time RE6 seems to be great fun after all – until all is smothered by lots and lots of atrocious quick time events, some of which are seemingly impossible to master. I made it through the first campaign - but I was enraged and determined to abandon the game, never to pick it up again. 

And then something happened: First I heard QTEs for RE6 were patched – you can now let the game do most of them for you. Second, I read that the QTE’s rage inducing difficulty was often simply due to lag. If resolution and graphics settings are too high for your system, not only do controls start to feel sluggish and clunky, but the timing for the QTE’s is totally off. Third, I read a FAQ detailing the “advanced controls” for movement and fighting, which the game itself does not bother to explain. In that FAQ, I also read that there are options where the FOV for the camera and aiming can be vastly improved. I eventually decided to give RE6 another go.

And what shall I say – I suddenly fell in love with it. If the settings are chosen just right, the controls handle like a charm and the game finally gets a chance to shine in its combat modelling. I also came to appreciate that the campaigns play vastly different: Leon/Helena get zombies and puzzles, Chris/Pierce is like playing a tactical shooter, Sherry and Jake get hunted by a “Nemesis”-type enemy (and Jake as an unarmed combat expert plays very differently from say Leon). Then there’s finally Ada Wong: She is also good in unarmed fighting, has some puzzles, stealth sections and her campaign ties up the remaining loose ends of the interweaving story lines. The story itself is ambitious, but of course campy as usual. Its main shortcoming is that the main adversary is not very impressive this time around. The boss fights, however, are all very good and the enemy variety overall is definitely the best in any RE-game as of yet. The sheer amount of content this game has to offer is huge! I eventually even began to like the sections where you have to drive a car, fly a plane etc. – these are all welcome diversions that add to the variety. 

My conclusion is that RE6 is severely underrated. For the most part, this is Capcom’s and the game’s own fault, but still! I will recommend it to you like this: If you liked RE5, then by all means give RE6 a chance! Buy it on sale, and if you heed the things I wrote above, you should be able get a lot of fun out of it.

After playing for more than 600 hours Resident Evil 6 is a beautiful work of art made out of garbage. In brief:
> The animations are amazing;
> The cutscenes are awesome;
> The character models are gorgeous;
> The story is good but it is needlessly complicated and each segment has a different tone.
My favorite story is Jake and Sherry. However, everything else is terrible.
The gameplay is severely damaged by:
> Limited awareness of your surroundings (the camera is horrible) and shakes alot;
> On rails sprint doesn’t work right and because you’re holding the action button the character performs actions that you don’t want to do, like vaulting.
> Dodging is clunky and doesn’t respond fast enough.
> Aiming is fine but it is impossible to be accurate with the grenade launcher and crossbow.
> The counter attack is great but sometimes it doesn’t work right. One-on-one is fine but against multiple enemies it can glitch.
> The driving is weird, it feels like you’re driving on ice. The plane is pretty cool.
> Some QTEs are ok but there’s to many of them. Seriously, QTEs for finding car keys?
> The worst part is this: your character can not pass through enemies. If you’re in a narrow corridor or cornered somewhere, you’re stuck. You cannot shove them aside. Even after an enemy dies you have to wait for it to disappear so that you can move on.
> The second worst part is this: enemies can interrupt your “animation immunity” and can stack damage. It is possible to be hit multiple times without any chance of reaction.
> The third worst part is this: the “near death” state. It is a waste of time. You cannot switch weapons, use healing items, reload or use your inventory.
Personally, if RE6 was supposed to be the last one, why not include Claire or Jill. I would have loved 3 stories like this: Leon and Ada, Chris and Jill, Claire and Sherry.
> The Mercenaries and Mercenaries no Mercy is awesome but as your skill grows Mercenaries becomes too easy and…
> The Mercenaries no Mercy only throws in your face how atrocious the game is: enemies spawn behind you, hand grenades and incendiary grenades kill up to 10 enemies and the actions cannot keep up with your skill. You die for the most stupid things: didn’t dodge on time, the counter glitches, quick shot hits enemies that you don’t want to hit, fallen enemies can block your path, etc.
In conclusion RE6 could have been an awesome closure but it fails miserably in almost every way. The only reason I keep playing is because I love the franchise and I like the way Mercenaries and No Mercy play out and it’s the only thing it gives the game replay value.
Also how about unlocking characters like Wesker, Barry, Jill, Claire, Rebecca, Sheva. Why Left 4 Dead characters?

When I first beat this game, I hated it like everyone else seems to. But after playing all of the campaigns and the Mercenaries mode, I realized that this game is a hell of a lot of fun if you go into it not expecting horror whatsoever. I actually kind of feel sad now that future Resident Evil titles won't be like this, because this game has systems in it that other games don't that make you feel like an action hero in a leather jacket. Things like the excellent dodge system that gives you unprecedented mobilty, the ability to Quick-Shot and do insane moves, the really good and responsive melee combat system, and all of the different unique animations for each and every character. I really enjoy playing it now as long as I skip all the cutscenes and play with a co-op partner.

Of course, the story mode is nothing special and it's filled with constant interruptions, bad pacing, and the writing isn't spectacular either. But I did enjoy seeing Leon and Chris again, off on another adventure. Jake isn't bad either, I guess, but maybe I just have a Troy Baker bias. And maybe it has to do with the fact that Jake can use kung fu while nobody else can. 

I think that the gameplay is good enough that if the campaign were better, this game would have been huge. It's a shame that the campaign doesn't give you the opportunity or necessity to really use all of your special moves, and I confess I beat the game just as a standard third person shooter without bothering to learn any of it the first time, which is why I hated it in the beginning. This is why you should at least buy the game on sale to play Mercenaries, which is so good here that it could be a game on its own. 

Still, I'd give this game a chance. Don't expect anything great out of the campaign, and expect it to suck every once in a while, but when it's good, it's REALLY good.

Resident Evil 6 is a good game in all the wrong ways. You love it for what it is and hate it for what it isn't. What it is, is a high-octane rollercoaster ride of loud noises, explosions and a lot of gore. What it isn't is a survival horror game with quiet, subtle moments and interesting puzzles. If your intention with a sequel is to change the genre of its series then going the complete opposite direction of the original with no regard to the source material is seldom the way to go. You need to pay homage in a delicate and deliberate way to the original while creating something fresh that both old and new players will enjoy. While the sales numbers for Resident Evil 6 could certainly claim that they were successful in the latter, the same can not be said of the former.  
 
The gore is pretty great and the guns feel like they have a lot of weight behind them when you shoot. The best part about the game is that there is no environmental exposition. This allows the player to fully focus on the gameplay instead of exploration. I don't see that very often and I believe it's noteworthy. There are some truly amazing set pieces in the game as well, such as the section in the streets in the beginning of the Leon chapter. Unfortunately these experiences are too few and far in between. 
 
Expectations can hamper anyone's experience of anything, be it a movie or a video game. Since I'd heard so many negative things about Resident Evil 6 I decided I was going to go into it without any expectations and judge it on face value. After launching the game my immediate reaction was frustration towards restrictive controls and movement such as the inability to run in certain sections as well as the inability to skip cutscenes I'd already seen. There's a part where you're supposed to protect someone and I didn't touch the controller through the entire encounter and it just automatically sent me to the next section. It all felt like the game wanted to only show me certain things at certain times and never give me the freedom to actually play the game by myself. I find it extraordinary that a game this action-packed can manage to be as boring as it is when it comes down to it. You can just run past the enemies most of the time and since they can't grab you they aren't any kind of a real threat. That wouldn't have been such a big problem had the story or the characters been more interesting. 
 
If the gunplay had been a little smoother and not as sluggish as it is I would have enjoyed the game a lot more. But it's impossible to move around and aim gracefully and accurately because of varying sensitivity. It's a true shame because shooting is fun and the gore looks great. Had they changed the controls and movement to be more responsive it would have been an excellent shooter. Instead it tries to be survival horror as well and falls short on both as a result.  
 
I was surprised at Leon's actions in the beginning of the game when he tries to reason with a zombie. Here's Leon, arguably the most experienced of all the Resident Evil characters and he's making a classic rookie zombie mistake in the opening scene. I just don't buy it. It wasn't until I got to the Jake campaign 15 hours in that I started to enjoy myself a little. It had more than just senseless shooting and loud noises all the time with some actual pacing and character development. This was actually the most shocking part of the whole game. Because at this point you've been sitting through so much mind-numbing action shlock that you've forgotten you were a human being. "Oh, that's right, I'm still alive, and I'm playing a game I guess... Wait, did something happen!?"

This game is good, if you go into it with the right set of expectations.  If you enjoyed Resi 5's co-op combat, this is going to be something you'll enjoy.  If you go into it expecting something like Resi 4, you're gonna leave disappointed.

Personally I liked Resi 5, and this game is more of that but better.  For one thing it feels a lot longer.  There are four seperate campaigns, each with two playable characters that have different equipment.  Thanks to this and the careful arrangement of enemies, each campaign feels like a distinct experience.  Chris' campaign for instance is very heavy on combat, while Leon's takes a slower approach and has more horror elements.  Jake's and Ada's are a mix of stealth and combat, but since the characters have different guns and melee attacks things work out very differently.

As far as the plot goes, it's interesting but flawed in execution.  I feel that they really should have forced you to play through the chapters in a certain order, as otherwise certain events don't feel as important as they should.  Particularly baffling is the fact that Ada's campaign is available to play at the start even though it spoils the entire plot and offers answers to a lot of the game's questions.  I would recommend looking up the correct chapter order on Google and following that instead, as it gives the story a much more connected feeling even if you have to go through certain areas twice as a result.

Another odd note is the game's settings, and boy howdy it has a ton of them.  You will want to fool around with things like the FOV setting so that you don't have the camera shoved halfway up your character's posterior, and I also recommend switching to classic aiming as it's a lot smoother.

The gameplay itself is solid.  There is one thing that is sort of a heavy change here, and that's the new stamina/movement/melee combat system.  Now you can punch/kick enemies (no need to knife-swap) by simply hitting the attack button without aiming.  This drains stamina, which is also used for dodges (something the game never actually explains but is critical for avoiding damage from certain enemies and bosses).  Jake is particularly reliant on this system as he has no melee weapon but has super-melee moves that kill easily.  Whether you think this is fun or not is gonna be on you - I can see why some people don't like it, as it's a marked departure from the formula, but I personally found it enjoyable.

You have a much larger inventory than in 5, and can carry all your weapons + some ammo for each fairly easily.  That having been said if you're going solo you'll find a lot of instances where you run out of space and have to make choices.  Health has also been changed: now you have cubes of hp that, similarly to Dead Rising, regenerate so long as you don't take enough damage to knock you down to the next cube.  One of the more annoying things about the game is that if you DO take a cube's worth of damage, you're frequently knocked down and have to stand back up, which can be obnoxious if it happens next to an enemy that can grab you for an instakill.

Speaking of instakills, I think that the game overall is fun, but there are sometimes cases where ♥♥♥♥ isn't spelled out very clearly and you just die as a result.  Case in point, during Leon's first mission there's a segment where a truck comes roaring through the area, but you're not told to get out of the way and it's pretty hard to tell where it's gonna wind up.  I got a Game Over to this three times as a result - once from not knowing what was gonna happen, once because I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and got grabbed, and once because my AI partner decided to commit suicide.  Funnily enough, this isn't even a QTE event, and lemme tell you there are some VERY fast ones in here that will instantly murder you.  Much like Resi 4, it's annoying when this happens, especially when there are long-ass death animations involved.

That having been said I enjoyed myself and I didn't even touch the multiplayer or co-op aspects of the game, which I imagine add a lot to the experience.  This game often goes on sale and I would highly recommend it to anyone looking for a fun zombie/bioweapon shooting experience.

Resident Evil 6 isn't what some die-hard fans would consider a Resident Evil game and yes it's not a survival horror game (except for the first 2 chapters of Leon's campaign). But when played as a third person action-shooter game it's one of the most fun third person shooters of it's time. Due to the multiple campaigns I'm gonna go through them in the order I played them Also note that my Resident Evil experience up to now is limited to playing a portion of 7 on PS4/PSVR, part of Revelations, and I happen to have the remake of the original on PS4. MINOR SPOILERS COMING UP:

Chris: Apparantly picking up 3 years after RE5 (2 1/2 years for the flashback chapter), this campaign follows Chris Redfield and his squadmate Piers Nivens as the former seeks revenge for the deaths of his squad while they and the BSAA are also fighting a bioterrorist attack in a fictional Chinese city. This campaign's gameplay is predominantly that of a third person military shooter a-la games like Gears of War. Stylisticly I feel it's similar to Call of Duty, particularly the Modern Warfare series. With it's Michael Bay eat your heart out setpieces, fighting of various terrorists, portion set in a war-torn country, and constant dude-broing. It does play well, especially when you enable the Item Drop Increase skill. Talking about the story, it's actually quite decent with a good performance from Roger Craig Smith as Chris. Though the blinded by revenge against the villain thing goes on for a bit too long. Piers is also great, he does a good job trying to keep Chris in line and I bought their friendship. Overall this campaign was a lot of fun for the 7 hours it lasted, unlike these next two campaigns...

Leon: 9 years after RE4, Leon S Kennedy is still part of the Secret Service, now protecting President Adam Benford. Whilst on a visit to college town Tall Oaks, an outbreak of a new virus called the "C Virus" occurs, infecting the president and forcing Leon to kill his zombified friend. Now he must team up with fellow Secret Service Agent Helena Harper to uncover the truth, avenge the president, and stop those responisible for the president's death and the outbreak. The first 2 chapters are a throwback to Leon's first 2 games. Featuring many zombie story tropes, there isn't many surprises here. After the 3rd chapter though things switch over to action. When Leon and Helena arrive in China things go off the rails, both literally and figuartively. By the end of the 6 or so hour campaign you will have killed a mutant shark, survived numerous vehicle crashes and death defying stunts, and fought a ridiculous multi stage boss. But none of this is any fun. Not even Leon's quips and one-liners that have been delivered appropriatly by Matthew Mercer could save this campaign. Also Helena is one of the most annoying and hateable non-evil female characters in all of gaming (and the one I hate the most since I first saw Stacey from A View To A Kill). By the end I was wishing that the easy to spot, different from the other campaigns and terrible main villain would just f**king kill her. Also while I'm complaining, the setpieces are terribly designed as well as being so horrible and implausible they put the infamous CGI surfing scene from Die Another Day to shame. While this one got off to a good start, it's by far the worst of the 4 campaigns.

Jake: Newcomer to the series Jake Muller starts out working as a mercenary in the same war-torn country from Chris' campaign. It turns out he has anti-bodies to the C-Virus. As a result government agent Sherry Birkin is sent to retrive him. However they go missing for 6 months and then have to find a way to the US while evading capture by the towering Ustanik. This campaign's setpieces are more styled like Uncharted. But like Leon's campaign the setpieces aren't that well done and they feel like discount versions of similar setpieces from Uncharted and similar action games from the early 2010's. Jake and Sherry's romance is surprisingly believable thanks to the actors chemistry, though it is cliche. Ustanik was alright as a recurring boss, though his death was contrived. Jake was also okay, despite Troy Baker's best efforts. Overall this campaign was just alright; nothing great, but nothing bad either.

Ada: This campaign sees Ada generally acting behind the scenes as she deals with both main villains as well as her own issues. This campaign makes use of a Splinter Cell Blacklist or Dishonored like stealth-action formula where you can choose whether you want to sneak or attack. Ada's crossbow is lot of fun to play with as is her move set in general. Doing a backflip and firing the crossbow at an enemy mid flip never gets old. I can't talk much about the story without spoiling the other 3 but it's actually quite entertaining and features a satisfying ending. I really loved this campaign just as much as I loved Chris'.

General Thoughts: The game's visuals do hold up quite well for an early 2013 DirectX9 title. The controls do work well on both a mouse and keyboard and an Xbox Controller. Also, in my experience, online coop is broken and split-screen coop doesn't work with the setpieces, so I played solo for the most part. This ended up being alot more fun, aided by your excellent and reliable partner AI. I actually missed the partner AI during Ada's campaign to be honest, though I see why it was initially single player only. The Mercenaries mode, paired with the fun and over the top gun-play is great and I see myself coming back to it for a while.

Overall I like RE6 as an action game. Those who come in expecting survival horror will be disappointed, but those expecting an over the top shooter will be satisfied. Just know that the coop isn't all it's cracked up to be...

“It's not Resident Evil!” That's probably the main criticism of Resident Evil 6, and to be fair, it's probably accurate. RE6 is an action packed cover shooter, and you know what? Leon has the slightly grittier zombie apocalypse, Chris fights uber bioweapons, while Jake plays homage to Nemesis. It's all larger-than-life, action packed, energy-charged, and I can't bring myself to hate it. I also like some of the changes to the mainline mechanics, like the stamina system changes, and melee combat.

Resident Evil 6 is like that popcorn flick that's trite and predictable, but you're still watching it due to the charismatic lead and the flashy action sequences. It may not have a whole lot of substance, but it has heart in spades.

Review for Resident Evil 6

Resident Evil 6 is an ambitious game that tries to do too much at once, with mixed results.

On the positive side, the game offers a huge amount of content. Multiple campaigns with different characters and playstyles keep things varied, and co-op can be genuinely fun, especially with a friend. The combat system is deep and fluid once you learn it, offering more freedom of movement than previous entries.

However, RE6 drifts far from survival horror. The focus on nonstop action hurts tension and atmosphere, and horror elements often feel secondary. Pacing is uneven, with frequent interruptions, scripted moments, and over-the-top set pieces that break immersion. Some campaigns are clearly stronger than others, leading to an inconsistent experience.

Enemy variety and level design can feel repetitive, and the story is bloated and confusing at times. It’s enjoyable in short bursts, but exhausting if played for long sessions.

Overall, Resident Evil 6 is a decent action game, but a divisive Resident Evil title. Fans of action-heavy gameplay may enjoy it, while those looking for classic survival horror may be disappointed.

[b]Resident Evil 6[/b] is the ninth installment of the series, and the sixth from the main games. It has always been a rough one for me to review and throughout the years my opinion has changed, or as some may say, evolved. After [b]Resident Evil 5[/b] release, when [i]Capcom[/i] announced this sixth title, there were a lot of fans among the community that had the strong impression which the series would return to the horror oriented experience. Including myself.

But why would [i]Capcom[/i] do that? [b]Resident Evil 4[/b], which further popularized the franchise, wasn’t horror oriented, and in fact, was a turning point for shooters alike, even inspiring other third person shooters for years to come. It’s one of the most important games in the industry, so why would [i]Capcom[/i] move from it? That is a good question, one I never really though much. Although my own self entitlement wanted the horror to be persistent, fans like myself had to wait five years for the seventh game, which in a way, returned to horror in a different, but pleasant way.

Following the main story, the U.S President comes clean for the first time regarding the events from Raccoon City in 1998. This is a major breakthrough, but not everyone is happy about such revelations. Meanwhile, other bio-terrorists attacks across the world are spreading, and it's Raccoon City reunion all over again.

The story is one, if not, the strongest pillar in the game. It features four different campaigns, and they are all connected through a thread of events which affects them, personally, or indirectly. The circumstances are the same, but the perspectives change from campaign and character. We have to give credit, where credits due, and as far as: story-wise, narrative, dialogues and overall direction, [b]Resident Evil 6[/b] shows a tremendous production value.

Character development has a huge impact, which undoubtedly was never presented before, not like this. Players get to know a lot more from all time favorite protagonists like Chris and Leon, as well as new ones which old fans immediately recognize, such as Sherry. Each campaign can be played from two different characters, such as Leon or Helena, Chris or Piers, Jake or Sherry. The last campaign is exclusively to Ada, therefore she is the sole option.

The gameplay always sets me up with mixed feelings. It’s an improvement from [b}Resident Evil 5[/b], at least in terms of functionality. New features may not appeal to everyone, but it's fundamentally an improvement. The biggest new feature is the ability to walk while shooting, or even running, which is the first time a [i]Resident Evil[/i] game allows it. A vast deck of difficulty tiers helps letting players enjoy their adventure based on their own skill and an extra mode was even later added, to extend the challenge.

The counters were pushed further and once you learn them, your gameplay approach will change entirely. Counters are perfect to save ammo and deliver a final blow with style. Every enemy can be countered, although some aren’t easy. In fact, even dogs can be countered. Unfortunately, the counters aren’t always a 100% successful hit, mostly due to the hit-detection containing flaws. Same goes for I-Frames during animations and some overall lack of optimization that could make this system extremely reliable and fun.

Another huge mistake is the lack of a proper tutorial, and since [b]Resident Evil 6[/b] has so many in-game technical details, such as shorkeys and character movements, unless you specifically search for these mechanics, you’ll never find them. Lacking a tutorial with these many features is stupid and a complete missed opportunity.

Another critic I strongly have against it, is how the game’s flow is constantly being interrupted, almost as reflecting Capcom's wish not to create a game, but to develop another movie, an interactive movie that follows the player, giving them a hand, or even better, playing the game for them. Cutscenes or dialogue scenes will stop the game, re positioning players in a different position, thus breaking the rhythm, and I found this perhaps the worst part of the experience.

Zombies are almost always never endingly spawning, which adds to the action factor, but loses a lot in my humble opinion. From someone who takes satisfaction in clearing a room or area, this is a nightmare. Although some seem to prefer the opportunity to grab more items or an extra exciting moment.

With an action packed campaign with some really original and awesome bosses, the multiplayer modes are an extra addition that is still popular to this day. Mercenaries is still being disputed competitively through Resi Net, with rewards and top positions. This mode is super fun with a co-op partner, but unfortunately suffers from the same issues I mentioned above, where hit-detection and the lack of decent I-Frames made me completely frustrated with it.

Design wise, it's top tier when comes to visuals. Zombies looks fantastic for a 2013 game, they are detailed and very impressive. Monsters are interesting and bizarre, and each area is pretty detailed and appealing. Visuals do look fantastic, but design is not always about visual realization. The level structures are linear, which doesn’t affect the game at all, and through the different campaigns, each scenario is unique and gets you a different vibe.

A nice little detail is how the User Interface changes for each different campaign, giving out an extended identity. Small extras like these are perfect, but I personally can’t say the same for the in game menus. I seriously struggled managing the inventory and just never felt comfortable to me.

[b]Resident Evil 6[/b] has definitely a considerable amount of problems, but it also improves tremendously for fans who seek an action game within a horror contemporary styled adventure. With different campaigns, diverse scenarios and various mechanics, it’s safe to say this entry is not what many of us wanted, but from where it stands out, it’s a solid game, especially if you have a partner to join you.

This will be a review for the campaign mode of Resident Evil 6.

Resident Evil 6 is often compared to Resident Evil 4 due their mechanics being very similar, as well as both featuring Leon Kennedy as a playable protagonist. This installment in the RE franchise does share the same campy, action feel of the last few installments whilst including very few new features, some good and some bad. I believe that it is a mistake to judge this game based on other RE installments, so I will judge it entirely on it's own merits.

The Good:
.  The campaign is a decent length, split into sections where the player takes control of different protagonists. This gives the narrative a rounded-out feel, as you are able to see the events unfold from the perspectives of characters who have their own motivations and reactions to the events as they unfold.
. The co-op mode makes the campaign far more enjoyable to play with a friend and allows you to play either online or splie screen (a rarity in modern games!)
. The game allows you to publicly match-make with a stranger to play as your companion, as well as giving you the option to turn online play off, which I found to be more enjoyable.
. Your AI partner is not a complete gumby and can look after themselves fairly well.
. There were precious few escort missions and the only time where there was one, it was mercifully short.
. Zombies are diverse and their models are fantastic.
. Character models are well designed and animated.
. Weapons function as they should and each weapon pickup serves its niche purpose well.
. Level design is linear (a series of hallways) yet rarely claustrophobic or irritating.
. Skills can be purchased with experience points and actually make a difference in a meaningful way.
. You can move and shoot at the same time and the ability to select between a crosshair or laser sight was a good choice by Capcom

The bad:
. Online coop is an experience that is dependent entirely on the person you are paired with. Capcom's fix to players with different approaches was to implement an option to select why you are playing the game. 
. Weapon handling is bad to terrible. The wiggly dot in your crosshair makes fine aiming impossible. 
. Sniper rifles should be useable without having to purchase & equip a 'steady-hands' skill. The reticle trembled worse than a rabbit at a Motorhead concert and this made the sniper rifle all but useless for me.
. Characters spout more cliched one-liners than any 80's action movie hero, even when completely inappropriate, which totally breaks immersion  at several points during the campaign.
. The J'avo enemies (similar to the Las Plagas) are far less varied in model and behaviour than the zombies.
. Bosses have predictable attack patterns, with their weak spots always appearing as easy, glowy patches, which removes the challenging aspect.
. There is no horror to the game- it plays as a camp action movie. The first chapter showed so much promise for a genuine horror game, but this was completely gone by the next chapter.
. Cutscenes are too numerous and they often serve to remove any player control over dramatic events. Why Capcom has a phobia of letting the player have control is beyond me...
. Quick time events.... QTEs rear their ugly heads often and even in situations where they serve no real purpose, such as to open a door, despite the fact that I have been doing fine using the space bar to do so until now! The QTEs are very clearly a poor-compromise for not allowing the player to actually play the game, instead forcing them to watch a cutscene of the action.
. Character development was nearly non-existent.
. Vehicle handling is so bad it nearly drove me to insanity more than once. Why a £10'000 superbike handles like a Penny-Farthing is beyond my comprehension.
. Scripted chase scenes; awful camera angles that require the player to hold the direction *relative* to the camera only works when you dont.keep.changing.camera.angle! The chase scenes are the buggiest part of the game and take several attempts to complete on higher difficulties.

In summary, I would give RE6's campaign a 5/10. If it were honest about it's status as an action game with horror elements, then the clunky movement and shooting mechanics would hopefully have been addressed. As it is, you can feel the decline in story-writing, character development and overall effort spent on the game the further into the campaign you get.

There are four campaigns that each have their own very distinct take on the Resident Evil formula. Leon has a more survival horror type feel while Chris take RE5 up to 11 and goes ape-shiz on the action. All in all a fun experience, especially split-screen On many occassions, some of these characters will cross-over with some of the other pairs' chapters, allowing you to play the same story section from a different point of view. The first three campaigns have each character take different paths, so all in all you get a lot of replay value from playing each chapter slightly differently between the two characters. Each chapter takes about 20-40 minutes to complete and every campaign has five chapters, so you have 15 chapters, plus the fourth character's storyline (was original solo, but a companion character was added to her story post-launch).

The game also features Mercenaries mode, a survival based arcade mode where you score points and kill monsters to increase the time you have to score further. This PC release of RE6 additionally features a few characters from Left 4 Dead in a special "No Mercy" variant of Mercenaries mode. Clearing through these missions can be challenging but fun, providing extended playtime. By linking to RE.NET, the central hub for Resident Evil activities, you can unlock some special costumes for Mercenaries mode, including some Resident Evil 2-era inspired costumes that are extra polygonal for those who might enjoy them. They can be unlocked by completing events which include replaying certain character chapters, accomplishing certain ingame tasks, or achieving a certain score in the story or Mercenaries mode.

Leon, Chris, Ada and newcomer Jake travel around the world fighting off all sorts of zombies and other nasties. Each of the four campaigns center on one of the four main characters and their respective partners, each telling the same story from a different point of view. As usual someone has gotten hold of some bioweapons that can turn everyone into zombies or worse, and it's up to our heroes to save the day.

The game plays pretty well. Just like Resident Evil 5, Resident Evil 6 also has little to do with the older games in the series. However, the controls in this game feel very smooth, and if you're able to master how the fighting and shooting works, it can be a lot of fun. Yes, there are quick-time events scattered throughout the game, but the main part of the game where you shoot, stab, hit, throw, run, dodge and so on, is very well done.

Personally, playing as Ada Wong was something that I had been wanting to do for a while, and getting to know more about her was a plus. The rest of the story, while maybe a bit over the top, was also pretty interesting. The only minus would probably have to be that the villains felt kind of meh, but that's a minor detail.

All in all I enjoyed Resident Evil 6, and do not think that it deserves all the hate it got on release. Luckily, going by the more recent reviews, more and more people seem to give the game the credit it deserves.

If you're a fan of the Resident Evil games (especially Resident Evil 5) or third person shooters in general, then you will probably enjoy this game as well.

A game that everyone seems to hate but I think I'm the only one in the world that sees this for its merits.

Pretty damn good as an action shooter, horrifying bad for a horror game as it takes a very huge departure from the rest of the series and instead sacrifices survival horror for a pretty in-depth shooter that has a very Capcom feel to its design and aesthetic. 

Hopping into this game thinking that it would be like the classic RE games would really disappoint you, and honestly I do think that the story mode is pretty damn bad and is only worth stomaching just to unlock more characters for the excellent Mercenaries mode. 

Don't really need to say much about the story other than its just a messy continuation of the series that tries to get the entire RE cast together for this huge Michael Bay-esque bonanza because UMBRELLA IS BACK, NOW WITH A NEO PREFIX. Starring incomprehensible monster designs, beautiful fashion model protagonists and MT Frameworks proving how well-oiled of an engine it is. Resident Evil has never been about the story, let's be honest here. 

Now that's out of the way, please for the love of god just play Mercenaries. As more of an expansion to RE5/Mercenaries 3D's ruleset (150 enemies max, rankings are D to S instead of stars, melee kills add time, etc) it shines much more due to the new moves that characters have such as sliding, counter melee hits, Coup de Grace kills, and many more beautifully animated Wrestling-inspired attacks which each character has their own specific modes. 

This game also includes all of the DLC for free such as the extra Versus modes (personal favorite being Predator- which allows you to play as Tyrant/Mr X/Nemesis 2.0 and hunt down survivors to see who of 8 people can cause the most damage) and the glorious Mercenaries No Mercy mode, which cranks up the enemy spawns to a stupid amount and raises the max enemy count to 300 while also adding a Left 4 Dead 2 crossover character/monster pack.

This game goes on sale quite often, so you're bound to get this for a very VERY cheap price. Very fun game that I wish people would be less brutal with and see that its one of the finest action shooters out there. If you want a survival horror game, stay far FAR away from this and get the RE1 Remake. If you want to play a very fun arcade/action shooter: get this and Resident Evil 4 and 5 [strike]And Vanquish[/strike] as well
