Well, if the amount of time I've spent playing this game is any indication, I simply cannot recommend [i]Resident Evil 6[/i]...enough. This is, hands down, my favorite [i]Resident Evil[/i], and I proudly say I own every single one they've released for the PC, including the (as of this writing) new ports of [i]Resident Evil[/i] and [i]Resident Evil 4[/i], not one but *two* copies of [i]Operation Raccoon City[/i], as well as both [i]Revelations[/i] titles; I even have original copies of both [i]Resident Evil[/i] and [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] in their original boxes. So trust me, I've devoted a lot of effort to this series.

Up until I finally got around to playing Re6, Re2 and Re4 had the honor of being my favorite games in the series to date (and we're talking about the original, terrible Ubisoft port of the latter, let's not forget). However, in this title, Capcom managed to somehow do just about everything right, in ways few developers can match. While it isn't the quantom leap-forward in genre mechanics Re4 was (and that game is honestly one of the most influential action games of all time and probably won't be topped any time soon), it still manages to take most of the things that worked in that title and improve them for a real-time setting...in short, everything Capcom failed to do in [i]Resident Evil 5[/i]. We can now move and shoot, and while we're still sadlled with real-time controls, we have a, for the most part, more streamlined inventory with hotkeys for things like grenades; there's even a designated "Combine Herbs and Put them In Your Pocket" and "Heal Yourself" button, not mapped with anything else, the former of which is exclusive to the PC and makes the mouse/keyboard controls the preferred method of play. For once, Capcom gave PC players the port we deserve.

Plot wise, the game itself is one of the better stories in the series. As most reviews will tell you, Leon's story is hands-down the best (and honestly the most relevant to the overall plot), with Jake's a close second, and Chris and Ada's unfortunately bogged down by poor writing and irritating mechanics, respectively.

Leon's story is the closest to the older games. Yes, it does feature zombies, but it's still faster paced than older games, with the exception perhaps of [i]Resident Evil 3[/i]. Still, I was a little unsure how Capcom would implement free-aim and move-and-shoot with zombies, but they pulled it off beautifully. The zombies themselves are a lot of fun to fight, especially in Mercenaries, and there's some nice variety to their designs. The highlight of Leon's game is the final chapter, which begins with he and his partner fighting their way through a city being overrun by zombies and ends with the game's final boss fights, which are themselves a nice call-back to William Birkin from Leon's debut game.

Chris's story is more action centric, and overall feels more like his last headline game, though fortuantely there's only five chapters we're saddled with him and overall the experience is improved by the game's superior controls. No more standing in the open casually shooting it out with five guys with AKs; despite what a lot of people say, that cover system is [b]incredibly[/b] useful in his scenario. The highlight of Chris's game is the second chapter, which shows us what modern warfare looks like in a world full of bio-organic weapons.

Jake Mueller, a series newcomer, has a story more closely reminscent of [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] in overall tone; Jake and Sherry spend most of it snarking at each other and generally not taking things very seriously, and for the most part it works very well. Their scenario is honestly the direction I wish the previous title had taken, since it never forgets it's a video game and never stops being fun. Unfortunately, there isn't a stand-out chapter for Jake, though the first mission (which parallels part of Chris's second chapter) is a good candidate; however, Jake's signature hand-to-hand attacks make playing as him a blast all its own.

Ada's scenario is probably the most spotty, since it's very similar to "Seperate Ways" from Re4; it's the only one to feature both zombies and the J'Avo Chris and Jake fight. Overall, I felt Ada's was the most uneven, especially due to a poorly implemented stealth mechanic (which is still extremely fun if you can get it to work) and immersion breaking co-op. While no part of Ada's scenario stood out, the opening of her first chapter is solid, as is her last chapter, esepecially her fight with the series' trademark chainsaw lunatic and her second bout with the game's final boss; unfortunately, between these two there's a horrifically broken helicopter segment that puts the HiND portion of [i]Black Ops[/i] to shame.

It wouldn't be right to ignore the game's extra modes, of course.

"Agent Hunt" is pretty much a Capcom take on "Versus" from [i]Left 4 Dead[/i]. Playing solo gets frustrating very quickly, and I honestly didn't enjoy it much.

I won't say much about Mercenaries, other than that's where most of my time spent playing this game was, and it alone makes the game worth the $60 USD I preordered it at.

There are also a few paid DLCs, which I also own.

"Survivors" returns from [i]Resident Evil 5[/i] and is honestly not much fun. Either the game crashes whenever I kill another player or it turns into shotgun spam very quickly, neither of which is an enjoyable experience.

"Predator" is basically "Juggernaut" from Halo, but with Ustanak. This can be a lot of fun, provided you have a full lobby.

"Onslaught" is similar to "Slayers" from the previous game. This gets intense in a hurry, but again, is fun.

Overall, [i]Resident Evil 6[/i] is one of my favorite games of all time, and as I said, I can't recommend it highly enough. Pick it up. Ignore the critical reviews (these same fools gave Re5 postive ones for crying out loud!). You won't be sorry.

Long time RE fan here (RE1 on PSX )! It was very hard for me to hit the recommend button for this game, and there are basically only three reasons why I am recommending it. 

1: It does offer a lot of content. This has four normal sized campaigns, even if some of them have a couple of interlapping scenes, it will offer you plenty of hours of playing.

2: With a good co-op friend this game can be extremely fun. People give these modern RE's a hard time because of the less survival horror, or the fact that they are co-op, but I think co-op is actually one of the series biggests strenghts now. In a world with very few co-op games, this game is a fun time if you have some good friends to play it with. I highly recommend playing on the higher difficulties. 

3: It's the Resident Evil universe. It's more of an already cool universe with enjoyable monsters and enjoyable characters. Yeah it's not perfect but it's still more RE. 

Now what do I not like about this game? The controls take awhile to get used to, I don't know why, but they just feel more awkward than even the older titles. I think pair that with the extremely tight corridors in some of the campaigns and it just makes it feel extremely sloppy. 

While the stories aren't bad, I felt there wasn't a good protagonist on the level of Wesker. I did like Chris's target for the first half, but although there was build up it did not end the way you would expect. 

Leon's story I felt had the most boring / easy monsters, as well as the least inspired easy boss fights. I feel like Chris's campaign was just better over all.

Then you have some minor nit-picks on things that they took steps backwards from RE5. No DirectX10 support, no LAN support, and over all I'd say RE5 even looked better. The share system for swapping items is gone, and unless someone tells you picking the setting as the host doesn't actually change the other persons difficulty setting. 

I think what disappointed me the most is that RE5 was basically a better game in every way. The only thing RE6 had going for it was length, but length is not important when RE5 just has more replay value. I think because I enjoyed RE5 so much more as a co-op game I will always just feel RE6 was one of the biggest let downs in the series. Don't get me wrong I still enjoyed it enough to recommend it, but barely.

[h1]Presentation[/h1]
The game runs just fine on my rig, and I haven't had any inexplicable FPS drops. There is gamepad support out of the box, it's a breeze to switch between devices. The game plays fine on a mouse and keyboard, however it does feel like the user interface was developed with controllers in mind. The online co-op and other gamemodes are functional. 

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Nothing fancy in this instalment. Environment and character models look decent, animation is fine.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
Voice acting is solid, weapons sound good, zombies still have that familiar "errrggghhh".

[h1]Story[/h1]
To be completely honest I found the story hard to follow. Despite the fact that it's built upon decades of wacky Resident Evil lore, it was more than a little convoluted. However I did like seeing the return of key characters such as Leon, Hunnigan, Ada, Chris and Sherry, as well as the addition of new characters like Helena, Piers and Jake. The decision to pair Piers with Chris made their campaign a bit of a sausage fest, and I would much rather like to have seen Claire, Jill or even Sheva there.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The game consists of four campaigns, each with two playable characters*. You can play online or offline. AI is not too bad here compared to RE5; your partner can usually hold their own and won't require much help. That's not to say I haven't had my fair share of Helena running in the opposite direction, but most of the time it works. There are points in the game where campaigns will intersect, and you can team up with another pair of players or AI to complete a section, which I thought was pretty cool. One interesting new game mode is Agent Hunt, where a player can invade other people's games as a monster, and try to kill them. I call this ♥♥♥♥ Mode, because I feel like a ♥♥♥♥ trying to halt people's progress in their game. There are about five or six other game modes, including Mercenaries which is really the only one worth playing.

*Ada's campaign when played offline contains just Ada without a partner. However when online, she is paired with Agent. I haven't played with Agent yet so I'm not sure how it works.

[h1]Lasting Appeal[/h1]
There are 80 serpent emblems to collect, and each chapter has a ranking for each character, on each difficulty, so you would need to play through the campaign at least 10 times (if my math is correct) to get S ranks for everything. Most of the online game modes are dead now, but you can still do some of them solo, such as Mercenaries. There is a lot to be had with this game, it just depends how much time you want to dedicate to it.

overall the new controls are  pretty cool, and a great idea. i think this is a step in the right direction to evolve the series as far as controls go.  brushing up against surfaces allow you to "lock" into place, letting you peak around corners and shoot safely (like every other third person shooter) and the camera is pretty good about letting you do it. sometimes you'll go into a psuedo first person view because of the lack of camera space, but they executed this well.  

unfortunately the camera is also your enemy . devs made a bad decision to randomly force the camera to auto focus on your objective about..half the time. this can often prevent you from even attacking the nearest threat because you can't turn around and see what's going on behind you.     there's also a nasty bug (at least i hope its a bug) in Chris and Pier's campaign where the camera can't even be moved and I can't aim or shoot. only run toward whatever the camera's pointing at.

unfortunately this is not a scary game, nor does it feel survival-ish.       your inventory is essentially reduced to a handful of guns and grenades, and healing.    there's nothing in this game you pick up that isn't ammunition, a grenade, or an herb and you can carry every weapon at once. the only real restriction is how much ammo you can carry (and half the time, you have too much. puzzle items fuse with your pathfinder

they stream-lined the entire inventory into a small scroll-fest that pops up during play. While I can say that the Resident Evil series makes me feel very warm and bubbly inside, I am sad to say that even though Resident Evil 6 is a very well created and beautiful title, I would not recommend it to long-time fans of the series. 

From the zombie-infested streets of Tall Oaks to the war ridden mountains of Edonia, Resident Evil 6 takes you through 4 different storylines, each containing two important characters (excluding Ada Wong's co-op partner, ingeniusly dubbed "Agent.") These four campaigns follow Leon S. Kennedy and his partner Helena Harper, Jake Wesker and his partner Sherry Birkin, Chris Redfield and his partner Piers Ivans, and Ada Wong, and progressively shows how their stories collide in China. 

Combat in Resident Evil 6 is unlike any other resident evil game, consisting of a stamina bar, more melee attacks, and a special coup de grace for each character (the latter is featured in Resident Evil 5). Each campaign has it's own arsenal that you will obtain throughout your playing, ranging from Auto-shotguns to Lightning Hawks, the Bear Commander assault rifle to the Semi-Automatic Sniper Rifle.  Quick-Shot and melee attacks take up one sliver from your stamina bar, and once said bar is depleted, your melee attacks are powered down to a weak, fatigued kick. The combo system is very well done, allowing you to quickly stun an enemy and go in for the kill rather easily. 

Mercenaries mode makes it's return in this title, as well as a special derivative named "Mercenaries NO MERCY". NO MERCY may sound familiar to fans of one of Valve's most successful series, Left 4 Dead, and you are right to feel such nostalgia. Mercenaries NO MERCY is a version of NO MERCY in which you can play as the iconic survivor cast of Left 4 Dead 2 (Coach, Rochelle, Ellis, and Nick, respectively.) In NO MERCY, music is replaced with songs by the game's fictional greasy rock band, the Midnight Riders, and it is also optional to apply a Left 4 Dead enemy pack which makes Witches, Tanks, and Hunters (from what I've experienced) available for your violent enjoyment.

A new addition to the Biohazard series is titled "Agent Hunt", in which campaign players can set their games to allow such mode to allow other players to join in as zombies or J'avo. This mode is /very/ addicting, but quite difficult if you are playing as the C-virus infected enemies. You control different versions of the zombies and J'avo, and can also control your J'avo after its Chrysalis mutation, allowing you the destructive power to wreak havoc in any way you choose.

All in all, in a review that sounds very positive, I must wrap this up with the negatives.
- Rather low replay value
- Decent graphics, some texturing looks unfinished
- Chock-full of cutscenes, long and short, many uneeded
- Clunky control system
- No pausing the game, at all (unless you're in co-op)
- Very limited array of weaponry
- Difficult to find ammo (but I suppose that is what you'd expect in an apocalypse)


TL;DR it's kind of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game. QTE. Don't buy it unless you want to experience vivid imagery of low-quality scares and body horror.

Tremendously disappointing.

Everything in this game's structure screams "Lazy". They even give you an optional infinite ammo cheat right from the start. The expansions to the combat system seem to carry a glimmer of effort, but the contextual commands to do them are so imbalanced and poorly timed as to suggest a lack of playtesting.

You get to carry far too many weapons at once, and it is far too cumbersome to select which specific one you want to use at any one time.  These guns have zero customization, and despite different appearances, many of them are even used the same way.
There are no real puzzles, and no exploration-- everything is totally linear to the point of being boring.
Even the combat difficulty has been toned down, with the only real bit of challenge being your need to adapt to the crappy UI aiming.
The skillpoint system for leveling up is anemic; you get the ability to freely switch between 8 sets of skill combinations, but only a few of them are really relevant. And since you can't swith what is IN those combinations mid-game, the barely-useful skill system becomes obtuse and irrelevant. 

And the overuse of Quick-Time Events ( something I despise to begin with) causes death to be nothing more than a constant annoyance-- there is no challenge in this game, and it is not scary.  As a personal gripe, the plot has gone totally off the rails as well. It is so disjointed and filled with plotholes and logic flaws that it is genuinely boring.

The online functions all sound like they should be fun;  but they all fall flat for obvious technical reasons:
Connecting to another player's game requires far too many circumstancial factors to be in alingment. Being able to play as a monster in another player's game might be more fun of the UI and controls for playing as a monster actually worked-- they don't. And even the overlapping portions of the character chapters fail to really present a gameplay environment where interaction  (cooperative/competitive, or even just knowing you are playing with another human being) are really utilized.

Right out of the gate, Resident Evil 6 is -not- the horror experience you would expect if you are coming from the first few games. Reviewing it would be quite difficult, and a recommendation would only be up for grabs for those who haven't played the original surival-horror RE games. I myself haven't played any of the RE games besides 5 and 6, and I honestly found them both to be great games despite their action-centric gameplay and bucket-loads of quick-time events. I'll make it as short as possible.

RE6 features several campaign runs with different characters and co-op focus(solo is available and not as difficult as RE5). The gameplay is, as most point out, very action-oriented with fancy dodges and organic movement that I found very enjoyable and is a massive step-up from RE5's movement and combat. There are loads of QTE's during cutscenes(as well as dynamic QTE's in combat to dodge attacks), although there is an option to disable the majority of them, or more specifically, the QTE's that result in game overs.

The big negatives are the boss-fights, being frequently reoccuring and never really stay dead. They also have a theme of being quite large and overblown, making most of them rather one-dimensional to fight. Some scenes in the campaign are beyond dreadful to get through(Jakes snowmobile for one), as well as some qte cutscenes like forementioned. The other elephant in the room is how little it lives up as a Resident Evil game, being quite the opposite definition of subtle. It never really builds suspense, you never feel vulnurable and you are often stocked up on supplies.

I won't blame anyone disliking the game for "not being a resident evil game", as I surely would dislike it as well had I been into the earlier games in the series, but for all its flaws, it's still bloody fun. Mercenaries is where it's at for me, with its unprecedented combat and movement shining the brightest! It takes some time getting used to for sure, but it's very rewarding once fully grasped!

All in all, it comes down to what you're after. It won't really live up to building an intriguing story, it won't scare you with psychological horror, and it will most certainly infuriate you in some campaign and QTE segments, but holy christ will it shine with the fun, dynamic combat and movement system! If you want action, get this or RE5. If you're more for horror, get RE7!

Resident Evil 6, is an action-adventure third-person shooter video game and the ninth installment in the Resident Evil series, developed and published by Capcom. It was released for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 on October 2, 2012 and for Microsoft Windows on March 22, 2013.

RE6's story is told thru the viewpoints of 7 characters, split between 4 scenarios which follows one of four main protagonists - Leon S. Kennedy, Chris Redfield, Jake Muller and Ada Wong and each one has its own unique flavour. (Eg: Leon's Scenario tries to recreate the original RE survival horror feel, Chris's scenario felt more gung-ho military styled.)

Prior knowledge of previous Resident Evil games while recommended, is not required to enjoy this game. I would personally recommend playing RE5 first though as this game's has a pretty similar feel to it, both controls and gameplay-wise. Story-wise, one of the main characters also has an important plot-connection with a character in RE5.

The story is interesting, if extremely over-dramatic hollywoodish at times. Expect to see gratuitous explosions, story bosses that just won't die unless the plot requires it, and stupidly cool but unnecessary action sequences.

Like RE5, this game's appeal is in its campaign co-op mode. 
The player characters from each scenario will have their own partners which are controlled by either the computer AI or another human player via online multiplayer. Co-op controls are pretty much the same as it was in RE5, but I didn't like that they removed the ability to trade a weapon / item to your co-op partner. Everyone now have their own loot drop.

Graphically, while the environments and lighting are good looking, I don't see much difference compared to RE5 and i'm assuming its using the same engine. While RE5 puts you in a mostly wilderness environment, RE6 has a more urban feel to it. Sound effects are crisp and sharp, and the english voice-over work is still very good with each character voices fitting their role well.

The controls, while certainly reeks of "consolitis" feels alot more fluid then RE5. This time, you can move while aiming down your sights. It still doesn't exactly feel like a FPS though so don't expect it to feel as such. 

RE6 now adds the ability to drive vehicles. You can expect to be driving cars in some scenarios,  or piloting a helicopter in some others. Controls are arcadey and simplistic of course, so don't expect much depth in vehicle controls. Still, it was a nice addition.

The best improvement is surprisingly the now classic Quick Time Events (QTEs). People who HATE QTEs, will be happy to know that there is now an option setting to actually skip them! If you are the sort that likes QTEs however, you will be happy to know that the keys to press them are now logically placed and isn't as silly as how RE5 did them.

Overall Rating: 7 / 10
Overall feels like a slight improvement to RE5's mechanics, using the exact same engine. As always, it is much more interesting to co-op the campaign with a friend. Definitely no longer a survival horror like the original Resident Evil, and it is basically a 30 hours rollercoaster hollywood action film all the way till the end. 

I'm giving it a slightly lower score then RE5 because for me at least, it gave me a "Been There, Done That" feel as I have played RE5 before. That said, if you enjoyed RE5, you will like this one.

RE6 makes for a solid third person shooter game. While the weapons do not have a realistic feel (nor do they attempt to give that impression), they behave in a way where it really doesn't matter. The gunplay is solid, with everything behaving as it should (with the exception of the hydra, being a 10ga sawn off, I'd expect a LOT more power than it actually offers). Knives and melee attacks do not make for insta-kills, introducing a dynamic of risk vs conservation.

Content in RE6 is FAR from lacking. The game has possibly hundreds of hours of gameplay with the MANY gamemodes offered (most of which I haven't even tried yet, admittedly), and fun side stuff to explore such as notes, figures, and backstory for down time between play throughs. Said content is also well thought out and very polished, making for a very eenjoyable experience throughout. 

Models and lighting (especially the wet-look shine) are superb, though the textures are a bit lacking in the resolution department. Then again, what can you expect from a console port?

That being said, this IS a console port, and it shows. Some of the controls (especially for the much loathed QTEs, or Quick Time Events) are finnicky at best, and maddening at worst, and the default binding layout is borderline insane and will frustrate any PC veteran. Then again, the developers did try to bridge the gap, and offer a lot of features that PC vets will love such as FOV settings and some control over the graphic settings.

On the note of the QTEs... Yes, they are possibly THE most annoying things in gaming besides BSODs and CTDs. For me, they ruin the experience and many players will agree. That being said, there IS an option where the game completes them for you, eliminating a lot of the frustrating nonsense that ruins an otherwise awesome experience. Unfortunately, I have noticed that if a player joins your game who does not have the feature activated, it will force you to complete the QTEs as if you had the feature turned off as well. While I suppose this makes sense as it will prevent players from having an unfair advantage over others, it's frustrating as you cannot control who can and cannot join your game.

Players joining, both as friendlies and enemies, can make the game even more fun, however it can also be the one thing, besides QTEs, that ruins the experience entirely. You can either make your game public, limit it to friends, or go solo, and thats it. You cannot set any preference for Mic or no Mic, QTEs, skill level, etc. Furthermore, there is no kick option, forcing you to leave your own game if you're stuck with an incompetent/trollish teammate, or enemies that would rather use exploits to get their kills. This issue is further exacerbated by the huge distance between hard-save points (there is a soft-save system of checkpoints which are lost as soon as you end a session) which can cause you to lose up to an hour of gameplay when you leave the game. Furthermore, the lack of a mute option when dealing with Hot Mic (never turning their mic off, or players who play in absurdly noisey environments, or players who are eight-year-olds) players can be just as maddening. 

When it comes down to it, Resident Evil 6 is a great game. I would strongly advise playing with people you know and work well with though, as this game is strongly geared towards a cooperative playstyle, and bad players can ruin the experience. Grab it while its on sale, and you won't be sorry.

Resident Evil 6 by no means achieves any sort of medium-pushing greatness at any point, but there its set of mechanics is capable of coming together to create a perfectly serviceable and sometimes-compelling action game. However, RE6 does completely fall flat as a survival-horror game, and its multiple campaigns are mostly awkwardly-paced and poorly-written, and the game tends to generally lack a consistent atmosphere or mood that made the earlier entries in the franchise famous. The game tends to achieve its highest points in its bonus and periphery modes (Mercenaries, specifically), where the player is afforded a lot more freedom to use all of the action mechanics at once. The interplay between shooting and melee, dodging and spacing, performing counterattacks, and utilizing environmental familiarity all gels together to be a pretty dang fun action game from time to time. None of these particular mechanics are best-in-genre or even the greatest available in the larger medium of contemporary videogames, but the combination available to the player feels pretty unique to RE6. However, it feels as if the vast majority of content in the game doesn't ever demand the player to utilize the full array of RE6's mechanics at any time. The 4 campaigns feel like they attempt to highlight different distinctive moods and playstyles, and it comes with the cost of sacrificing that interesting and unique interplay of mechanics that RE6 houses under its hood in order to match whatever arbitrary "feel" each campaign strives to achieve. In setting up its separate campaigns this way, it also feels like the game fails to communicate clearly the amount of options the player has during combat sequences, and its unfortunate, because it took me a long time to even realize some of the options I had when it came to evading certain attacks, performing counterattacks, and the variety of movement and spacing options available. It feels like the game barely just tries to set itself up as RE5 with move-and-shoot, but it actually contains a lot more nuance than that.

With that said, RE6 is far from perfect, but it sometimes shines during a few moments sprinkled throughout its huge campaign offerings, and Mercenaries is a nice highlight of the game's distinctive action game feel that can be revisited either casually or hardcore. For anyone that's looking to experience a somewhat unique action title, I personally recommend it, but I understand that it won't carry universal appeal due to its largely incohesive design. If you're an action fan and have played all of the action game darlings (Devil May Cry 4, DmC: Devil May Cry, and Metal Gear Rising get my nods), you might not be too bad off grabbing RE6 on sale and approaching it as an action game. Even more power to you if you can convince a buddy to play cooperative with you.

I want it to be clear from the beginning – I am a Resident Evil fan. And I liked most of new Resident Evil games. Most, but not this one. 
While I completed totally unfriendly RE 4 PC without mouse support mods and enjoyed the hell out of RE5 by playing both single and local co-op with my brother, this game just fatigued me after a few hours. 
Its main problems is terrible controls allocation and a ton of useless commands spread throughout most of the keyboard. Don’t fool yourself – you’re not going to use even 30% of them, and if you try you get dead while you look for the correct kay. I honestly cannot imagine if the controls are easier with the gamepad, since some of commands required two keys, plus a correct direction key. 
Another issue is  that it’s bloated to four separate campaigns whose structure is at least inconsistent. So is storytelling. I was disappointed when after completing the first (Leon) campaign I got through most of weird Chris Redfield campaign, and discovered, that some sequenced I did from the same perspective, instead of opposite. The pinnacle of WTF was when at the end of first campaign i reached the part already shown in prologue, and it was completely retold in different way. That’s not how you are supposed to tell viewpoint related stories.
What’s good about it? Probably graphics are okay, but they don’t impress me much after RE5, or rather introduction of X360 generation graphics. Really nothing else was better than in 5. The graphical low point for me was the new image of Ada Wong, who now looks as a china doll with much too wide cheeks, and too small mouth. Maybe it was an attempt to make the game more realistic, but I preferred the more manga-like version from RE4, and CGI movies. 
The worst part is that I was genuinely interested in the story, and gave up on it near the end of second campaign. My recommendation? RE Revelations is a much better game even though it was converted from Nintendo DS. So either try this one, or wait for the upcoming sequel.

Once again a game I can neither recommend nor downrate which proves there should be a "neutral" button. It is difficult to evaluate this game considering the issues and also the good parts it has. I am in between and being offered the two extremes only is not sufficient.

The good stuff:

--- The game offers not one but four campaigns! This is pretty cool considering the 4 couples you have which means 8 characters - each with a different personality, extra attack or weapon and importance when it comes to the storyline. Also, enemies approaching you differ in each campaign. The same goes to the locales. While Leon and Helena traverse through the big city, a cemetery and a cathedral offing dozens of zombies Chris and Piers do the same but in China. They are attacked by J'avos - these are infected people with the ability to plan their attacks and can also use firearms.

--- Graphics / cutscenes / sound effects -> production value. Well, after episode 5 it was obvious the creators would take this to another level.  The game looks stunning and the atmosphere is there. The coop and action sequences once again decrease the horror elements but nobody can say they did not try! Also, there are dozens of cutscenes and in the game's menu you can rewatch all. Altogether I'm sure it will take at least 2 hours to go these in one sitting.

--- Longevity. Once again we have collectibles that come in the form of emblems. I have found many but could not find a lot either. There are no more treasures as collectibles. Instead, there is something else that is dropped by the enemies and they represents points. This amount can be used to purchase skills. These can then be levelled up. 3 skills can be active at a time and there are enemy-specific ones, too. So, you and your coop partner need to work together and decide who equips what. Multiplayer also returns in the form of Mercenaries and there is now a new game mode called Agent Hunt.

The bad stuff:

--- 4 campaigns: In terms of story and characters this is really good but there are too many intersections. In fact, there are boss battles you need to play twice. Really? Of all this it is Ada's (4th) campaign that is the worst. First of all, almost all the areas are familiar and you encounter hardly any new enemies. Throughout all the campaign you know what's going to happen and the ending is a total letdown. Not only this but Ada plays alone. Your friend assumes the role of a so-called Agent - a guy who's just there so that the creators can tell they did really make a coop game. Agent wears a mask and does not have a real name.  In the cutscenes you see Ada alone and throughout the campaign Agent cannot interact with anything. You cannot open doors or chests, you cannot solve any puzzles and no QTEs for you (which is actually good). You can pick up bullets, of course and fight with Ada but feel like an unnecessary character who does not even have a story.

--- Cheesiness: If you thought episodes 5's dialogue was bad you are in for a great surprise. Some of the conversations the protagonists have are just dumb. In fact, you can easily guess what will happen next. The script should have been reworked at least 3 times to eliminate some of the worst dialogues this franchise has ever seen.

--- Boss battles: They are waaaaaaaay toooooooooo loooooooooooooong! You battle the same guy while he assumes at least 3 different forms one after the other. The tactic is different as well as the environment. It is not necessarily a problem but the game is very difficult and also you are 100% sure you eliminated your foe when he returns once more to annoy you. I have to admit the enemies are great (each one of them poses a real threat) but you battle them for too long. This gets boring and aggravating considering the difficulty of the game.

--- Difficulty level: This game is annoyingly difficult. From time to time you get a QTE which is next to impossible to complete for the first time. Missing it will result in a death cutscene - well, I appreciate the developers wanted to show me what cutscenes they had conjured up in their mind but this is still pretty annoying. Boss battles can be a pain and the controls do not help either. It is a sad thing to say since this game enables you to do pretty much everything: you can run, do fistfight, dodge and even slide. And finally: you can walk while aiming at an enemy! The problem is with the turning and the speed. Also, the camera does not help and sometimes you get attacked because our heroes are looking at what's going on elsewhere in the distance.

For me Resident Evil 6 was annoying. I could handle 5 but the latest instalment was just too much. Campaign and firefight was good but Ada's story was a silly way to end a game and the difficulty level did not pose a real challenge (it was annoying instead).

If you are a newcomer, do not start with this one. If you liked the predecessors you can pick it up but buckle up as the ride will be long, tiresome and irritating! Of course, for hardcore RE fans the 6th instalment is a must.

Resident Evil 4 on PS2 was what brought me to the Resident Evil series, and I enjoyed it a lot. That said, Resident Evil started out as Survival Horror, and started to lean towards a more of an action game, which is perfectly fine if B.O.W.'s were the main focus.  

Resident Evil 6 provides a mostly linear gameplay which provides you with a specific objective after another. I feel that it takes out the exploration, which I enjoyed from the previous games. They also have route mechanic that functions similiar to that of the Dead Space series that tells you where to go. There were no need to back track.

Ever since RE4, the melee mechanics has been evolving for resident evil. RE6 offers counter-attacks, melee without the need to stagger enemies, environmental kills and more. The counter-attacks are dependant on the enemy's attack as well as the weapon you are wielding. Meleeing on command also depends on the weapon you are wielding. The combat system just makes the game a bit more fun, especially in the mercenaries mode. 

I never really got into the story into older Resident Evil games, for the exception of Veronica: X, but the Chris's story really stood out for me. Leon's story was similar to previous RE games. I was playing RE5 on the PS3, and getting matched with other people was always an issue. Playing RE6 on PC, however, coop is pretty common. There's even a matchmaking group for any multiplayer modes. It's always a better experience to play online.

LONG REVIEW - BE PATIENT. 

The best advice I can give if you are going to play RE6, is start with the Leon missions. Do missions in the order they appear; Leon, Chris, etc. I thought you chose one character and played the whole game with that person and skill set. I chose Ada, the last character, and it was incredibly difficult with hardly any ammo. Sheer desperation made me mention how hard it was in a forum, and I was told start with Leon.

 The game is cram packed full of cut-scenes, either long or short. The short ones are on average about every two minutes. It constantly pulls control away from the player. It might just be that  the ground rocks, but then you lose control, the camera sways, and the character wobbles. Then you have to press your control keys again to get going. There are parts of the game where it happens less, then there parts when it's non-stop. There are even times when it takes camera angle control from you and expects you to carry on.

 Over-all though it is a constant wrangle to maintain control. When you get to a ledge, you can't just jump up it. You have to wait for it to say 'space', then you can press space and jump up. Nearly everything is controlled in this way throughout. Endless, endless pressing keys.

 That brings you onto the quick-time-events. Non-stop button mashing that has nothing to do with normal control. It's Ok to an extent, but even the most patient person gets annoyed. You think, "what is this for".

 Then onto how difficult it can be. There is one part I recall. 3rd Chris chapter, you have to run across a load of boats and moorings. You have to make it within time, or wherever you are you die. Checkpoints make you repeat it until you get it right. I can not tell you how bad that whole event was. I was screaming. (Not the only time I was screaming in this game either.)

 5/10 is generous, but I don't quite think it's a 4/10. It's strong points are that sometimes the combat is great. The sets can be OK, but mostly they are dimly lit. The cathedral chapter in the Leon campaign is epic. If only they had made the whole game like that.

 The bosses are just unbelievably annoying. The Leon boss kept coming back at various latter stages of the Leon missions. I became sick of the sight of it, and sick of shooting it. Completely stupid method to kill it. I had to search online to find out how. What they have done is build up the difficulty over each character's campaign. Only it doesn't work. It feels like catastrophic insulting garbage from the developers, and you want blood as compensation. They try to make it a huge experience. However all it does is fall flat on it's face by kicking you in the teeth non-stop.

 Falling over is something that happens a lot with your character. Endless boom, flat on your back. It's noisy a lot. In fact they should have called the game - 'Boom, flat on your back'. I honestly don't know if I can finish it. I have given it a good go. I sold RE5 (CD-copy) unfinished as well.

I can recommend this game, with caveats.  The story is passable, but the dialog is almost universally unbearable.  Cheesy bordering on sickening in some parts.  If I hear another character say "Are you serious?" or "You gotta be kidding me!" in a Resident Evil game, I will probably close the game right then and there and throw my wireless mouse at a baby.  

The gameplay is... unpolished? To say the least.  The degree to which the game starts to get annoying / hard to play / needlessly complicated varies depending on which campaign you play.  I saved Leon's story for last since I was hoping his would be the best / most entertaining / interesting.  Mistakes were made.  In order of enjoyable gamplay, I would rank the campaigns Jake > Ada > Chris > Leon.  In order of enjoyable story, I would rank the campaigns Ada > Jake > Chris > Leon.

Leon's campaign really makes me upset.  It has a different set of enemies than the other 3 campaigns and even on normal difficulty, you will die a lot.  I have played almost every Resident Evil game and consider myself to be pretty experienced in the gameplay, I still found myself dying a lot to a lot of stupid things, most of which you cannot control.  For example, there is one boss encounter where you are forced to take constant damage for a brief period.  If you are below half health before this segment starts, you will die instantly and cannot be revived by your partner.  In another section, you are attacked by concealed enemies and without prior knowledge of the encounter, there would be no feasible way to avoid incoming damage (it's a semi-submerged area).  Again, if you are attacked in this spot with low health, you will immediately die with no chance to heal or be revived by your partner (you get knocked down and then instead of triggering the "hurt" state where you can crawl away to safety, you will instantly drown).

QTE's are also a big part of my problem with this game.  They are more intrusive than RE4 or 5's, in my opinion, and very rarely add any enjoyment to the gameplay experience.  Having played RE4 somewhat recently, the QTE events in that game were never as punishing and always at least gave you a brief warning before you were expected to react.  A lot of QTE in this game expect you to know what is coming and react to it with prior knowledge.  I died a lot of times to random QTE events during cutscenes that had no warning and didn't really provide any good context or necessity for them.

The prologue would make you think that Leon's is the campaign you should start with, I would put it at second or third.  If you play it first, you might quit the game entirely before you get to the more fun campaigns.  If you save it til the end like I did, you will leave the game with a bad taste in your mouth.  Leon's campaign has some of the worst dialog and the weakest plot of the 4 main campaigns, in my opinion.  While the whole story is traversed by most of the cast, Leon's portion just feels icky.  Helena is a terrible partner and Leon himself is basically a one-liner spouting husk of his RE4 self.  Other campaigns have bad dialog, but at least I didn't actively want the characters in those stories to die so that I would not have to endure it.

I have not personally played co-op but from the single player missions, I can tell that the co-op experience here is almost identical to that of Resident Evil 5.  You and your partner will often be working together nearby, followed by sporadic sections of splitting up to help each other through obstacles while covering one another.  It lends itself to an "easy" co-operative experience, meaning there is low performance stress on you and your partner.  At most, you will find yourself running to knock an enemy off of your partner, whereas most of your co-op interactions will involve pressing buttons and spinning the stick to move a platform or open a door.

All in all, if you like Resident Evil games or third person shooters involving zombies, you'll enjoy this game.  If you're not a fan of the Resident Evil franchise or only casually looking at this game as a co-op option, I would recommend looking elsewhere.

This is from the perspective of someone who has played the Xbox version first, and the PC version second. The Good of this port is the same for the Xbox version, and I will review it as an action game, not a horror game. It is clearly not meant to be scary, but to be fun and make you feel awesome for breaking through all that it can throw at you. If you are unable to accept that Resident Evil is no longer meant to frighten you, you will likely hate this game for straying so far from its roots and reputation for scares. If you are able to look past the reputation of Resident Evil, read on.


The Good: (what to consider when purchasing)

Resident Evil has never had such tight, fluid controls. The new movement and dodge mechanics make you feel like a badass, tucking and sliding out of the way in real time, through your own skill rather than a contextual quick time event as it used to be. Reversal attacks add a layer of cool that no other entry in the series before it has had. You're now able to turn the flow of combat from hectic run-and-gunning into a scene straight out of a kung-fu B movie, rewarding you for your quick reflexes and giving you much needed breathing room when the enemies swarm you. What could be more awesome than grabbing a leaping zombie out of the air and stomping on it before whipping around, kicking another so hard it spins backwards on its heels, then slamming it into the ground with a DDT from behind? Probably while doing it as classic Resident Evil characters, which this game thoughtfully provides.

The gameplay varies between campaigns, as you would expect. Leon's focuses more on melee combat than the rest due to scarce ammunition and the zombies' resistance to bullet damage. Expect to be punished harshly for not getting your reversal timing down, as zombies behave unpredictably; Leaping at random, tripping over their own feet, lunging from the floor to pull you down with them, etc. Chris' campaign is full on testosterone infused action, hardly a dull moment to be found and plenty of fun enemy types to encounter and learn the weaknesses of. J'avo are much more predictable than the zombies, but are able to use ranged weaponry, making combat much more reliant on cover. Ada's campaign is a little more like the Resident Evil we recognize, with more puzzles and being rewarded for avoiding enemy contact, though obviously that's not possible most of the time as this is still an action game. Jake's campaign is a mix of the three, combining the over-the-top melee combat of Leon's campaign, the cover based shooting of Chris' and the enemy avoidance of Ada's. It works well, though can be a bit schitzophrenic as you would be required to change playstyle often.

The game has a wealth of content because of these four campaigns, and if playtime is something you consider when buying a game, you'd get your money's worth here for the sheer amount of it all. It's not Skyrim levels of vast, but for the type of game it was aiming to be, it certainly could have been a lot less. *cough-cough-OperationRaccoonCity-cough*


The Bad: (nitpicks and gripes)

While all that's well and good, there are moments where the camera will suddenly yank away from your perspective and focus on something in the background, but still have combat continue around you. This leaves you helpless as enemies are allowed to swarm in closer, or your precious ammo is wasted as you start shooting at a door that just opened because the game insisted on pulling the camera away to show it to you. Though the gameplay is varied between the campaigns, all of them begin to lose steam half way through. Leon's campaign recycles boss fights to the Nth degree, so much so that you may get frustrated as you have to repeat the same fights over and over with little to no variation between them. Past chapter 3, Chris' campaign just throws more and more enemies at you in the despirate attempt to heighten tension more than it had the previous chapters, though because there's nothing really different from them it just feels like an annoying slog. There is a moment where you take control of a jump jet, but it never happens again and it's over in about five minutes. Jake's campaign remains the freshest the longest, with cheesy car chases and one liners that put a smile on my face, but his final chapter reuses a fair amount elements from Chris' campaign. That's to be expected though, as Chris and Jake are meant to meet here, but they still feel a little too similar at times. Ada's later chapters recycle a lot of the same scenes from the other three chapters with minor tweaks here and there, so you end up feeling as though you're going through the motions, tying loose ends rather than playing as a seperate character.


The Ugly: (the game's major failings)

The PC version's load times and compatibility issues with most computers and hardware make it unquestionably inferior to the console versions upon which the game was built off of. It can take anywhere from 8 minutes to 15 minutes just to reach the main menu even on a good computer, while far more graphically intense games zoom past it, which is completely inexcusable in this day and age. It absolutely cripples this port's lastability by comparison, and though infrequent, the occasional crash will make that 8 - 15 minute wait between startups feel all the more brutal. That the game has been out this long for PC and still has these issues is a shameful neglect of its players who are already wary of this game's reputation for being so unlike any other Resident Evil. There isn't even a chat box to use and communicate with the rare person who joins your game, so if you don't have a mic, you're left with only the character's generic "thanks!" or "look out!" commands. It's no wonder the PC multiplayer lobbies of this port are ghost towns when it takes so long to load and your ability to communicate is being harshly limited without such a basic feature. Imagine having no way to explain a monster's weakness while your partner continues to get hurt by it, not noticing what the monster is doing and soaking up resources for it. It would be very frustrating, naturally.


Final Verdict: (CONSOLE version) 7/10

Resident Evil 6 is a very functional, varied game full of cheese that'll give you many hours of brainless fun. If you go into it with the same mindset that you would when approaching a John Woo action movie, you'll have a blast. It's silly, but it seems to be fully aware of that, and just tries to do its own thing.

However, and I cannot stress this enough, play the console versions.

Were it not for the load time, the occasional crash wouldn't be such a big deal and would have remained merely in the Bad, but when combined it makes the experience of playing the PC version not worth the awesome collaboration with Valve's own Left 4 Dead 2 gang and the inclusion of the 250+ enemy minigame, No Mercy mode. Were it not for the lack of a chat box, newbies wouldn't be such an annoyance, but without the ability to explain a bosses weakness or where to go, they simply slow down your game rather than help you in any way that your AI partner couldn't do better than them. It all contributes to the game's lonely multiplayer scene, with more than a third of the game's content going purpetually unplayed (nobody plays Mercenaries, No Mercy, Agent Hunt, or even the other campaigns, just Leon's). It seems unlikely at this stage, but I hope dearly that Capcom fixes the unforgivable startup times, as well as the compatibility issues for many common brands of graphics card. Until then, I recommend Resident Evil 6 as a whole, but not this version of it. There is no excuse for missing basic PC gaming features and 8 - 15 minute load times in the modern era of gaming. Shameful display.

Having played this game that much, I decided to give it a proper review.
First off, I'd like to mention that I got this game back when it used to cost 60 bucks, with all dlcs, and it's worth every single penny. You can't just ignore how much love, effort and attention was put into the story and gameplay. The game itself is very replayable, even in campaign mode, because there are so many tiny details, that I am surprised to find even as of today. In certain locations, you will even intersect with other players, providing with richer understanding of the story while also allowing you to play through certain parts briefly with the 4 of you together. Unfortunately this feature is skipped by most public players these days, but you can still use it with friends. The controls are difficult, I agree, it took me over 100 hours to get the hang of it, but once you do, you should feel invincible with all the action stuff possible here.


Now about that action part: Most of us Resident Evil fans hate it, but not me. Back when I was a kid, and played the first Resident Evil, I felt helpless and thought, "why the hell I can't roll, push or just straight kick that slow ass zombie in the face?" Not anymore. This is the first and probably the last game in the franchise that let's you initiate physical attacks without having you to do anything else. Some of you might say "But that's the whole point of Resident Evil!" I agree, but I still don't mind.



Aside from the story mode there are also extra modes that give tons of fun, and even though there aren't as many people, it is entirely possible to get full lobby :[olist]
[*]Mercenaries: Classic mercenaries, but with RE6 mechanics. Can be played with a friend or alone. I actually dislike Mercenaries for praising so much counter attacks to score high, because it quickly gets repetitive. Still, if you don't care about score, it's worth trying.

[*]Mercenaries No Mercy: Same as original mercenaries, but double the enemies both the amount and on the screen with Left 4 Dead 2 survivors added. In case, you need more challenge. If there were Left 4 Dead 1 survivors instead of L4D2, I would have liked this mode much more :)

[*]Survivors: The most unbalanced of them all and the worst just like most competitive modes. I don't recommend to touch it in public games. Mostly you will encounter players using Piers abusing quick switch exploit with anti-material rifle that let's you skip reloading and rapid fire any weapon, quick shot or worse - cheaters, which makes it very toxic. Still if you can play with preset rules, it is fun. Can be played in Deathmatch or Team Mode (up to 3v3)

[*]Onslaught: My second favourite. It uses the same concept as mercenaries - rack up the combos to send the enemies to your opponent. The higher the combo the more dangerous enemies are sent. Can get real messy after a few minutes :)

[*]Predator: Now this mode is addicting, my most favourite and the most balanced of them all. You take turns playying as Ustanak that big frigging Nemesis-like behemoth in a 5v1 game. Ustanak is very fast and strong. You and your team need to cooperate to take him down. Many complain that he is op. Nah. You guys just need to learn the controls and have a good strategy. The controls thing applies to Ustanak as well. He is the only creature in the game with good controls, but can still be killed as easily as Agents.

[*]Siege: This needs to be reworked, which is not happening since the game is long abandoned. Very similar to Left 4 Dead versus with the added protect-the-civilian detail. You take turns as Agents and Creatures. Agents need to protect the BSAA agent from being killed, until time runs out, while creatures work together to kill the agent. There is no delivery location. So you just either run around or hold out in a certain location, which is probably not going to work. 

[*]Agent Hunt: Mentioning this mode the last, because it has wasted potential and could have been much better. It let's you join other people campaign modes to try and hunt them down as one of the creatures. So why is it bad? Controls are terrible and not much can be done about it. Creatures to play as are limited, you will mostly play as zombie or J'avo and sometimes will be lucky to mutate into something stronger, which won't make much difference because of terrible controls. And not all locations are available. Some of the available ones are bad and you will be forced to watch unskipable cutscenes, which make already difficult hunt even more frustrating.

[u]Summary Review[/u]
Not a bad game at all, so as long as you don't treat it like your typical RE game. Recommended to be played with online friends, or else it'll suck.


[u]Detailed Review[/u]
When I first played this on the PS3 on release, I was completely appalled with RE6's control mechanics. Trying to turn the franchise people knew and loved into a typical FPS shoot em' up, this is not what people expected after RE5.

However, as time passed, this game has found a place in my heart. Not as another RE game, but as a coop game to play with friends online, and this is where the game really shines.

When you play this game by yourself or play on split screen, the game is a chore. AI buddy is too retarded to be of any help, and playing split screen really can strain the eyes, especially if you don't have a monitor bigger than 27".

Honestly, I wish Capcom put the option to play offline coop on dual display, rather than being forced to just stick with two cropped rectangles on one screen, then this game would have gotten more thumbs up on my end.

But regardless, if you have a friend to play with and both of you have steam, get this game when it's on sale and play with each other online. You guys will have an awesome time.

Also a warning: If you guys are here for the story...yeah, you might want to chuck a good portion of that out the window. Most of the story is garbage, and won't be fun for either of you if you guys plan to take this game seriously. I tried playing this game both serious and both as casual fun, and I found myself loving to crack jokes at this games' story than actually being sucked into the story. And I'm all [b]for[/b] story when it comes to games.

If you still plan to get the game, just know the controls take some time in getting used to. But if you're familiar with playing AAA fps games, then you'll get the hang of the controls faster. But if the only thing you've played is Resident Evil...you might curse the controls until the day you die.

But all in all, this is a game that people should try out for kicks. Just make sure to catch it when a sale hits.

Resident Evil 6 is hands down the single worst Resident Evil game ever made by Capcom.  Basically if Resident Evil 5 and Operation Raccoon City had a deformed digital game-love-child using Call of Duty as a surrogate, RE6 is what would come out of it. The game seeks hard throughout its 30 - 40 hours of game play to find an identity, and unfortunately it finds 4 different identities, none of which are stellar and ALL of which were lifted directly from other games that unsurprisingly did it better.

Leon's campaign is a contrite, try-hard amalgamation of Resident Evil 4 and 5's Tomb Raidery, Mario-ey parts filled with nonsensical obstacles, endless holes in the earth, exploding air vehicles and cars, and poor excuses for zombie scares. - not to mention a clear disregard for the intelligence of the Biohazard fanbase when they repeatedly make Leon an unlearning single celled organism whose only display of personality is to make quips about his luck with women. Ignoring the tutorial which attempts to Tarantino the story, poorly, and introduces the main trope of Leon's game: Everything is always on fire and will always explode, you start out in what almost seems like it might be a throwback to Resident Evil 2, until the first 5 or 6 pseudo-jump-scares officially turn you off of any notion that this is a survival horror game. When you finally do meet "zombies", they are fast moving but boring engagements often composed of QTE and they don't even necessarily die from headshots. If this wasn't bad enough, there is no logical consistency whatsoever to the plot and the game tries offensively, pathetically hard to convince you that "This is just like Raccoon City." Yea, the god awful game Operation Raccoon City, maybe. Certainly nothing like RE2 and maybe a bit like RE3 considering that's where the franchise went action-centric.

Sherry's campaign (because I refuse to call it Jake's) is a mixed mess of third person shooter elements and stealth gameplay wherein a pathetic emulation of Nemesis and the Tyrant happen to be in multiple chapters. It's not even a matter of Ustanak "stalking" you like Tyrant or Nemesis did because he doesn't stalk you. You are just forced via linear progression to be in the same area he is and then occasionally run from him and try not to piss him off. In fact, it seems like Capcom made it their goal to copy as much of Binary Domain as possible, but the thing is....Binary Domain was so  much better and it was pure third person shooter. There is far too much stealth gameplay involved, and don't even get me started on the horrid snowmobile sequence. Did I mention Jake is complete retcon and ruins the entire game on his own? Sorry Troy baker i.e the only voice actor in gaming. My issue isn't with you, you're good - but with this awful, awful, awful storywriting.

Chris's campaign, and this is the absolutely disgusting part, is the only solid one out of the original 3. It is pure, 100% third person shooter. Not the slightest trace of "survival horror". You're in the BSAA, obviously - ignoring entirely that his partner Jill is inexplicably no where to be found at all despite the numerous times they've been in the same situations and should be working together still - and you end up chasing "Ada" around the world, with biohazard outbreaks happening to be there each time, or happening while there. Frankly, if this had been it's own separate game in which terrorists and rebel armies are using BOWs and viral weapons with some over-arching story that made sense, it would have been a solid game. Obviously not resident evil, but a solid game. But this is Resident Evil. Like I said though, Chris's campaign is the only one of the main 3 which maintains consistent game mechanics and never forces you into complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, out of place gameplay sequences like flying airplanes except for the one extremely long and ridiculous car chase scene. On top of that, the dudebro sentiment of the story is at least commiserable. 

That leaves Ada's campaign. Before Capcom noob-patched the game, Ada was on her own. No partner - could not co-op. It was the only one that resembled survival horror and it was actually fun to boot. Not to mention, you HAD to play it to actually piece together the god awful story that tied the entire game together. Now it's co op and the entire allure of that campaign is gone.

Despite those massive failures, the game does have some decent non-story multiplayer, and mercenaries mode is the best it's ever been. It's just too bad the game, like all modern Capcom titles, got pounded into oblivion by oversaturated DLC.

This game is an aberration.

As a Resident Evil game, it fails completely. There is almost no horror or tension at all in the game. Some inklings of it in Leon's campaign is all you will get.

Story wise, it's completely non-nonsensical and doesn't really advance anything. On the other hand, it's a fully self contained story with almost no references to other games in the series.

It also falls completely flat as a third person action shooter. The pacing is terrible, there is a tiny amount of enemy variety. Getting shot instantly knocks you on your back. You will have to drop stuff from your inventory every few minutes even on higher difficulties.

The game is also plagued with a constant stream of Quick Time Events. All of them different, and all of them extremely tightly timed, to the point where you'll have to take your hand off your mouse to mash your keyboard with both hands to beat them. It's absurd.

The camera is used to increase the difficulty of certain boss fights for no clear reason. It'll switch from over the shoulder to fixed angle with no warning, sometimes making you about-face right into instant death.

Even the COOP is messed up. Ada's campaign gives you a token faceless companion who can't even interact with doors or the environment, unlike in the other 3 campaigns. It was obviously meant to be a single player experience.

The characters look nice, have a good amount of detail to them, but the environment textures are terrible. You will constantly get closeups of textures so blurry you can't even identify what they're supposed to represent.

Avoid this game at all costs. It manages to be worst in every way than Resident Evil 5. It fails as survival horror, 3rd person shooter action and even COOP. Do not touch this turd.

This is probably one of the best examples of "mixed bags" that I can think of. Resident Evil 6 is both great and horrible in so many ways I won't be able to go over them all but for that reason alone I feel it's a game for anyone who considers themselves a "gamer" should play at least once to see what I mean. 

  RE6 is an action title with the occasional horror aesthetic thrown in to tie itself in whith its lineage. While best played with a friend it's very much playable solo. Players will take control one of 3 pairs of characters (or possibly an additional duo or a single character for the fourth campaign) as they experience the story of the game from three different perspectives and this is where the idea of the mixed bag begins. Instead of a single cohearent script, its divided amoungst three different stories that constantly leaves the player confused and in a stupor. Even with all the campaigns completed I had to read some of the in-game lore from the easily missed extras menu once I shot enough blue emblems in the game. While the Resident Evil series isn't known for its story, previous entries were at least easy to understand, not the case with this title, often throwing characters at the player that even veterans have no idea as to who they are.

  Controling the characters is another issue for this game. In many games designed with a controller in mind, often times a button is used as a modifier for every other button. In previous games, what would be holding down the left trigger would then make the character aim at which point the right will fire. While that is a simple method, RE6 has layers of these that are poorly explained if at all. New players should take their time figuring out the controls as even into my second campaign I was still learning what certain combinations of buttons and motions did. However once learned, the complex control scheme actually makes for excellent stylish feats but not everyone will get used to them.

  Probably one of the best things about the title is how it can incorporate multiplayer into the campaign. With certain options selected, a player can allow others online to join the game as a co op partner, random players to take control of basic enemies for a little extra challange, and even run into other players who are in other campaigns in overlapping story sections where up to four players can take on a segment of their campaigns together. The only problem with this is that due to the small playerbase many of these things wont happen without coordination with other players such as through Steam groups.

  While there is definitly more to say I feel that these are some of the biggest issues. I do enjoy the game despite all its faults, however I will say that it may be my least favorite of the RE series that I have experienced. Many others damn this game as complete garbage, and while not all of their complaints are invalid or wrong, it does have entertainment value and some excellent points. If you are looking for a coop third-person action title, there are not many on the market but you should not settle for this unless you are already played through better titles. Give it a look but be aware it is flawed.

Resident Evil 6 (RE6) is the third Resident Evil game I’ve played (only played 4, 5, and 6 since I don’t have a Playstation). The game has a relatively low metacritic rating (69 last I checked) but I found it to be exactly what I expected after playing RE5 a year earlier. If you’ve only seen the Resident Evil movies then you may not be aware that the games have a completely different storyline and I think they’ve been retconned a few times as well.  You would probably recognize a bunch of the characters though since almost every Resident Evil character I know appears in RE6.

The game is a third person “over the shoulder” game played in coop with another person. Just like Resident Evil 5, if you don’t have a friend playing with you, the computer controls the other guy. There are 4 campaigns for you to play and in each of them you can play one of the 2 characters. The campaigns all intersect multiple times so you might be playing the Leon campaign and run in to Chris Redfield. Then when you’re playing the Chris campaign you run into Leon and play as the other side of the encounter. It’s a great way to see the plot from various viewpoints and you’ll understand why characters are acting in a certain way. After you’ve completed the game you can go back and play as the second character in each campaign as well. There’s over 50 hours of gameplay to be had in single player alone. Each campaign is divided into chapters and each chapter into sections, for example Leon Campaign Chapter 1-1, 1-2, 1-3, etc. The game saves at checkpoints during each section, so if you’re knocked out and your partner doesn’t revive you in time, you restart at the checkpoint. Your inventory is saved between sections and you can replay previous sections freely. There is no more “inventory screen,” now it’s just a quick menu where you hold a button to display and scroll through your items. There is no level up system, but you can gather “exp” points to unlock perks such as improved damage or better aim stability. Then you can pick which 3 perks you want equipped between missions. So you can replay levels over and over for more exp or replay some of the bosses a few times for fun.

I believe the complaint that a lot of Resident Evil purists had was that beginning with RE5, the games aren’t really “survival horror” anymore. Now the focus is on action and shooting. I remember in RE4 that conserving ammunition was a big challenge so you use melee attacks as much as possible. The melee system has been enhanced a great deal since then and ammunition has become a lot more plentiful (you can also replay levels to grab ammo and then just save + quit). You’ll definitely do a lot of shooting, but you should definitely master the hand to hand (or knife fighting depending on which character you’re playing). 

Storywise, the game picks up a few years after Resident Evil 5. The world is continuing to circle the drain as various warlords around the world use biological weapons to create zombies and other super powered monsters. Each campaign has its own antagonist though they cross over a lot, as mentioned earlier. If you haven’t played the previous games you might not understand a few “peculiarities” of the playable characters. I certainly didn’t know who some of the people were and the ways that their backstories drive the game’s plot.  It is mostly understandable though if you play the whole game through. Just accept that everyone knows each other from previous games.

Pros:
+Excellent built in co-op play for the campaign, and for different game modes like Mercenaries. Steam sells the “complete pack” that includes everything, kind of like a Game of the Year edition.
+Very long game (at least 35 hours even if you rush), you’ll get your money’s worth.
+A lot of replay value (you can unlock “perks” by grinding for exp).
+You can play as a monster! Join someone’s game and ♥♥♥♥ them up. A few people tried dropping into my brother and my games, but since we were on levels with only normal zombie enemies (so they spawned as normal zombies), we blew them away easily lol.

Cons:
-Multi player is kind of dead now. Hard to find a game to join unless it’s a friend inviting you or vice versa.
-According to Resident Evil “purists” the game is more action than “survival horror.” If you’re new to Resident Evil games and just looking for a co-op shooter, this won’t bother you.
-There are a few times when you need to run through an area in a short amount of time (like escaping a giant enemy) and the camera keeps subtly shifting so you slightly change running directions and hit a wall or something, then you die. This is VERY annoying but only happens in a few areas. Most of the time you can play leisurely.

Overall I would definitely recommend Resident Evil 6 if you like action games and / or zombie bashing games. The visuals are disturbing and the monsters are grotesque, as expected in a Resident Evil game. The game is 100% better if you have a friend to join your game for coop play. And once you’re done with the campaigns you can spend a lot of time on the various game modes that are included, most especially the Mercenaries mode, which returns from Resident Evil 5. It’s kind of like a survival mode where you try to live to the end of the timer killing as many enemies as you can. The enemy types keep changing until you’re fighting mini bosses.

I'm writing this review as a gamer who owned and played Resident Evil 6 at launch, on console. Keep this in mind. Though so far the PC version is a very good port. 

Now, before you start calling me a newbie and etc. Let me post my Resident Evil credentials. 

- Heard about Resident Evil in Game Players magazine when I was in junior high
- Earned allowance and had mom buy me the original tallbox RE on PS1
- Loved it, got Directors cut and Resident Evil 2 as soon as they released. 
- I bought a Nintendo Gamecube JUST for the REMake. 
- I feel Nemesis doesn't get enough credit. 
- I have owned Resident Evil 4 on it's original release on Gamecube, plus the PS2 rerelease, Wii version, original ♥♥♥♥ PC version, and the recent HD re-release on PSN - as well as the Steam HD Re-release. 
- I bought a Dreamcast with Code: Veronica and feel it's the most unsung game in the entire series. 
- I believe the true downfall of the series stands with it's fanbase being Republican about game changes.

Resident Evil 6 gets A LOT of hate from critics and gamres alike, and why wouldn't it? The game is plagued by many of the issues that later RE games suffered from that caused the series to fall into extreme ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. 

That being said, Resident Evil 6? Is perfect. 

I love this game, you know why? It's EVERYTHING Resident Evil. And no one wants to admit it, we can all make jokes about Chris's campaign being Call of Duty: Zombies 3rd Person Umbrella Edition all we want, but that's what RE5 was. 

Resident Evil 6 is the evolution of the Resident Evil series in the current generation formed into one compilation. It's a prime example of nostalgia meets current gen. Look at Leon's campaign, obscure puzzles, slow moving zombies and dogs, etc. It's all evolution. Chris has more of the high octane heart pumping action zombie gaming associated with the series, whereas Jake's campaign mixes different elements from other horror games, it's genius. 

I enjoyed this game immensely and would recommend it to anyone with an open mind.
