Resident Evil 6 is the current latest numbered-entry in the long-running action-game series from Capcom. RE series (Resident Evil) has been evolving & moving further away from its survival-horror roots and more so into action-game territory with each entry - and in many people's opinions, this has been ringing more & more true with every entry since RE4. Regardless of what you may think of the changes in direction, there's one question still lingering: as a game, whatever it may be, is RE6 actually any good?

To answer the above question, one must also ask this: what does one actually want out a Resident Evil game? Do you want that Resident Evil 4 & 5 level of awesome action-packed gameplay and style? Leon's campaign certainly delivers this - and I think is the best overall campaign in the game; especially in the gameplay department. Leon's campaign is nothing short of awesome. Are you looking for an action-packed shooter-game w/ that "bro-feel" w/ lots of soldiers (that are AI) often surrounding you and often comes across feeling like Call of Duty and Gears of War games often does? RE6 has that - and it has its own twist on that, since you do have Resident Evil elements (i.e. Inventory and can combine items); well, Chris Redfield's campaign delivers this. 

What else would you like in a Resident Evil game? Do you want a more hand-to-hand & melee-based, more-acrobatic, more stealthy experience, and some driving element with some of the well-known Resident Evil elements? Jake's campaign certainly delivers this. Would you like a more single-player style campaign (if you play it w/out another player) that has similar elements to Jake's campaign, but also actually has some puzzle elements like other survival-horror games do? Ada's campaign delivers this. Not only that, but Ada's campaign has the actual best story in the game - delivering more elements of story-telling; big twists and reveals; and filling-in many of the gaps that were left lingering from the other 3 stories.

Do you like all of these types of games? Then, certainly, this game's definitely for you. Then, the "sums of its parts" factor will certainly speak to you, as it delivers all of these gameplay experience and does them all very well. Because each campaign often feels so different and so focused on different gameplay elements and styles - RE6, in a sense, often feels like 4 different Resident Evil games rolled into one entire ridiculously huge package. 

All of these campaigns, they can be played with Co-Op, if you like. All of these options can be set, when you load-up a saved game or start-up a brand new game. Each character has a partner with them, where the partner can be played by the game's AI (for all you offline and/or solo gamers) or even be played by another player online (for all you Co-Op gamers). Ada's campaign is the exception - as that is a solo-campaign by herself and without an AI partner if played solo (as it was originally built) - but it can be a Co-Op experience if you want to play online with a partner. 

(SIDE NOTE: The option to make Ada's campaign an additional Co-Op experience was added later by the dev's). 

In an interesting twist on things - when playing online, gamers can play a monster in certain parts of the game and invade other player's actual game at certain times.

One of the best & worst things this game has going for it and against it is its overlapping story & intersecting elements. You might run through an area again entirely that you did in another campaign - and it might not be much different; or you might do a different actual one part of the map in one campaign, but then a different part of the map - and it feels totally different, until they intersect somewhere, if they actually intersect. Chris's campaign does the same exact certain boss fight a few times (which is overly repetitive); and then we run into this same exact boss fight with Jake. The problem here is - you pretty much play this same boss fight the same exact way every time, whether you're doing Jake's campaign or Chris's campaign. 

Now in another campaign, you might do the same boss fight - but you're doing it as a different character with a different element and role to it, making it another kind of awesome. For example - in Leon's campaign, you do a boss fight on the ground like you normally would in a typical action game and shoot it on-foot, even though other characters are there and have a different role; while in Ada's campaign, you do this boss fight totally in a helicopter, shooting the enemy & firing missiles. You can always skip cut-scenes, which is a plus, if you don't want to see the same cut-scenes when any of the overlapping of the 4 stories take place. It's unfortunate that if you did a boss-fight on one campaign already, there's no option just can't skip that same boss-fight in another campaign - especially if the roles for the characters aren't too much different and you don't want to go through the repetition. It's when your character has a completely different role and element entirely, that you actually will really want to do the boss fight.

The graphics in this game are pretty good, for the most part. While the character models and especially the monsters are all excellent-looking, all loaded with detail galore and plenty of excellent art direction; it's the in-game textures for the objects in-game areas that can be of low-quality, when up-close. While game-areas and environments its art direction often do look great, it's the details within them that can vary. Thankfully, RE6 is not in a case like a Bioshock game would be in - where the signs, posters, and anything that's on them is important and need to be seen and read at its best quality, all so you can gather more detail and information about the game's story, lore, and get immersed in its game-world. 

Most of the story-telling is told via cut-scenes and while playing in-game - and there certainly is plenty of this. While each story itself on its own is actually good - it's b/c of the overlapping of its stories, which makes this great. A lot of things that may not add-up entirely in one campaign, this can only be realized only from playing a different campaign entirely. Ada's campaign ties together a lot of the story elements, filling in most of the gaps and blanks that might've been lingering and left-over from the other 3 campaigns. Once a chapter is unlocked and finished, gamers can jump to any Chapter and even replay them. You are graded for how you perform in each campaign - so fans of this game and perfectionists might want to replay the game and certain chapters just for those reasons alone. If that isn't enough, the game has an experience system where players can upgrade specific skills for each character and actually roll all of that into New-Game+ Mode.

After 33 hours of gameplay and taking on its 4 different campaigns - where two of them are at least good and try something different for a RE game (Jake's campaign & Chris's campaign); one campaign is absolutely an fantastic campaign especially for its gameplay (Leon's campaign); and one campaign that is a stand-out just for telling the best story of the bunch and giving us the most clarity (Ada's campaign) - this game is an absolute flawed-gem of an action game. If it wasn't for some of the repetitive boss-fights & certain areas that couldn't be skipped when tackling another campaign (b/c you feel like you've done some of this before), this game would be absolute masterpiece. The "sum of its parts" factor in many ways are often what makes this game as great as it is - but in a few other ways, that also can be one of its few minor flaws. Resident Evil 6 is experimental, ambitious, grand, epic, and ridiculously huge in scope - and because of this, it might not always deliver the best Resident Evil experience, but it most of the time will deliver such an experience.

Final Grade = B

This is not a recommendation, exactly. No, sirree. It's a bit of a warning. 

I've played almost all the other iterations of the Resident Evil series (and enjoyed them), but this one is simply punishing. And that makes it largely un-fun at times. 

I'm not implying that the controls, or the game itself, are broken - in fact, the dialogue, the characters, the cutscenes, and production/creature design, are quite good. Those aspects I enjoy. It's more like the game simply isn't sure what it wants to be (action, thriller, horror, shooter, co-op, stealth, etc.), and in so doing, tries to shoehorn a little bit of everything. And doesn't do any of that particularly well. It's the age-old issue of quantity over quality. Personally, I find that all that variation really disrupts the tone of the game, which is supposedly survival horror with action elements.

There are many lethal cutscene QTEs, and a plethora of "races" away from insta-kill threats. In some cases, you get both - over and over again in a single event. And more often than not, the events themselves are too long - making it difficult to complete without making some critical mistake. After which, you have the option of continuing from checkpoints - which penalizes you in the in-game report-card-style ranking system at the end of each level.

It's also not helped by an AI ally system that is, at best, occasionally helpful/useful.

It's a 50/50 shot, that in the midst of a minor scuffle, he/she will be able to save/help you. And it's much more likely the AI will be haplessly fighting something else (or off-screen, making a sandwich) while you're getting curb-stomped by enemies. 

I'd liken the gaming experience to feeling more like studying for an important exam, frustratingly trying to memorize where to be and where to go, just to pass. It's less suspense from horror and environment, and more suspense from not wanting to die and do the level over.

As a fan of the franchise, I'll continue to try and power through this game, but for the most part I'm somewhat disappointed in the turn the franchise has taken.

This game is underrated.

There is no other way to say it. The fans attacked this game right off the bat and have subsequently abandoned it.

That being said, this is not for the fans who I presume will not listen to anything I have to say. This is for the curious gamer who is looking for a fun zombie-survival-action game to play with a friend.

First and foremost, this is not a survival horror game (nor have any of the numbered REvils ever been) but an evolution of the original game concept that has been present in all the numbered games.

It is highly action oriented, designed more to get your heart racing than scare the piss out of you. There are no supernatural gimmicks or creepy solos through mansions here. You are fighting a war against bio-terrorism, and you are losing.

What is perhaps most ironic about this game is that it follows the formula of the popular movies, and yet has received such heavy attacks for doing just that while actually being better than any of the movies could ever hope to be.

The characters are more memorable, developed better, and even more likeable to the point where you actually care when one of them dies. The gameplay is solid 3rd-person with the exception of camera steal happening when they want to show you a particular sequence.

One complaint I've heard is that the game makes it too easy for you. I don't know what difficulty these people have been playing on, but the game is not easy, you will die quite a bit and not simply because a quicktime event got you but because the enemies will overwhelm or overrun you.

Perhaps the most interesting thing I've found in this game is that no two characters (with the exception of the Generic Agent Man) play quite like any of the others. They all have their own unique HUDs, weapons, and even melee moves which keeps the gameplay interesting as something you have access to isn't always the same as your partner and vice versa.

The intersecting stories are handled well and if you play through the game in order it weaves a fascinating intertwining plot where you can see everything develop in each from different points of view. I even had my opinions about different characters change as I played the different campaigns and was allowed to see more into their rasons for what they do in the game.

So to sum up, this game doesn't deserve the bad ratings and poor reviews it has received. It's a solid zombie-action game with survival undertones and a solid cast of characters with a story filled with all the action cheese of the movies.

At the end of the day, you should give it a shot. It might surprise you.

Honestly I can't justify why this game got the lukewarm reception it did. A negative commonality between most critic and gamer reviews has been focused on how the game strays from being survival horror. The truth is though that Resident Evil has not fit that genre since 1999's Resident Evil 3 - Nemesis (as far as the main series is concerned). That being said critics and fans have had nearly a decade to either accept this new direction or simply walk away from the franchise. 

With that said, if you're looking for an actual survival horror game you might want to look elsewhere. As a more action-oriented horror/sci-fi title however you can't really do much better than this game right here.  

RE6 gives you four campaigns that each feature their own characters and story-lines (which tie into the main story arc) as well as gameplay styles that, for the most part, are different from one another. Three of the four allow the player to choose between two playable characters in singleplayer mode or allows for online co-op play. In addition, three of those campaigns will take you on average five to eight hours to complete with the final taking somewhere between two or three. Add it up and you've got a game that can take you upwards of seventeen hours to finish.

There are some issues with the game though. While each campaign has its own series of events, most of them share some common locations and you'll feel like you're playing through the same thing each time during certain areas just with a different character. Also I found that Chris' campaign lacked in some parts. Clearly his campaign is intended to be more third person shooter-based but the cover system is a little wonky (though MUCH better than the one in Operation Raccoon City) and I found myself running out of ammo way too often. Beyond these two gripes the only other negative aspect worth mentioning is that the main story can be a little confusing sometimes despite seeing it from four different perspectives. Hunting down the break-able symbols (thus unlocking info files) certainly helps but there definitely needed to be a little more clarity.

Overall RE6 is actually a pretty good game. It might have completely stripped most of things that made the franchise the definitive survival horror experience it was but if you can look past that you'll find an enjoyable experience.

[h1]Resident Evil 6 – An Icy Adventure in the World of Bio-Terror[/h1]

[i]Author: Kiba Snowpaw, the Alpha Male Ice Wolf from HowlStrom[/i]

[h2]Introduction[/h2]

Howl and hello from the frostbitten realm of HowlStrom! I'm Kiba Snowpaw, your alpha ice wolf with 37 years of gaming wisdom and a penchant for survival horror. Today, we're diving into the frigid depths of [b]Resident Evil 6[/b], a game that has stirred as much love as it has controversy. Strap on your fur, grab your ice magic, and let's explore the chilling and thrilling world of RE6!

[h2]Basic Plot Summary[/h2]

Resident Evil 6 is an action-packed survival horror game developed and published by Capcom. Released on March 22, 2013, it follows the intertwined stories of four main protagonists as they battle the virulent C-virus across North America, Eastern Europe, and China. With distinct campaigns for Leon S. Kennedy, Chris Redfield, Jake Muller, and Ada Wong, the game offers a blend of horror, action, and dramatic storytelling.

[h2]Originality[/h2]

RE6 introduces several new elements to the Resident Evil formula. The game’s unique "Crossover" mechanic allows up to four players to experience interconnected storylines simultaneously. Each campaign offers a different gameplay style, ranging from classic survival horror to high-octane action. This blend of genres and perspectives provides a fresh take on the series' traditional gameplay.

[h2]The Studio[/h2]

Capcom, the legendary studio behind Resident Evil, has a storied history of crafting iconic games. Known for their innovation and dedication to quality, Capcom has delivered numerous classics over the decades. However, with RE6, the studio faced criticism for deviating from the series’ survival horror roots in favor of more action-oriented gameplay.

[h2]Analysis/Evaluation[/h2]

[h3]Character Development: Main Characters[/h3]

Resident Evil 6 boasts a robust cast of characters, each with their own unique story arcs and motivations.

- [b]Leon S. Kennedy:[/b] The former Raccoon City police officer turned government agent is back, tackling a new bio-terror threat in Tall Oaks. Leon’s journey is filled with emotional depth as he grapples with trust and betrayal.
- [b]Chris Redfield:[/b] The seasoned BSAA operative faces his own demons in Lanshiang, China. Chris’s campaign focuses on his struggle with PTSD and his relentless pursuit of justice.
- [b]Jake Muller:[/b] The rebellious mercenary and son of series antagonist Albert Wesker, Jake’s story is one of redemption and self-discovery. Partnered with Sherry Birkin, Jake seeks to escape his father’s shadow.
- [b]Ada Wong:[/b] The enigmatic spy’s solo campaign adds layers of intrigue and complexity. Ada’s motivations and allegiances are constantly in question, making her storyline a thrilling ride.

[h3]Supporting Characters[/h3]

- [b]Helena Harper:[/b] Leon’s partner, a secret service agent with a tragic past.
- [b]Piers Nivans:[/b] Chris’s loyal BSAA comrade, representing the new generation of soldiers.
- [b]Sherry Birkin:[/b] The daughter of Umbrella researchers, who plays a pivotal role in Jake’s campaign.

[h3]Character Arcs and Relatability[/h3]

Each character’s arc is deeply intertwined with the game's overall narrative. Leon’s steadfast heroism, Chris’s battle with inner demons, Jake’s quest for identity, and Ada’s mysterious motives all contribute to a rich, multi-layered story. Players can find aspects of themselves in these characters, making their journeys all the more engaging.

[h2]Structure[/h2]

RE6’s structure is ambitious, featuring four distinct campaigns that intersect at key points. This interwoven narrative provides multiple perspectives on the unfolding bio-terror crisis, creating a dynamic and immersive storytelling experience. The game's pacing varies across campaigns, from the slow-burn tension of Leon’s campaign to the intense action of Chris’s missions.

[h2]Mechanics[/h2]

The gameplay mechanics in RE6 are a significant evolution for the series.

- [b]Combat:[/b] The ability to shoot while moving, slide, roll, and use cover adds fluidity to combat. The enhanced melee system allows for visceral hand-to-hand encounters.
- [b]Health System:[/b] Players must find health packs instead of relying on herbs, adding a new layer of strategy.
- [b]Skills:[/b] The Character Skill system lets players upgrade abilities, tailoring their playstyle to their preferences.

[h2]Implementation[/h2]

Capcom’s implementation of these mechanics is largely successful, though not without its flaws. The control system, while comprehensive, can be overwhelming for new players. The game’s diverse gameplay styles ensure that there’s something for everyone, but the sheer variety can sometimes feel disjointed.

[h2]Impact[/h2]

Resident Evil 6’s impact on the series is profound. It represents a bold shift towards action, which divided fans but also attracted a new audience. The game’s ambitious narrative structure and crossover gameplay mechanics influenced future titles, including Resident Evil: Revelations 2 and Resident Evil 7: Biohazard.

[h2]Hook and Thesis[/h2]

Resident Evil 6 is a love letter to fans of action-horror, offering an expansive and multifaceted experience. Its blend of storytelling, diverse gameplay, and cooperative mechanics make it a standout entry in the series. While it may not be a pure survival horror game, it delivers a thrilling ride that keeps players on the edge of their seats.

[h2]Praise and Critique[/h2]

[h3]Praise[/h3]

- [b]Varied Campaigns:[/b] Four unique storylines provide diverse gameplay experiences.
- [b]Crossover Mechanics:[/b] Innovative multiplayer features enhance the cooperative experience.
- [b]Graphics and Sound:[/b] High-quality visuals and voice acting bring the world to life.
- [b]Action-Packed Combat:[/b] Fluid and dynamic combat system.

[h3]Critique[/h3]

- [b]Lack of Focus:[/b] The game’s shift towards action can alienate fans of traditional survival horror.
- [b]Convoluted Story:[/b] The complex narrative can be difficult to follow.
- [b]Poor AI:[/b] Partner AI can be unreliable, detracting from the experience.
- [b]Inconsistent Pacing:[/b] The varying pacing across campaigns can feel jarring.

[h2]Personal Opinion[/h2]

As a seasoned ice wolf from HowlStrom, I found Resident Evil 6 to be a thrilling, albeit flawed, adventure. The game’s strengths lie in its ambitious storytelling and varied gameplay. However, its departure from survival horror roots and occasional mechanical clunkiness can be off-putting. Overall, it’s a game that offers intense action and dramatic moments, but it’s not without its icy patches.

[h3]Highlights and Drawbacks[/h3]

- [b]Highlights:[/b] Engaging combat, impressive graphics, and the sheer variety of gameplay.
- [b]Drawbacks:[/b] Convoluted story, inconsistent pacing, and unreliable AI.

[h2]Evaluation[/h2]

Resident Evil 6 is a game that defies easy categorization. It’s an action-horror hybrid that pushes the boundaries of the Resident Evil series. Despite its flaws, it offers a compelling experience that’s worth exploring, especially for fans of action-packed gameplay.

[h2]Comparison[/h2]

Compared to other Resident Evil titles, RE6 stands out for its ambitious scope and varied gameplay. While it lacks the pure horror of RE7 or the tight pacing of RE4, it offers a unique blend of action and story that’s unmatched in the series.

[h2]Overall Conclusion[/h2]

In the icy expanses of HowlStrom, Resident Evil 6 remains a game that’s both cherished and critiqued. Its bold approach to storytelling and gameplay mechanics makes it a memorable entry in the series. Whether you’re a long-time fan or a newcomer, there’s something in RE6 to captivate and challenge you. Embrace the frost, brave the bio-terror, and experience the multifaceted world of Resident Evil 6.

Compared to Resident Evil 5... this game is not as good.  The problem boils down to trying to do WAY too many things at once.

--Compared to RE5, there's a few Dead Space esq grotesque elements, but they are extremely insonsistent in how they want to place such elements.  A few deaths are gruesome while others are laughably tame or even literally non-fatal.

--The storyline is more than aa bit disjointed due to sudden-skip and explosion-prone transitions, almost like a bad action movie.

--The combat is alright with several different variations of enemeies depending on the campaign selected, but again there is some inconsistency.   Normal zombies damage you just by grabbing you regardless of any visual violence while other enemies do not.  The bosses are basically all puzzle bosses and really quite forgettable, even the recurring ones.

--The cover mechanics are rarely useful and often clunky, and the controls are in general more than a bit unwieldy when it comes to turning.  Aiming is for the most part fine.  The camera can be nauseatingly claustrophobic when in certain indoor areas.  Adjusting the FOV helps a bit

--QTEs return, and like the cinematic ones in RE5 they dont really add at all to the enjoyment of the game nor are a meaningful part of the gameplay.  There is one egregious instance with an enemy that has an instant-kill grapple attack, but takes a several-seconds long cinematic to actually perform which the Co-Op partner is (both mechaically and thematically) pointlessly prevented from interrupting.  This happens cinematicaally too later in the game's first campaign with a one-button-or-you-die QTE.  These sorts of situaations are neither fun nor interesting for the player.  'Oh sudden QTE I missed, gruesome game over.  Mistimed it, forced to watch again.  Mistimed it, forced to watch again.  Repead until you get the timing right.'  Devs need to learn that this is not fun, challenging, or rewarding, especially when presented with a gruesome visual afterwards.  Heavy Rain does this right. with cumulative QTEs required for complete success or complete failure, as well as possible middle-road results.

--The inventory system is bad becaause you can carry too many guns and they can't be quick selected like in an FPS, you have to scroll through about 4-5 to get to the one you want.  RE5's limited inventory, while sensical for a controller, was also VERY nice as a game mechanic because it let you customize your loadout.  You could carry many items to be ready to fight, or few in expectation of collecting in the level.  You could take one gun and a lot of ammo, or many guns with less ammo each.  You could take more armor and health and less guns, all your choice with the limited inventory space.  That and you would never get ammo for a gun type you weren't carrying.

--Items in the world are instanced so co-op ammo or health management is not as interesting.  As opposed to sharing found health items to your partner to hold and use, healing yourself while near them miraculously heals them too.

--There is an added versus mode where players can enter the games of people playing campaign mode, and take the role of the enemies to kill the hero characters, but there really isn't much point to this except as a sort of pseudo versus mode.  Luckily this is a disablable feature, which lets newer players avoid potential abuse from veterans.  I haven't tried it myself, but from what I have read there is no benefit to the hero-player aside from a slight chance of a health item drop.  It is merely for potential added difficulty.

A few other complaints but you get the idea.  There's a whole lot of things done not-that-great.  Its still an OK game to play in co-op and the production value of the game is fairly high (especially with facial animations).  It uses Steam instead of GFWL now and still runs great with no hitches or lag, and the graphics options are good too so its glad to see that it still runs well like its predecessor.  Its not awful, but a bit underwhelming.

As divisive as it may be for "fans" of the franchise i must say that i had a blast with this game.

Re6 is a game that has its quirks; abrupt camera angle switches, an abundance of QTEs, dated visuals and overly ambitious yet lukewarm set pieces.

Underneath those flaws however lies a combat system so unique and well made that i'd go as far to say that it's without a doubt one of the best ones i've had the pleasure to play this gen.

If i were to keep 3-4 TPS combat systems from this gen then RE6 would definitely be included alongside the likes of Vanquish, Max Payne 3 and maybe Space Marine with its intense mix of ranged and melee. 

RE6's combat is based upon awareness, precision and evasion. Each encounter requires you to know your enemy's weakpoints, be aware of your environments and use them for massive damage and finally evade and properly time your strike to deliver a counter attack.

Enemy weak point knowledge is a must as nearly all enemies can be downed with a few well placed shots. Failure in focusing on said weakpoints will find you spending mag after mag in an attempt to kill an adversary.

While chest-high cover is in the game its only purpose is to regain stamina as the game forces you to go toe to toe with enemies finishing them off with melee and exploiting invincibility frames.

Range of movement is also incredible with 4 way roll/evade, slides, 180 degree spins on the floor, quick recovery from attacks, quick attacks that stun enemies and consume stamina points,etc. 

Inventory management is also the best the franchise has seen so far, allowing you to mix, match and discard items on the fly and the tablet system makes healing a breeze. 

Another thing to applaud is the enemy mutation system with foes reacting on each and every hit differently, forcing you to constantly adapt to their forms and attack patterns.

In place of gun upgrades there is a perk system this time arround that lets you customize and fine tune your play style; you can focus on ranged and/or melee, opt for more in-game drops or equip perks that boost your healing capabilities and that of your allies.

The game's story is a 20+ hr long roller coaster ride through a wide gamut of emotions and the story itself can be described as a mix between Lethal Weapon, 28 days later and Maniac Cop (?!) with the everpresent (and personally always welcome) RE6 cheesiness.

There's a bit of Demon's/ Dark Souls flavor in the campaign as there are options to invade ones game as a creature and at certain points in the plot where paths entwine between characters, two pairs of players can join forces. 

Mercs mode makes a welcome return alongside its frantic PC only variant: No Mercy with guest cameos from L4D characters and foes. If you also opt for the season pass there are 5 more modes each with its unique play style.

The PC version while not looking spectacular, is still way better than the console variants with many options in the menu and no frame cap for the 120+ Hz crowd. 

Due to the game's idiosyncrasies i'd suggest to 1st play (classic) mercs on the very first stage (Urban Chaos), fine tune the controls and FoV to your liking (choosing laser sight aiming is STRONGLY recommended) and then proceed to familiarize yourself with the combat system until you can get at least an A grade consistently. Then go into options and turn QTE assist on. While most QTEs are not hard by any means there are a couple of them that are rage-inducing so it's better to save yourself from the mental breakdown alltogether.

Finally the game criminally forces you to go through the prologue when you fire it up for the first time, prohibiting you from even changing some gameplay options. My advice? Stick with it! It's not indicative of the in-game experience by any means and all it manages to do is to outline the game's flaws. Why did they choose to give such a bad first impression? I'd guess to set a cinematic "feel" but it fails miserably imo.

Highly recommended for TPS aficionados and action enthousiasts in general with an appetite for something exotic and distinct.

Невозможно отрицать тот факт,что геймплей и атмосфера игры далеки от классических первых трех частей,что разумеется,не понравится любителям классики.Как и "новые" Resident Evil 4 и Resident Evil 5-эта игра шутер.Хоррор отсутствует,однако тем не менее в отличии от 5ой части,здесь делаются какие то намеки на него,в кампании Леона.
Кстати,насчет кампаний и сюжета.В игре 4 кампании,три из которых расчитаны на двоих игроков,где уже знакомые персонажи(Леон,Крис,Шерри) действуют на пару с новичками(Хелена,Пирс,Джейк),последняя же 4ая кампания играется за Аду Вонг.Несмотря на огромную продолжительность всех кампаний,как ни странно,они не надоедают(ИМХО).Сюжет не плох,ролики сделанны вполне себе хорошо,а геймплей не жданно не гаданно цепляет(ИМХО).Здесь вам и обычные перестрелки,и битвы с боссами и поездки на мотоцикле и прочем виде траспорта(включая вертолет),короче говоря,заскучать попросту невозможно(ИМХО),тем более,что патронов мало и часто приходится сражаться в рукопашную.
Думаете,пройдя кампанию можно смело забивать на игру?Только не в творении от Capcom,уж эти японцы умеют заставлять игроков засиживать за своими играми(пример-Devil May Cry 4).Помимо классического режима "Наемники",появившегося еще в 3ей части,имеется,впервые введенный в 5ой режим "Наемники:Возмездие" и еще около 3-5 новых режимов.А помимо "Дополнительного контента" здесь имеются всякие фигурки и документы про разные события и персонажей.
Теперь менее важные вещи:
Графика очень даже не плохая,радует глаз(ИМХО)
В саундтреке нет ничего примечательного,однако некоторые композиции можно выделить.

Получилось полноценное продолжение серии,сделанное на самом высшем уровне.(ИМХО)
Здесь они решили угодить всем,что стало их ошибкой,(кампания Криса полностью лишена атмосферы),однако игра в целом замечательная,не шедевр разумеется,но превосходный продукт,поглощение которого не надоедает очень долго,пожалуй никакая из игр серии Resident Evil доселе не имела настолько широких возможностей ни геймплея,ни дополнительного контента.Симбиоз всего лучшего из 4ой и 5ой частей.Если разработчики продолжат в том же духе и еще более приблизят последующую часть к классике,то Resident Evil 7 однозначно будет шедевром.

Resident Evil 6 provides an interesting take on the journey this series has had throughout the years. While it looks slightly dated in comparison to games using DirectX 11, it still manages to mantain a fun experience across all the different campaigns.

Resident Evil 6 splits itself up into campaigns that translate roughly into different "eras" for the Resident Evil franchise. You have Leon Kennedy, while with the B.S.A. now, feels very familiar regarding the slower paced and claustrophobic gameplay of the earlier parts of the series. You have Chris Redfield, still capable of bench-pressing 600 pounds in his more action oriented and over-the-top military-based experiences. You have Jack and even Ada Wong as well rounding out the people involved.

The controls for the PC are a bit awkward, but thankfully it manages to provide for mouse support that hasn't really irritated me in any particular way. Control keys seem to be a bit awkward in their defaults and some keys are used for more than one thing which can cause some confusion in frantic fights.

One thing that really bothered me was the number of QTEs in this game. The "tutorial" consisted of no ability to save and had far too many QTEs which made the entire segment feeling much more like a zombie/explosive version of Dragon's Lair. Thankfully it eases up over time and while they are still a bit more common than I'd like, they aren't overbearing.

Weapon upgrades was another bit of disappointment for me as well. Instead of gathering money during your exploits and spending it on weapon upgrades specific to pistol X, Y, or Z; you pick up "Skill Points" and spend them on basic skills that improve things like extra pistol damage, extra rifle damage, round penetration and so on. This feels a bit disappointing since it reduces the impact your inventory has on how you operate in the game, meaning that instead every pistol of every time is suddenly better without any visual representation to show it.

On the multiplayer side of things, we have a number of different ways to play. You can essentially "infect" another player's game by joining in as a monster or creature with the sole goal of killing one of the human players before they manage to finish the chapter they're on. This is neat as it feels a little like Dark Souls, though lacks the heart-pounding result as it's declared and the human players are well equipped to handle it.

You have Mercenaries and the like as well, with Mercenaries also getting a Left 4 Dead crossover. It's the same Mercenaries game mode we've had for awhile with very similar rules. The downside is that the Left 4 Dead crossover feels hamfisted with the characters not really having anything special here as they feel like they were just reskins.

Despite it's flaws, Resident Evil 6 proves to be a fun enough game with various different paces to suit many different moods. The crossovers for the stories of each campaign compliments each other without getting in the way and gives you a reason to hop around the chapters once you unlock them all for a second playthrough.

Make no mistake, Resident Evil 6 is no longer a (survivor) horror game; it's a full blown action game with horror themes here and there. The story is rather poor (great characters interactions but overall the is full of cliches and most of the backstory is crammed into documents you get by shooting snake emblems) and the campaign itself is full of highs and lows. When it shines, it really does - you get great setpieces, boss fights, interesting over the top action sequences etc. But when it blows, man - it really blows: you will rage in frustration over instadeath QTEs, stupid design decisions, frustrating stealth sections, slow-walk sections (the whole beginning of Leon's campaign), camera control being taken away from you (while enemies can still move and hurt you), annoying vehicle sections... ugh, there's a lot of that.

However, the combat system is fantastic... once you learn it, because Capcom forgot to include a proper tutorial to teach you how to play the game. But when you do get how to play - it's marvelous. It's the most technical and versatile third person shooter that has been released in years, topped only by Vanquish. Forget about boring pop and shoot cover shooters that flood the genre nowadays; this game is all about slides, dodges, counters, stunning enemies and performing melee combos. :D If you spend most of the game hidden behins a cover or standing in place and shooting enemies, you're playing the game wrong. :P

Also, Mercenaries is the best bonus mode ever. EVER. Very addicting and time consuming and at the same time, very satisfying, mostly because it focuses on the game's strengths (the combat system), while throwing away everything else (those highs and lows from the campaign design).

Each one of the 4 campaigns focuses on a different aspect that the RE games have covered. Starting with Leon's campaign we have a more old-school and slower-paced experience that aims to recapture the urban pandemonium of Raccoon City, except on a much larger scale as it takes us into China. Zombies and their assorted variants are the only enemies you'll face here (with the exception of the Rasklapanje, which shows up in all the other campaigns, and Ustanak) and you can tell that Capcom made a conscious decision to make sure that any other types of enemies did not appear within this campaign. The overall theme of horror is maintained all the way up until the middle of the 4th chapter when all hell breaks loose. Ending in true Resident Evil style via the use of a rocket launcher on the antagonist of that campaign.

Next up is Chris' campaign. As you'd have guessed after playing Resident Evil 5, his campaign focuses on mostly action with one segment that is a tribute to Yawn from the original Resident Evil. Enemies in this campaign are strictly the gun-toting J'avo and their subsequent mutations. The J'avo are not to be confused with zombies, and as such do not fit any criteria of that word's definition. J'avo are the main reason for the more action-oriented segments within that campaign. Chris' story ends in one of the more dramatic scenes in Resident Evil history that truly sets the overall theme of redemption and sacrifice which his campaign covers.

Jake's campaign sees the illegitimate son of Albert Wesker being pursued by Neo Umbrella. I'd say that if there were one word to best describe the aspect that his story covers it would be "Retreat". Appropriately so, as the C-Virus B.O.W "Ustanak" hunts Jake down every step of the way in a clear nod to the Nemesis Tyrant from the game of the same name. Again, J'avo are the only enemies you'll encounter within this scenario.

Lastly we have Ada's campaign which is the most varied of all the stories, though it focuses more on stealth, survival and puzzles. In it you'll fight both zombies and J'avo as you try to unravel the mystery of Ada's doppleganger.

So now that we've covered the overall themes of the campaigns, let's get into what really sets this game apart from other Shooters. This game easily has the most fluid controls of any TPS I've ever played. Though at first glance, the game's controls seem pretty straight-forward for a TPS. L-trigger aims your weapon, right trigger shoots when your weapon is readied and melees when it isn't, while L3 makes you sprint. There is a cover system as well, but it's rudimentary and not nearly as elaborate as something like GoW or AoT. (Think of its inclusion in the same way that multiplayer functions in Dark Souls. It's implemented on a basic level and usually won't be used, but still useful when you find yourself in a bad situation.). Here, the game passes itself off as a generic shooter until you actually discover the dodging and melee mechanics. There is a good deal for me to cover, but let's start with the basics and a video of how well the combat system works when mastered https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hUjmW5GgU_c

Hitting A or L3 (360 Controller) while your weapon is readied will cause you to dodge in place. Combining this with different directions on the left stick will allow you to dodge in the corresponding direction. Releasing the left trigger allows you to resume normal movement, but holding on it will cause you to lie prone with your weapon drawn. While prone, you can move in the same directions that you can while standing. Flicking the left stick will cause you to either roll to the left or right, or make you scramble backwards. This is an invaluable skill to learn for dodging/animation cancelling and setting yourself up for retaliatory attacks.

Sprinting while hitting the L-Trigger will cause you to slide on your back. This can be useful for getting through a bunch of enemies relatively safely, or to stun them for a melee attack. As with dodging, if you keep the L-Trigger held after sliding you'll go into a prone state. Quickly reversing your direction while keeping your weapon drawn will also allow you to flip yourself in the opposite direction while going prone. Next up is Quick-Shotting. Quick-Shotting is (as far as I know) a mechanic unique to Resident Evil 6 that allows you to fire a non-precision shot at your target. It is a crucial mechanic to master for quickly dispatching enemies with melee or for stunning them so that you can get into a better position. A Quick-Shot is performed by hitting L and R at the same time while using either the left or right analog stick to aim the direction of your shot. Keep in mind that the tracking radius for Quick-Shotting is rather small and it will target the nearest enemy in the direction you aimed. A Quick-Shot is always a guaranteed stun on most standard non-mutated enemies. Finally we have counters. Countering in this game is a mechanic that allows a player to evade an enemy attack and respond with one of their own. A counter can be performed on most non-boss enemies by hitting the R trigger (without your weapon drawn) at the appropriate time. Not only does this grant invulnerability frames, it also allows you to dish out a massive amount of damage within a short time (and is particularly useful for extending the Time Limit in Mercenaries mode.). Some enemies have counters unique to them (such as Bloodshots) that allow you to severely damage, if not outright kill them.

So yeah, sounds complicated? And you're probably wondering how well all of what I've mentioned in the previous paragraphs functions together. Well, sometimes Quick-Shotting can hit the wrong target if you fire it into a group (Though this rarely happens if you're keeping track of where enemies are around you.). The contextual action to parkour while sprinting is also a bit too sensitive, but can be easily managed by learning what you can and cannot parkour over, and when you should sprint. As for the cover system. You'd think that going into cover when your weapon is drawn and you're close enough to something would be a horrible game mechanic, but the game is very, very strict about how close and which way you have to be positioned for this to even happen. The cover system does its job well enough despite lacking a bit of polish, as this isn't a cover shooter. Control of the camera in this game will also be sometimes taken from you to focus on a point of interest or objective during the campaigns (you are usually invulnerable while this occurs, though enemies still move around), but generally not in a way that feels disorienting as long as you're actually paying attention to the game. Though, since you're not invulnerable once the camera control is returned, it can somtimes lead to enemies getting a cheap hit in on you. It's a minor issue, but is something that happens from time to time. There are a fair amount of QTEs in the game, similar in number to RE4's, but if you were able to handle the QTEs that RE4 threw at you, then RE6's should pose even less of a problem to you. There are also about 5 brief driving segments in this game (they're not really anything special, but they're handled well enough for what they are). Most bad reviews of the game like to hyperbole the camera and QTES in the game to absurd degrees. Again, as long as you're paying attention, you should not be failing the QTEs in this game (and there is an option that was patched in to allow the game to perform them for you, for the most part). One last thing to note is that the progression of chapters is pretty much straight-forward and linear (though there hasn't been an RE game since Dead Aim that wasn't as such).

Overall, the game has a lot to offer for those actually willing to learn and master its controls, despite some poor design choices.

RE6 uses a very different approach. This time it's more action, more shooting, more explosions, more dead people, more monsters, more zombies, more melee, more acrobatics, more martial arts, a long series of boss fights, a huge pile of QTEs (seriously huge pile), extreme amounts of dying (on Professional difficulty), less running around, less puzzles and less looting, and then an endless row of the usual challenge modes if you're into those. If you're playing the story on a higher difficulty, then you'll probably run into situations where it's going to be pretty difficult to progress. In my opinion this is one of the game's positive properties. You'll keep trying and trying and you'll advance sooner or later. Make sure you DO NOT use infinite ammo, no matter what. The tension is partially about how you manage your ammo and resources. The other aspect that adds to the tension is the mysterious pieces of the story. As a matter of fact, the speciality of the RE franchise is that as the story unfolds and while you're witnessing the horrific events, everything becomes more and more interesting and just draws you in. It is just like that in this case. I can't tell you how many times I've rolled out of the way to run from a zombie, just to interact with that table next to me and slide directly into the arms of another zombie. Good, but not perfect.   In short, this is an experiment in the Resident Evil series with some experimental results. 

It offers some fun gameplay that takes RE to places that it's never been before.   Along with that, there are a few shortcomings that gnaw the overall experience.  If you're one of the pure traditional horror and tension over all things than you might want to look elseware.

Is it better than RE5?  In my opinon, Yes, but I still like RE5.   Is it a groundbreaking horror-fest like the first several RE games?  No, not even close but that doesn’t mean that this is a terrible game.  

Expect for your characters to be the most mobile that they have ever been before in an RE game. Even more mobile than in many 3rd person action games. You can run, roll, side roll, dodge, fight from the ground, evade while on the ground, engage in physical combat, and that's just a bit of it. This is a godsend from when I was playing RE2 back on the N64 in 2001. I always found myself cursing at the screen because of the bad camera angle or when Leon or Claire just couldn’t figure out how to use some low level martial arts against many enemies that had negative IQ's. Some people are complaining, but I enjoy many of the changes.  

Not saying that there wasn’t times when I cursed at the screen while playing this game. Although most of those were due to the few camera angle and controls that tried to stick to the series. RE6 is much faster paced than previous RE's. This can be a big problem when a camera angle gets stuck and you can’t see your character or when your character jumps in the exact opposite direction that they were supposed to (the run button is the same as the leap over obstacle button). Thankfully this only happens a handful of times between otherwise good gameplay.

The area where I had the most fun with this game is the same that I had with RE5.... The Mercenaries No Mercy.  Its basically a time attack horde mode where you get points for combos while you survive until the time runs out or until you kill 300 enemies. An impressive amount of said enemies can be on the screen at a time.   This teamed with online gameplay makes this game a worthwhile venture if you dont mind action (and a bit of WTF were they thinking) in your Resident Evil game.

Amazing game with an awesome plot. I recommend this game for both those who played some/all of the previous games and those who never did. Here is a little summary of the game's features:

CAMPAIGN & PLOT

After years and years "playing safe", this time, things really get out of control. Bioterrorist attacks take place in some major places worldwide. This time, just like Raccoon, you get the feeling that you just can't save everyone.

In this game, you get to see more than meets the eye. You're able to see what hapens "behind the scenes" at certain events, thanks to more immersive cutscenes provided by different campaigns.

Story intersection is another curious feature. I've never seen anything like that in any other game. It is really fun to play with 3 other players in campaign, specially against Ogroman and Ustanak.

Old friends are back, and some revelations are made.

I really liked that they brought Sherry (that's right! It is NOT Ashley, for Christ's sake) back. She was missing since RE2, and all we had after that was an epilogue file in RE3 saying that the US government wanted her. Capcom really loves to disappear with some characters.

IMPROVEMENTS & ADD-ONS

The combat system has improved a lot since RE5. Dynamic cover, dash, counter attacks, dodge and melee dedicated buttons are in the features list. The most interesting addition, however, is the Skill system. There are tons of things to choose from: enhance your firearm power, melee power, defense, aim, etc. It's very nice.

CO-OP

Co-op mode in RE6 is more dynamic than it was before. The host don't need to restart the game or stop whatever it is that he/she is doing to allow someone in. The lag seems to be less of an evil this time around, but it is still an issue, specially at some QTE events, where the game should sync the players before the scene, but that's not the case everytime.

But putting that aside, it was a real pity that Capcom got rid of the lobby system for each separate chapter (like 1-2, 3-4, and so on) and the "magic chest" where you could store your items. I find it extremely annoying to always have my inventory full. Got too few space for so much different bullets, herbs and grenades.

DOG TAGS

That was an interesting add-on. You can customize your dog tag your way to distinguish yourself from other players.

EXTRA CONTENT

In Agent Hunt mode, you join another player's game as the enemy. Your goal is to kill the player.

Mercenaries is back, just like in the previous games. Thankfully, still very familiar. The notable difference is that Coup de Grâce and Counters add more time to the clock.

If you're a fan of Left 4 Dead, you might want to try Mercenaries No Mercy. I think you'll enjoy.

Onslaught is a fun mode where you kill enemies to send more enemies to your opponent's side. You can't see each other, though.

Survivors is back, too. But, this time, it is much more fun. You can play with up to 6 players in the same room. Melee moves, little ammo to spare, random spawning weapons and enemies lurking around will turn it into a challenge.

In Predator mode, you play can play as Ustanak, a virtually indestructible creature, which reminds me a lot of Nemesis. Each turn, someone will play as Ustanak and try to defeat as many Agents as it can. This mode can be played with up to 6 players.

Resident Evil 6 has gotten some hate over the years, but honestly, I think a lot of it is undeserved. It is a fun game despite all of its flaws, and I think that it is worth playing if you are a fan of the Resident Evil games.

Gameplay wise I think that the formula for RE6 is pretty good. The gameplay style matches RE4 and 5, but I found it to be a bit smoother. Yes, RE4 is overall a better game, but RE6 feels better to play. That does not mean it is perfect though. Some of the camera angles can be pretty rough and it has killed me many times. The inventory system is annoying too, I never liked how you went through items and how you couldn’t space out your inventory instead you just have slots. The upgrade system is a little weak as well, but it never really hampered my fun with the game. Some of the enemies are BS, but those exist in every RE game, so though it is not excusable to create fun killing enemies but it is nothing new for the franchise. Actually, that brings me to a thought, I feel like a lot of the flaws RE6 has are just flaws that exist within several games in the series as a whole. With the Remakes coming out now it appears as though that is becoming no longer the case, but I am surprised that people have chosen to be so critical of RE6 when RE4 has some of the same BS; wonky controls, cryptic puzzles, poor movement and camera angles, and so on. Those are all problems in RE4 but people make it out to be worse in RE6. One thing I both greatly appreciate about this game and hate is that it heavily encourages having a friend to play with. On one hand, co-op games have become too much of a rarity (especially nowadays it appears), but it is nice to be able to go through a story campaign and experience the game together. I played this game both with my brother and my sister and each time was quite satisfying and was a fun bonding experience, especially when we got to complain about some of the BS this game throws out. On the other hand, if you play this game alone the AI is pretty much a handicap I remember people joking that for both RE5 and 6 they were purposely making the AI terrible so that they could sell people two copies of the game instead of one. The jokes on them, I played split screen like a real gamer. And as a final small side note, the DLC game modes are fine and they are worth trying out and seeing if you like the way they play.

I think the real reason people give RE6 flak (then conflate it to the gameplay) is because of its lackluster story and world-building, and it is warranted. As far as RE stories go it is so over the top and unnecessarily epic for what else the series has to offer. At the time this came out I thought for sure this was the end of the series, how could you top the absolute chaos that is a global scale massively destructive cataclysmic reality of RE6? But you know what, despite how off the wall the game is, the underwhelming character development, and the fact that RE6 went away from its horror roots to move into the action genre I still love this story! No really. It is so stupid that it is kind of funny and when you have a friend to ♥♥♥♥♥ to it can be an absolute treat just like watching a so bad it’s good movie with your friends. I understand the hate this game gets for really giving the middle finger to its roots, but I don’t know. I just find it oddly charming really.

The music to this game is standard RE music it is nothing really special but it never retracts from the experience. The sound effects are all pretty good overall as well. Guns sound as they should, and the enemies' and allies' voice lines and sounds are good. The voice acting by the main characters is all really good especially compared to some of the older RE games. And the ambient noises never felt out of place. RE6 is not outstanding in its sound work, but it is good overall.

Graphically this game is a product of its time, but for the time it looks pretty darn good. The lighting is solid, the models look great, the textures are generally pretty clean, and nothing ever came out as distracting. I have never really been a fan of RE’s enemy design and that continues here, but I can say that I enjoy all of the styles of the main characters especially Sherry and Leon (though Leon still has better style in RE4). I am really surprised that this game doesn’t feel colorless either, there are plenty of scenes that are vibrant and yet still fitting to RE’s darker vibe. Overall I think that this game was better than many of the time and it comes off as impressive to me, even today I think that this is a pretty good-looking game, though to be fair the PS3 and 360 era of gaming is generally where I think most games will never feel overly aged.

In conclusion, I like RE6. It is not perfect, it can be a pain to play with odd controls, camera angles, enemies, and objectives, but it is overall a pretty good game. I am glad to see that the game has aged well and in recent years has had a more positive reception than when it first came out. I think it is well worth buying nowadays, though definitely not at its full price of $40 for the game plus the DLC. You can get this game dirt cheap when it goes on sale (which it often does) and I think that it is worth the play if you are a RE fan or are looking for a solid co-op game. I liked this game enough to write my first review on it to counter the negativity, and I like it today. It is always nice to see a game age pretty well.

Le numéro 6 de la célèbre série suit très bien les traces de ses prédécesseurs tant pour l'histoire que pour ses vidéos léchés. Les graphiques en jeu sont aussi dans les standards auxquels Capcom nous a habitués au fil des ans.

Le bas est au niveau de la jouabilité. Depuis le 4e jeu, les aspects horreur et survie ont été relayés à l'arrière plan au profit de l'action.  Si cette action était bien gérée dans le 4e et 5e, elle est tout simplement ridicule dans le 6e. Les actions sont imprécises, le nouveau "recoil" des armes rend leur utilisation pénible, les boutons d'actions apparaissent souvent lorsque le temps alloué pour les utiliser est déjà en parti écoulé et les angles de caméra, surtout lors des scènes animées, rend certaines parties du jeu frustrantes, voir enrageantes. Lors de parties multijoueurs c'est problèmes sont doublés.

Somme toute, le jeu n'est pas injouable mais pas à la hauteur des attentes malgré son contenu varié et ses multiples défis.

I played enough of this game to recommend it to you. There's everything to love and nothing to hate. If we consider the last trilogy, Resident Evil from 4 to 6 this is easily the best of them all, the culmination of the action Capcom offers. You can do all sort of new moves which are awesome, you can slide, dodge, land on your back and shoot from the ground (which can be done when enemies drop you too), you can fight in melee with combos or switching to a melee weapon. I really like the fluidity of the game and it's even more fun with a friend. The coop of this game is great, you are not helpless per sé, you can counter enemies' grapples, you can even "stand up" for yourself if you survive long enough in a down state, but, of course, it's a lot easier if there's a team mate helping you out but that may not be always possible due to tactics gone wrong or levels where you have to stay apart for some time.
There is much to explore, some campaigns have more exploration than others, graphics are really good for my standards (which may be low since I don't really care) and it goes at 60 fps even if the benchmark told me it would go at 20-30. The campaigns are a great idea, different enemies, different characters, different playstyles and it's a hard game too! I play at Professional difficulty, invested 23 hours in the game right now and I'm something as halfway through (I'm doing chapter 3 with Chris now after doing 3 chapters with Jake and Leon). I really can't find anything wrong with this game, it gives me the challenge I seek, the adrenaline, the fear (the fear of dying but there are some jumps too), the gameplay is perfect as I see it, this was much more than I anticipated, I'll definitely play this multiple times.

 I don't really understand why this game gets sh** on so much. I've been a fan of the Resident evil series since its inception, and have had to grit my teeth along with the rest of the fans through the movies and games like Raccoon City. Resident evil 6 may be flawed, but the PC version is a true successor to RE5, let me explain.

Many people's main complaints about RE6 are either the bad AI, the muddy graphics, or that it is a poor console port. Anyone who has played RE5 recently will recall just how bad the AI was in that game. Playing single player would mean that you would have to call Sheva 5 or 6 times to get her to help you open doors or do objectives. Sheva would constantly get knocked down or held in place, and she would knock you down with her attack reaction. The zombie AI in 5 was also pretty terrible, where J'avo would climb up things and then immediately jump off in order to attack you, or they would get stuck inside each other because they wouldn't understand where to go. In RE6, I feel like I never have to worry about my AI partner, and the enemy AI always keeps me on my toes(on Professional difficulty) with their new running leaps and ground grabs, and the large numbers of regular zombies make them feel actually threatening.

 Though the graphics/ textures may be muddy at times even on the highest settings, the shaders and effects are great. and the underwater effects in Ada's campaign may be some of the best I've ever seen in a video game. That being said, there's not much of a graphical change from consoles to the PC version. Whats also important to realize though, is that Capcom has tried very hard to rectify their mistakes from the console versions, and has added tons of new options that will help tweak the game play to your preferences. 

The story is in a similar vain to the RE5 story, where it's mostly action, losts of Quick-time, and some exploration. This time around, there are 4 campaigns, and though they may be shorter than RE5's full campaign, they keep the action varied and prevent it from becoming stale. Unfortunately, the action-oriented nature of the campaign seems to confuse some players, as if they forgot how much action/Quick-time that RE5 brought to the table. 

The difficulty this time around has really increased. I vividly remember RE5's Professional difficulty being somewhat of a pushover, with zombie's movements and attacks being perfectly telegraphed and predictable. This time, Professional mode really increases the survival horror feel, as being grabbed or missing a dodge can spell death for your character. As I mentioned before, zombies have new attacks like running jumps and crawling grabs, and the special zombies can ruin your day quite easily. 

All and all, the game is the next evolution of the RE series, which in my opinion is a great installment (we should be thankful they didn't continue to go the Raccoon City route). The new crossover instances and Agent attack modes can be fun, and are great ideas that I hope they continue with in the next installment.

There's a key phrase that aptly describes Resident Evil 6:

"Flawed, but fun."

This game takes its' predecessors pedestal of being the most polarizing entry in the series, although it may divide players more than ever. Each of the 4 campaigns present will appeal to certain players and not so much others. The same can be said for some of the features in the game such as the intersections, Agent Hunt, and the co-op mechanics. The real safe bet is that if you're an action fan who likes to play with friends, Resident Evil 6 is an easy recommendation. It's not the greatest action game and it's definitely not a good horror game, but there are some fun moments and good replay value to keep you coming back for more.

However, if you come at Resident Evil 6 expecting another Resident Evil 1 or Resident Evil 4, then you will not only be severely disappointed, you will hate this game immensely. This is a game for open-minded players who like action, players who are willing to take the time to adapt to its' systems, and players willing to overlook the flawed design choices and story to have a good time.

There is a lot to enjoy here, but only if you're willing to sit down and enjoy it.
